speechtext: Hon. FRANK OLIVER moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 125) to amend the Land Titles Act.

maintopic: LAND TITLES AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: LAND TITLES AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The Bill is to make necessary provision for the registration of titles in what is now the Northwest Territories. At present registration must be made within the territories. In a few instances property within the territories is in such condition as to require registration, but it is not thought advisable to establish a registry office in the territories until the business to be transacted is much larger than it is at present. It is therefore proposed that for the present registration of titles of properties within the territories should take place at Ottawa, and this Bill is to provide for that.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-MR. CON-MEE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. Some few days ago an article appeared in the ' Free Press ' of this city in regard to evidence or a statement that was taken before the Committee on Mines and Minerals. Some discussion took place the day following in this House, the matter was brought to the attention of the House by the hon. member for Nipis-sing (Mr. Gordon) and the minister and myself made some remarks. I find in an issue of the 'Citizen ' of this city what I consider a very gross piece of misrepresentation, which I wish to call to the attention of the House. First I desire to call attention to what was complained of. The article published in the ' Free Press ', which I shall not quote in extenso, makes reference to statements made before the Mines Committee, and goes .on to say:
Thar it is the duty of the Canadian government to step in and take over those nickel deposits for the benefit of the Dominion and the empire was the proposition which was

placed before tlie Mines and Minerals Committee of the House of Commons this morning by Mr. Arthur Wilson, at present of Toronto, but officially engaged in an investigation on behalf of the British government into the nickel deposits in Canada.
Continuing further, the article contains this paragraph:
He advocated that the government should take over the nickel deposits as a matter of imperial urgency, which would give Great Britain an enormous advantage over all other countries in the construction of warships, and would insure for all time that the material which is a feature in the construction of modern battleships would be retained for the empire.
I may say, as was explained by myself on that occasion in my remarks, which will be found in ' Hansard,' that Mr. Wilson was very much annoyed at having been misrepresented as this article does misrepresent him. I stated on that occasion that I had gone with Mr. Wilson to the editor of the ' Free Press,' and that I gave him a correction of that statement. Let me read the correction which was published:
I was much surprised at the report contained in your issue of this day with reference to Mr. Wilson's remarks before the Committee on Mines and Minerals this morning. Nothing he said could have warranted any one in stating that he was officially employed in an investigation on behalf of the British government into the nickel resources of Canada, nor had he advocated that the government should take over the nickel deposits as a matter of imperial urgency. He merely attended before the committee at their invitation to give evidence as to the present condition of the nickel industry and suggested that it would be in the interests of the country generally if the larger deposits of nickel ore at Sudbury could be worked on a larger scale, and that not only should the matte be refined in Canada but that the government be recommended to foster the production of nickel steel in the country.
Sir, notwithstanding the fact that that correction was published, there appeared the following day in the same paper an editorial to the effect that its statement was correct. The paper insisted on this, notwithstanding the remarks made both by myself and my hon. friend from Nipissing (Mr. Gordon).
Then in the Ottawa * Citizen ' of a couple of days ago, appeared this article, which is the one I rose more particularly to complain of. It is headed the ' Nickel Monopoly,' and goes on to discuss what it alledges to be Mr. Arthur Wilson's statement. I shall not read the article through, but only that portion which it is necessary I should read in view of the remarks I propose to make:
A discussion subsequently took place in the House of Commons regarding the purport of Mr. Wilson's remarks, and Mr. Gordon, M.P., and Mr. Conmee, M.P., undertook to Mr. CONMEE.
describe the report as inaccurate, and furthermore denied that there was any such thing as a monopoly of the nickel production in Canada.
Let me call attention to the fact that what was complained of in the article and corrected in the letter written to the newspaper and signed by myself was not the question at all of a monopoly, but the question of the misrepresentation of a witness who appeared before this committee. I take it .for granted that it is not only the duty of the committee-and I feel that responsibility as being chairman of that committee-to protect those who come before it and give expert evidence or information, but it is also the duty of this House to protect its members and those from whom it may obtain information on such important questions. Then this article goes on to say:
Mr. Conmee expressed something akin to pained surprise that any one should allege such a thing and conveyed the impression that Mr. Wilson had repudiated the reports of his evidence which appeared in the press both Liberal and Conservative.
As to that statement, Mr. Wilson came with me to the newspaper office. I introduced him to the editor, and Mr. Wilson explained where the misrepresentation occurred and the editor replied that it was not his regular reporter who had attended to that matter. If it had been, he explained, the mistake would not have been made. Yet the editor returned to the same misrepresentation the following day. The article in the * Citizen ' continues:
Mr. Templeman, the Minister of Mines, reinforced the other two gentlemen by stating that the chairman of the committee had assured him that the reports of Mr. Wilson's evidence which appeared in the press were inaccurate. In what detail the report of Mr. Wilson's evidence may have been inaccurate, it is difficult to determine; but whether or not he stated that a monopoly of the nickel industry is enjoyed by the International Nickel Company of the United States, the same is true, the chairman of the Mines and Minerals Committee, Mr. Gordon and Mr. Conmee to the contrary notwithstanding. The two latter gentlemen in making the statements that they did on the floor of the House were simply engaged in the congenial occupation of gold bricking parliament with an engaging air of candour. They pointed out that, so far from the nickel resources of Canada being monopolized by the American company, there was a large area of nickel mineral claims which were not owned by the Americans. This is true, but it by no means disproves the monopoly charge. On the contrary, it is the strongest evidence against it, seeing that this territory is lying idle and its development paralysed.
I wish to call the attention of the House to the extravagant language used by this writer. He represents that the witness did make statements which that witness

has not only denied, but has taken every reasonable means of contradicting, feeling that he was injured by the misrepresentation. He says also that two hon. members of this House are engaged in the work of gold-bricking the House in regard to what was placed before the Mines Committee. The press is an important medium of information for the public; no one is stronger in his belief in the press than I am; but I do protest against the gross injustice of a writer, who knows nothing about the subject-for this article is proof that this writer is absolutely ignorant of the conditions that exist in connection with this mineral-and who has no personal knowledge of what took place before the committee, seeking by these extraordinary statements of his to misrepresent members of this House. There ought to be some decency in conducting discussions in the press. Members of this House have some responsibility, and, in carrying on their duties they ought not to be wantonly and grossly misrepresented at the mere will of some one who happens to write for a newspaper. I do not think it is to the credit of the newspaper itself. I will not go further in the matter. I think these gentlemen have committed an offence which deserves some punishment; nevertheless I shall not do more than call the attention of the House to the wrong that has been done. I shall not take up the time of the House in discussing fully all thi3 writer's opinions and the policy which he advocates for the country as elaborated in his article. But let me say that what it was stated that there was a monopoly of the nickel deposits of Canada in the hands of a particular company. That was denied both by the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Geo. Gordon) and myself. There was also the' statement that Mr. Wilson had represented himself, wrongly, fraudulently, before the committee as a representative of the British government; yet the very contrary was the case, for when Mr. Wilson was asked by a member of the committee if he did represent the British government his answer was, ' No '. Yet this misrepresentation is persisted in notwithstanding what ha3 taken place. speechtext:

House resumed adjourned debate on tl -* motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier for the ap-

pointment of a special committee to investigate certain allegations of Mr. Hugh D. Lumsden against a portion of the engineering staff of the National Transcontinental railway.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not the advantage of being in this chamber when the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) introduced his resolution to appoint a committee to investigate the circumstances surrounding the resignation of Mr. Hugh D. Lumsden as chief engineer in charge of the construction of the Transcontinental railway. But, after a careful perusual of the motion and of the speech delivered by the Prime Minister on that occasion, I shall take the opportunity to make a few remarks, first, upon what should _ be _ the object in introducing a motion of this kind; and, second, what I think is the apparent object of introducing that motion.
In 1903, this government conceived the idea of building a second transcontinental railway, or rather some person else conceived that idea, and, as we afterwards proved, the government took to itself that idea and claimed it as its own. However that may be, the record of this House shows that, while we were in favour of the idea of constructing a great national transcontinental railway, we objected-and we still object-to the manner in which the government carried that idea into execution. And, because we did not approve of the principle of carrying that road to successful completion, it carried with it, I think, a corresponding duty on the part of the members on this side to see to it that the road was constructed in the most economical manner.
Now, without going into the figures, let me say in a cursory manner that there is no doubt-it has not been disputed-that this railway has cost a very much larger sum than was estimated. We were told that the government had most reliable information upon the subject, and that the construction of the road would cost in the neighbourhood of $51,000,000. And to-day, as we all know, according to the latest revised figures of the Minister of Railways and Canals, produced in this House in December last, it is costing over $114,000,000.
Now, I would say, in the first place, need we go further than that? That change casts a very serious reflection upon, makes a prima facie case against, the government of the day, that there has been recklessness and mismanagement, or at least, carelessness, in the construction of the National Transcontinental railway. From 1903 down to 1907, while there were occasional grumblings, so far as I know there was no Mr. CONMEE.
distinct eruption in connection with the construction of that road. But in 1907, Mr Hodgins, who was then in charge of district ' B ', came out boldly and said, in effect: ' I have been endeavouring, in my own way, to keep down the estimates, to cut down the classification in respect of the division over which I have charge. But the commission is not satisfied with that, the commission, he said, have been urging me to be more liberal in my classification.' That is the charge he made. That charge wa3 investigated, to a certain extent. A committee of this House was appointed,' a majority of whom were supporters of the government; and, while it it true that to a certain extent Major Hodgins withdrew his charges, it is equally true that the reason why that committee did not proceed was that the matters to be investigated were matters that came exclusively within the jurisdiction of the tribunal of arbitration appointed under the Act of 1902. Matters went on until 1907. The man in charge of the railway, the chief engineer, is the man upon whom this country must depend for honesty in the construction of that railway, because there is no man who has greater powers, or should have greater powers, he certainly has greater responsibilities than the commissioners themselves. The commission is composed of men who know nothing whatever about railway construction. So far as I know, not a single gentleman on that commission to-day has ever built a mile of railway, or any portion of a railway, or has ever, in his lifetime, had control of any railway or any portion of a railway. So I say that as regards the position of the chief engineer of the Transcontinental railway, I thoroughly agree with the hon. the Minister of Railways that he i3 the most important person that we have under our control in the construction of that railway, because he is the man that can return common excavation into loose rock, loose rock into solid rock, or solid rock into common excavation. That is the man who can turn $25 into $50, who can turn $50 into $150, who can turn $25 into $150. Therefore, I say he acts in the position of guardian of the treasury of this country.
Now what do we find? We find that in 1907 the chief engineer, being unable to agree with the most liberal classification being made by his sub-chiefs, resigns his position because he cannot countenance what he claims to be an unjust, unwarranted and dishonourable manner of classifying, especially on sections ' B ' and * F ' of the Transcontinental. Now I say this fact, coupled with the fact that this road has cost $12,000,000 more than double what was originally estimated, these two facts alone, I submit, make out a prima facie case against this government, that the road has not been constructed in an eco-

nomical manner, and that therefore we are called upon to investigate. Now, having in view' these circumstances, what is the duty of the government upon this occasion? I say it is the absolute duty of the government to place such an instrument in the hands of a committee of this House of Commons that we will be able to go thoroughly into the cause of that gentleman's resignation. A committee of the House should be given full power to say to Mr. Lumsden: You have resigned because you say that certain of your engineers have forfeited your confidence by reason of their over-classification; that means that you have resigned because certain of your engineers were changing 25 dollars into 50, and 50 into 150. You say that in consequence thereof you have lost confidence in them. We ask you to say why you have lost confidence in those men, we ask you to prove your allegations. Until we do get a committee that will enable us to ascertain whether these charges are true, we have not done our duty to the country. If the government do not give us that power, I maintain that they are afraid to give it, they are afraid to let the country know what is taking place under the regime of that commission. I maintain that the government are in a worse position if they grant a commission which does not give that authority, than if they granted no commission at all, because they might consistently take the attitude they took on the Hodgins inquiry and say: We did not grant this commission because these matters were under the exclusive jurisdiction and control of another tribunal which we appointed in 1903. But when they appoint a tribunal and do not give it the powers which they should give it, then we are justified in saying that if they-take this position, they do it for the purpose of deceiving the public.
What have they offered us by this motion? Mr. Lumsden says in effect: I, Hugh Lumsden, having lost confidence in the engineers in district ' B ' and ' F ' hereby resign my position. The government says:	We will investigate that.
Now that, boiled down, is what the government have offered us. But how does the Prime Minister look at it-I take his own words. The Prime Minister says: This is altogether a question of classification, that is the reason that Mr. Lumsden resigned. You can investigate that, but you cannot investigate whether that mistake, or improper classification, arises from carelessness, negligence or bad faith. Why, Sir, those are the very things which caused Mr. Lumsden to resign, he would not have resigned, as he says himself, unless he had lost confidence in his sub-engineers, and the reason he lost confidence in them was because they had been guilty of over-classification, and that can only arise by reason
of carelessness, incapacity or had faith. The Prime Minister, himself says that if this investigation led to that conclusion, namely, that Mr. Lumsden was resigning for either of these reasons, incapacity, bad faith or dishonesty on the part of his subengineers, then you cannot go one step further in that investigation. If that is so, then I say that the whole investigation proposed by this government is an absolute farce.
Now, let us see what the Minister of Railways had to say. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has a very unhappy method, a very unhappy manner, a very unhappy custom, I might say, of interjecting questions which go to the whole root of the matter. The hon. member for North Toronto asked the Minister of Railways what, in his opinion, in his own language, we could investigate under this motion, and the Minister of Railways was absolutely dumbfounded, and could not say what was to be investigated. I will read what the minister said:

I would not like to detain the House longer recapitulating what is so plain.
-So the Minister of Railways himself cannot explain what there is to investigate, under his leader's motion. Then we take the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), and what does he say? The hon. member for Pictou says, at the bottom of page 2488 of ' Hansard ' of the 25th January:
And the result is we get down to this question as to whether or not there have been mistakes in classification-
Now, a mistake in classification is an improper classification and if it is an im-

proper classification it is not a proper classification. I think that goes without saying. That means that the mistake that he was referring to was not a proper classification. Then he says:
-whether or not Mr. Lumsden was correct in his statement that there was disobedience of instructions and failure to record what he had told these men should be done.
Well, failure to follow instructions leads to overcharge in classification, and overcharge in classification means improper classification. So far as the hon. gentleman has simply said that the matter to be investigated is whether or not there has been a proper classification. Now he says:
These are proper subjects for the committee.
He says that whether or not there has been over-classification is a proper subject for the committee. But then he says:
The question as to whether there was proper classification is a matter entirely for the tribunal constitued by parliament in 1993.
So that he says in one case that the question of classification is a proper one for this committee and in the next case he says that the question of classification is a matter entirely and exclusively within the jurisdiction of the arbitrators appointed under the Act of 1903. It is impossible to reconcile these two statements. It shows that there is nothing whatever to investigate under the resolution proposed in this House. I will put a concrete instance. We will say that we have a committee appointed and we will say that we have on that committee the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) and the hon. member for Carleton, N. B. (Mr. Car-veil) who have done such herculean service in the Hodgins inquiry and who succeeded so well in burking that inquiry.

speechtext:
I was proceeding to give a concrete instance of what would probably happen if we had the hon. member for Carleton and the hon. member for Pictou as two of the members of this committee. We will proceed now to show what exactly would occur. We have a committee of five, three of whom are government supporters, stalwart henchmen of the government. The chairman is put in the chair. My hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), we will say, calls Mr. Lumsden and puts him in the box:
Q. Mr. Lumsden, you were, until June 25, 1909. chief engineer of the Railway Commission?-A. Yes s'r.
Q. You resigned your position on June 25, 1909?-A. Yes sir.
Q. Why did you resign your position?-A. The letter I wrote to the Chairman of the Transcontinental Railway Commission shows that.
Q. What was that?-A. I resigned because I had lost confidence in the engineers on sections ' B ' and ' F ' of the railway.
Q. Why did you lose confidence in these engineers?-A. I resigned because they had classified contrary to my instructions.
Q. What were these instructions?-A. I have them here in my pocket.
I propose now to prove that by reason of over-classification against these instructions this country has lost, say, $500,000.
The hon. member for Pictou rises and says:	This resolution does not authorize
this committee to try the question of whether there was over-classification, it is a matter, according to my speech on this motion, which comes exclusively within the jurisdiction of the arbitrators appointed under the Act of 1903 and in proof of that I cite the speech of my own leader, the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, in which he says that whether that over-classification arose from bad faith, incompetence, or carelessness, this committee cannot determine such a question. There we stop. That is the very foundation upon which this inquiry proceeds and yet we are blocked from going into the case. What can we ask the man? We can say to him:	Tell us some other
reason why you resigned. Was it because your engineers smoked bad tobacco, or was it because he was not wearing a proper kind of clothing, or was it because of any other
habits he had? There would be no objection on the part of my hon. friends because this is quite within the purview of this resolution, but when you go into evidence to substantiate your charges and which relates to the taking of a dollar out of the public treasury, these gentlemen are justified-and I make the statement advisedly-under this resolution in saying not one tittle or iota of evidence are you entitled to give here. Then it goes back to the very same tribunal which my hon. friend from Pictou helped to send it back to in 1907, or 1908, because he said that tribunal had the exclusive jurisdiction in the matter. In order to be precise I will read the hon. gentleman's own words on that occasion:

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext:
-Now the fact is before us that Mr. Lumsden and Mr. Woods have gone over that section ' F ' of this line. They have looked at various divisions there and at this very moment they are performing the function which was contemplated would be performed by section 7 of the agreement and endeavouring to agree' upon what the proper classification is, and in the event of their being unable to agree as to that then the third arbitrator would be called in. In other words these gentlemen are now dis charging the duty assigned to them and are going to arrive at some conclusion upon the differences which I understand my friends to be arguing this committee should engage in.
The absurdity of the position suggested by my hon. friends will be recognized when we consider that at this very moment the two gentlemen who are appointed by statute are performing their statutory functions and they are bound to come to some conclusion on the matter. Upon that conclusion the accounts will be adjusted. At the same time, if the view of my hon. friends were concurred in we would be taking up our time in dealing with a purely academic question. I do not understand my hon. friends to urge that there is anything improper in the position of the commissioners in dealing with the engineers, so it is purely a question of a difference of opinion between these engineers as to what the classification will be.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman ays, hear, hear, but if he follows the reasoning of his leader he will be found to acknowledge that the moment the question of classification comes up in this committee, it will be sent to these three arbitrators. Well, if that be the position taken by the government it simply means that there is not a single thing concerning the expen diture on this railroad which can be inquired into by that committee or any other tribunal appointed by this House. The very minute you touch the kernel of the matter which should be inquired into, the supporters of the government will say: these matters are solely within the jurisdiction of this arbitration tribunal and you have no right whatever to interfere with

them. Therefore, we can come to no other conclusion, but that this committee is now being appointed, not for the purpose of investigating, but for the purpose of whitewashing. We will go before this committee and we will present our evidence, but our evidence will be rejected and the next morning the ' Globe ' newspaper will come out with great big headlines statins that after the most thorough, searching, and impartial investigation that has ever taken place Mr. Lumsden's charges have utterly fallen to the ground, that the skirts of the government are absolutely clean, and the opposition had to withdraw every charge. That is what the government want to do, and that is the reason they put this resolution on the order paper. But if I am wrong I now ask the right hon. gentleman to set me right. The Prime Minister knows that the gravamen of the charges made by Mr. Lumsden is over-classification which simply means taking money out of the treasury of this country illegally and unlawfully. I ask the right hon. gentleman in his place now, will he allow us to ask these questions and to prove these charges when the matter comes up before this committee. The right hon. gentleman is silent; he does not answer. I can quite appreciate his silence. I ask the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) will he declare in the committee that we have the rigiit to investigate the question of whether or not, there ha3 been over-classification and money taken out of the treasury? Let the hon. member (Mr. Macdonald) tell us that before we go to the committee. The hon. member is also silent. 1 ask the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) who no doubt will be in the committee, what will he say if we offer to prove these charges? Will he allow us to do so or will he tell us it is a matter to be sent to the arbitrators who have not yet sent in their report. That is a fair question to put to these gentlemen. The hon. gentleman is also silent.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: They are dumb.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext:
They won't answer. Since it is quite evident that we will not have an opportunity of getting these matters before the committee let me now say a word or two on the merits of the case. In 1903 the right hon. the Prime Minister proposed the building of the National Transcontinental railway and he told us he had mountains of information upon which to base an estimate of the cost. I have a right to suppose that he sent out a staff of engineers who went along the route of this railroad and got the levels, and took the estimates of quantities that were to be removed, making borings in the different hills to find whether there were solid rock, loose rock, Mr. MIDDLEBRO.
or common excavation. That wa3 their duty and I presume- they did it. I make this statement here-not as an engineer, but on what has been told me by experienced engineers-that an engineer can ascertain more correctly before a cut has been made than he can afterwards, what amount of material is in that cut. That is especially so in the case of	a partial
cut, say where the railway is going round a hill and only a portion of the hill is taken off, because he has the actual geographical formation of the hill to be removed in his eye, whereas afterwards he has not. In the case of a straight cut I will admit that he could measure that afterwards as correctly as before, but I say that the experience of engineers proves that in a location such as I have referred to, they can estimate more accurately before the actual cut has been made than afterwards. Now, that being the case, can any one conceive why there should be a difference of from 100 per cent to 150 per cent between the estimate- and the actual cost in this road. The geographical position of the country is the same as it was when the estimate was taken, the geological formation is the same, and practically the only thing that has caused a difference in the price is, the classification of solid rock, loose rock, common excavation, and the over-break. It is because the juxtaposition of these four that the extra additional cost of the railway has come. It i3 very easy for a man to change commop excavation into loose rock, an engineer's certificate will do that. It is very easy for him to change loose rock into solid rock, if the engineers are in any way in collusion with the contractor and if they will do it, and it is a very hard matter to detect when they have done it. But, in going along and boring down into a hill to find what was the character of the soil, how much was common excavation, how much loose rock and how much solid rock, was it possible for them to have made a mistake to the extent of from 100 per cent to 150 per cent. The best engineers say that it is not possible, nay, they would not be very much surprised if there was a difference of more than twenty per cent in the calculations of an engineer made in that way; but they say that when you get beyond a difference of twenty per cent there is a prima facie presumption that there is something wrong. Now, in this case the difference is not only twenty per cent between the cost and the estimate, but the cost has risen from $51,000,000 estimated-to which you may add twenty per cent as the outside difference that may arise and that will give you $62,000,000 estimated cost. Then the estimated cost ha9 risen from $62,000,000 (including an allow-| ance of twenty per cent) to $114,000,000, and there you have an increase of 100 per

cent and $12,000,000 additional to 3pare. Is there any common sense in that? Does not that very circumstance cast upon the government a prima facie case of negligence, mismanagement, or dishonesty? I think I am justified in saying it does.
I desire to say a few words in reference to Mr. Hodgins. As we all know Mr. Hod-gins was district engineer in charge of district ' 1'', the district lying immediately east of Winnipeg. Mr. Hodgins, so far as we know, enjoyed an enviable reputation until the time he severed his connection with the Transcontinental Railway Commission. He was selected for that position because of his exceptional qualifications as an engineer, because of his great experience in other portions of the world in railway engineering, and, so far as we know, no suspicion had been cast upon him on any occasion. Why was Mr. Hodgins dismissed? I make the claim that Mr. Hodgins was dismissed because he was keeping the classification down too low to suit the contractors and to suit the commission. I prove that in this way. In 1907 complaints were coming in from the contractors to the commission that the classification which Mr. Hodgins was making on his section ' F ' was altogether too low as compared with the classification that was being made in the province of Quebec. This commission sent out their inspecting en-giner, Mr. Gordon Grant, to investigate whether or not Major Hodgins was giving estimates that were too low for the contractors. Perhaps that was not putting it fairly; to investigate the question whether Major Hodgins was not giving a3 liberal classifications as he should. What did Mr. Grant say? After examining the work he came back and reported to the commission, under date J uly 23, 1907, under the head of ' classification on district ' F ' as fol lows:
Classification, on this work, where the vast majority of it is solid rock, is not a serious matter, and where material has been moved that could be classified-and the greater part of it was moved last winter when it was frozen, such as the opening of cuts, the stripping of rocks, &c., I found, from questioning the resident engineers and from looking over the progress estimates, that the classification given the contractors has been very low, and in many cases absurdly low, and for that reason alone there are probably
1,000	men less on the work to-day than there would have been if the work had been fairly and justly classified. Classification is left entirely to the resident, engineers, and they are all to timid to give the contractor what he is entitled to in that line.
Mr. Gordon Grant reported to the commission that Mr. Hodgins was classifying too low, yes absurdly low that his resident engineers were afraid to give the contractors what they were entitled 80
to. What was the result? Two months afterwards Mr. Hodgins was made to walk the plank. It is not the inference that he walked the plank because he was keeping the classification down too low to suit the contractors? Now, what is the truth? Fortunately we have, I think, Mr. Hodgins being justified by after events. The hon. member from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) went very carefully and concisely into the amount of over-classification on the different divisions of the Transcontinental railway. So far as I know the calculations he made are absolutely correct and they have not been denied by the Minister of Railways. I am, therefore, assuming that what he gave us in the House on Tuesday is absolutely correct and is justified by the returns brought down by the Minister of Railways and Canals. According to these returnes we find that there has been an over-classification on the same district ' F ' of $2,798,791-and Mr. Hodgins was removed from that section before that because he was keeping down the classification. Mr. Poulin, his successor, was appointed. Do we find then that his estimates were too low? Do we find any contractors making complaint that his classification is kept down too low? Not a bit of it, not a word of complaint. What do we find? But we find Mr. Lums-den, the chief engineer, of the commission, finding fault with the classification there and we find that the reason Mr. Lumsden resigned was because there was over-classification in that district. We even find Mr. Gordon Grant himself, after he is appointed chief engineer, after he goes over that road, coming back and cutting off $360,000 voluntarily. Is that not proof that Major Hodgins was justified in the charge he made? Is it not proof that the commission wanted Major Hodgins to give more liberal classification? Their inspecting engineer came back and reported that Major Hodgins was not liberal enough. Major Hodgins is discharged and an engineer put in who allows over-classification of $2,789,000, and Mr. Grant himself comes back, and, of his own volition, not as an arbitrator, but simply as engineer for the commission, lops off $360,000. Yet we hear it said that Major Hodgins did not do his duty when he came to the conclusion that they were trying to make him over-estimate the classification. What could an honest man do but to resign. The Minister of Railways yesterday put on record a great number of letters in reference to this subject, many of them not very germane to the discussion. I, therefore, propose to quote from some of the letters to be found in this return from Mr. Woods, assistant engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific, in which Mr. Woods makes complaint as to over-classification in differ-



ent portions of the contract. The first letter appears on the first page of the return. It is a letter from Mr. Woods, dated October 7, 1907, shortly after Mr. Hodgins had been removed from his position. So far as I know, certainly so far as this return shows, there were no complaints by ine Grand Trunk Pacific against Mr. Hodgins while he was in charge as to over-classification. This return shows that in October, 1907, shortly after a successor was appointed, there were serious objections to the classification on that section from the Grand Trunk Pacific. He says:
With the latter portion we had detailed percentages for each cut and were greatly surprised at the allowances made for solid and loose rock. In nearly every case, where the cuttings were not entirely all ledge, the estimate given for solid rock is double, or more than double, what it should he. In fact, the specifications had been entirely ignored and an excessive allowance made, not by reason of any error in judgment, but, as I understand, by special instructions from the assistant district engineer.
Let me give you some illustrations:-
Take the cutting from stations 5818 to 5826. Estimated 71 per cent solid rock and 29 per cent loose rock. Slopes taken out 1J to 1. Very little ledge in this cut. Some large boulders but a very large percentage is common excavation.
Station 5812 to 5860. Classified 91 per. cent solid rock. 6 per cent loose rock. Slopes taken out 1J to 1. Solid rock over-classified at least 100 per cent.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: What distinction does the hon. gentelman draw between the slopes of solid rock and common excavation?

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: In common excavation you will naturally remove more material, because you will require to have a greater slope irom the perpendicular.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: What is the percentage?

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: Not being an engineer, I cannot say; but if one and a half to one is a proper slope for common excavation, it is too much for rock.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: What is the proper slope for rock?

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: As I have told my hon. friend I am not an engineer, but I have sufficent common sense to know that if one and a half to one is a proper slope for common excavation, that slope is not required for rock. Notwithstanding, Mr. Woods says that in this particular excavation solid rock is over-classified at least 100 per cent, yet the return of the slope is given as one and a half per cent to one. That means that you have allowed the contractor to go back from the slant twice as far as you should, and back of that legitimate slope, he has taken rock at $1.50 per yard. That is properly over-break.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext:
He takes that at $1.50 a yard and uses that in the next grading and calls it filling and gets paid for it as such. Although they are cu tting solid rock, they are returning it as one and a half to one slope and getting $1.50 per yard for it. The next letter I shall read is on page 5. It is dated 20th February, 1908, from Mr. Woods to Mr. Lumsden:
I do not know the date of those instructions or when they are supposed to have become effective, but from reports of my assistants at Winnipeg and at Quebec, there does not seem to have been any change in classification of work previously reported, the percentage of classified material being steadily increased. We are satisfied that on some parts of the line the work previously estimated was not classified according to your recent instructions, being overestimated in both loose and solid rock. The attention of your district engineers has been called to this fact, but apparently without effect. If your instructions were effective when the January estimates were made, we certainly will have to object to the classifications as rendered on certain parts of the work.
On March 24, 1908, Mr. Woods again writes Mr. Lumsden as follows. He is referring to sections ' B ' and ' F,' the two sections concerning which Mr. Lumsden sent in his resignation because of the insubordination of the engineers:
In examining these estimates I find no apparent change in classification since your instructions to district engineers of January 28, 1908. On the contrary the percentages of classified material seem to be constantly increasing and are even higher than when we made our objections in September last.
I am quite aware that during the winter season it is natural that classified material should run higher than at other times, as little earth work is opened, but I had hoped to see a reduction in classified material so reported prior to January last.
1 have before me a detailed sheet showing classification as made on district ' B,' and am surprised to find material classified as solid rock which, if 1 am correctly informed, under your instructions could onlv be classified as loose rock. 1 also find very large quantities returned both as loose and solid rock in borrowed embankment. On the work east of the Quebec bridge a large amount was done with teams, side borrowed material, and yet the entire contract for the 150 miles only shows 24 per cent of the work done as common excavation. It appears also that the item ' assembleed rock,' No. 5 in your instructions, is made to cover most material where explosives are used in handling.
In excavations for foundations, where hard material is found, under this item it is classified as solid rock, giving the contractor three times the usual price for that material. Onr district engineers are not satisfied with the classification as made. On district ' P ' the objection lies in the first and second divisions.
It is imposible at this time to go over the work with a view of examining classification, but, from reports from my assistants, I cer-

tainly must object to the classification as rendered being: considered final, and request that as soon as the season will permit, you accompany me over at least a part of the line, that I may have your views in regard to this most important matter of classification.
H. A. WOODS, Assistant Chief Engineer.
Then on April 2, 1908, Mr. -Woods again wrote to Mr. Lumsden:
There are a few exceptions to be taken to these estimates so far as" I am advised, except to the classified material, which is constantly increasing, and a very large amount of overbreak in solid rock cutting also increasing and representing in all a very large amount.
The next letter I shall quote is dated June 19, 1908. This is'rather an important letter from Mr. Woods to Mr. Lumsden:
Dear Sir,-I have before me estimate of rock excavation, district ' F,' for the month ending April 30, 1908. You will recall these statements as being made showing the overbreak on each division from month to month.
It is a little surprising to find that the total overbreak on this district to April 3J. is over 500,000 cubic yards. From the column furnished showing how some of this might have been used where rock borrow otherwise would have been required, and earth borrow, and deducting the.same, I still find about 151,000 cubic yards of overbreak.
I have nothing to show how this overbreak is estimated. Articles 37 and 38 would indicate that a large amount of this overbreak might have been estimated as loose rock rather than solid. Can you say if this has been done? None of my reports indicate such to be the ease. I think you will readily agree with me that if these cuttings are being measured month to month by actual quantities taken out, and no allowance deducted, little effort will be made by the contractors to keep overbreak within reasonable limit and in the end we shall undoubtedly be paying $1,000,000 additional for the work on this section probably not contemplated in youi a, proximate estimates.
Dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge receipt of your favour of the 19th instant, together with the copies of settlement sheets of contractors' progress estimate returns for the month of May, as follows.-
District ' A.'-Grand Trunk Pacific.
J. W. McManus & Co.
Lyons & White.
Willard Kitchen & Co.
District ' B.'-Grand Trunk Pacific.
M. P. & J. T. Davis (east).
M. P. & J. T. Davis (west).
Macdonell & O'Brien.
E. F. & G. E. Fauquier. District ' D.'-Grand Trunk Pacific.
District ' F.'-J. D. McArthur.
Upon comparing these estimates with those received since January last. I find that utou percentage of classified material in districts B and ' F ' remain practically in the same proportions as in former estimates received since January last. As I cannot believe that this classification, as rendered, as in accordance with the specifications, or with your letter of instructions to your district engineers of January 30, I must again object to the classification. Our recent visit to certain portions of the line on district * F ' confirms my views relative to classification on both these districts.
H. A. WOODS, Assistant Chief Engineer.
The next is dated July 8, 1908, and will be found on page 35. It is from Mr. Woods to Mr. Lumsden, and the portions I shall read are as follows:
Dear Sir,-Referring to our recent visit to the work on district ' B ' east of the St Lawrence river, our examination of classification as rendered at points visited, and our conversation regarding same, I hope to repeat in writing what I stated to you verbally-that we still vigorously protest to the classification as returned to date. For example: The first cut we visited, station 7135 to 7112 Gravel cut with little or no ledge. Classification returned 7,900 yards solid rock, 12,100 yards loose rook.
Then he goes on to say:
H. A. WOODS, Assistant Chief Engineer.
There you have the engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific, a very experienced engineer, saying: If you go on in the way you have been going, with respect to this very question of overbreak-that is taking out more material than you should on this contract alone, the government will lose one million dollars. In order not to weary the House,
I desire to put on record without reading them, the following letters.

That will give the House some idea -of the complaints that were being made by the Grand Trunk Pacific and whether or not Mr. Lumsden was justified in the position he took when he resigned his office because he could not submit to the classification made by his subordinates. Let me give an instance. I cannot give the exact monetary sums involved-my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) did that. Stations 6030 to 6046. Estimated 40 per cent solid rock, 10 per cent loose rock. This is the large sand-cut west of O'Brien s camp. Of the 95,000 yards moved to August 31 in tins cut, at least 80,000 yards were pure sand.

Now, let me come to this tribunal of arbitration about which so much has been said. In 1903, it is true, provision was made for the appointment of a tribunal of arbitrators. But they were only to act in case of disagreement between the engineer of the company and the engineer of the commission. ' Well, after Mr. Hod-gins had made his charges, after Mr. Woods had repeatedly and yet again sent letters to this commission objecting to the overclassification, the commission finally decided that they would have an arbitration. And whom did they appoint? They appointed, of course, their own engineer, Mr. Lumsden. The Grand Trunk Pacific appointed their engineer, Mr. Kelliher. And these gentlemen looked around to find a third man. The government, in its wisdom, having confidence in the ability and integrity of Mr. Collingwood Schreiber, suggested that that gentleman be appointed third arbitrator, and the Grand Trunk Pacific acceded to that suggestion. So that two out of three arbitrators were nominees of this government. And this government should have had confidence in at least that number of the arbitrators. The arbitrators, as a body, were considered bv this government and by the railway company as the most competent men in the Dominion to decide this question. They went to districts ' B ' and * F ' the districts in question. Using their knowledge as engineers-the best that could be obtained in this country-they went over the work. The sub-engineers watched the proceedings. I do not know whether they should be there or not. But I do know that these arbitrators were then taken on the ground, and that they had this matter, as the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. E. M. Macdonald) sayssub-judice; they were considering these matters as a court. After going over these two sections they came back again. In the ordinary course of events, if public decency were the guiding principle, everybody would naturally wait until the commission made a report, and especially would this be true of the government of the day, since they had appointed two of these gentlemen practically themselves. But what happened? The district sub-engineers, Messrs. Doucet, Poulin and Huestes, who were subordinates of Mr. Lumsden in district 'B', rushed home and framed a

report and submitted it to the Transcontinental Commissioners. Why? From what they had observed of the action of these three arbitrators, the men who were best qualified to know what had taken place, the best qualified to know whether there had been over classification, from what they had observed they came to the conclusion that that Board of Arbitrators appointed practically by this government, was going to come home and say:
' There has been over classification'; and with a consciousness of what they were going to do, they came home and undermined the authority of the arbitrators, and the most shameful part of the whole transaction is what the commission submitted to it. What did they do? These three commissioners came home, and one of them wrote a report reflecting upon the action of the arbitrators; then every man of them wrote a report of that kind and submitted it to the commission. Now I propose to read from these reports. The first is that of Mr. Doucet, dated on the 22nd of June. After reciting a lot of things which he said the arbitrators did, and which in his judgment was not proper to do, he said, on page 23:
On Thursday a start was made at 5 o'clock in the morning, reaching the 1.50th mile at 9 o'clock. The first cut inspected consisted of classified material in which 1,000 yards of solid rock in masses had been returned by our engineers. Mr. Schreiber turned to me and asked me to point out where the 1,000 yards of solid rock were. I answered him that the cutting was classified material, and that the boulders of which it was composed were in the embankments. I was asked to point out where 1,000 yards of boulders averaging one cubic yard each could possibly be; to which I said that as the material was classified, it did not matter whether the boulders were a yard each so long as the mass consisted of boulders large and small cemented together. Mr. Iielliher. the chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific, then spoke up and said that if I read the specifications I would see that boulders to be estimated as solid rock must measure one yard each. I at once saw that the arbitrators had made up their minds to throw out everything which our chief engineer had returned as solid rock except ledge rock and boulders, each of which measured one cubic yard.
I just read that portion of the report to show that Mr. Doucet knew that the arbitrators were going to report against him, knew they were going to come home and say that there had been over classification. Now, I will read from the report of Mr. Huestes on page 26:
At about the 132nd mile cut station 6576-92, resident engineer Girdwood was questioned as to how he got his 1.174 cubic yards of solid rock, and he replied in boulder measurements, and led the arbitrators to believe that each individual boulder measured one cubic
vard, which I knew he did not mean, and which afterwards Mr. Bourgeois informed me was not the case, as the cut in question was a mass of boulders cemented together, and Girdwood had taken measurements of all boulders for a certain time to arrive at a means of estimating the percentage of solid rock in the cutting, based on our interpretation of ' assembled rock ' as the material was cemented together.
The rest of the report shows that they were not at all satisfied with the classification being made by the arbitrators, because it was going to exceed what they thought it should exceed. Now, I will quote from the report of Mr. Poulin, on page 21:
I do not know of what nature the reports of said inspectors may be; but as district engineer in charge, I must protest asrainst the manner in which such inspection was made as being altogether inadequate and too * superficial to form a correct idea of what the material was like at the time the work was
done	The only question asked me
by Mr. Schreiber about the work was, how I would return a certain portion of one cut. On my answering ' assembled rock ' he answered, ' you are wrong, the chief engineer meant there should be at least 80 per cent of large masses of rock.' I said nothing, but wondered how he knew so well the meaning of that which the chief engineer had apparently in his mind, but did not say in the interpretation given to us.
Now, the point I desire to make is that these understrappers were criticising the proposed decision of the board, the arbitrators consisting of the most expert engineers in the whole country, two of them appointed, as I said, practically by the government itself. It would have been decent to allow the arbitrators to come back and make a report, and to ascertain, first, whether or not that report was going to justify the subengineers. But they did not do that. They came back, and to my mind, concerted a conspiracy, because I find that one of the reports of these sub-engineers is made on the 22nd of June, another is made on the 23rd of June, and the third one is made on the 23rd of June, and all these reports are sent into the commission, and each one of these reports is an attempt to undermine the authority of the chief engineer and the probable result of that Board of Arbitration. What were the duties of the commission in that case? It was the duty of the commissioners to say: We have ordered a board of the best and most experienced engineers in this country to go and see whether or not there had heen over classification in these two districts 'B' and 'F'; what business have you to come in here and attempt to influence our judgment until we receive the report of these arbitrators? Did they do that? I am sorry to say that the most unwarranted and humiliating spectacle is presented to us of the commis-

sion, not only apparently being only too willing and in too great a hurry to receive these reports, but of receiving each one of them at the same meeting of the commission, and considering the reports of these understrappers at 11 o'clock on the 25th of June last, without consulting the chief engineer, without consulting the Board of Arbitrators, and without first submitting to the chief engineer the reports of his subordinates. Does not that look as if the commission did not want over-classification to be found out in districts 'B' and 'F'? Is not that just what they wanted in 1907 when they sent Mr. Grant to inspect district 'B' under Mr. Hodgins, and he came back and said Mr. Hodgins' classification is absurdly low, he has not given the contractors enough, and so Mr. Hodgins is displaced two months afterwards. These understrappers come back here, the commissioners first get their reports in hand and turn round and send these reports to their own chief engineer and say: Mr. Lumsden, what do you think of that? Under the circumstances what could any self-respecting man do but say: If that is the kind of treatment that is accorded me I will resign my position as chief engineer. The records show what took place. At 11 o'clock in the morning on the same day the meeting took place. The same afternoon, and without notice to Lumsden, they sent to the chief engineer, Mr. Lumsden, the report of these three sub-engineers which favours the contractors as to said classification. On the same day, as soon as Mr. Lumsden got this impertinent communication, he did as any self-respecting man would do, resigned his position. Now, what I want to show is this:	I will quote the
words of the Minister of Railways in this House on Tuesday last. The Minister of Railways said: If there is one man we ought to stand by, it is our own chief engineer. These are his words on page 2435:
Surely the chief engineer of the Transcontinental Commission ought to be able to look after the commissioners side, which is the public side, ought to be able to defend his own work, the work of which he has approved in the months past, and be able to give reasons for the decisions arrived at.
I thow these words back to the Minister of Railways and ask him: Why didn't you do as you say ought to have been done, give your chief engineer the right to defend his actions, instead of allowing the commission to undermine him by his own understrappers, without giving him the slightest opportunity to define his attitude?
But for the life of me I cannot conceive the action taken by this commission. This commission seems to think that it is their bounden duty to do what?-to fight the Grand Trunk Pacific when the Grand Trunk Pacific say there is over-classification,
Mr. MIDDLEBEO
when they should, if the contractors are not doing the honest thing, be right in line with the Grand Trunk Pacific, because every dollar that the Grand Trunk Pacific successfully objects to means a saving to us of 50 cents interest as I hope to be able to show in a moment. But, they seem to think that they are fighting for the interests of this country when they are fighting for Over-classification. Yet, they are opdosing the Grand Trunk Pacific when the Grand Trunk Pacific are trying to lessen the cost. The facts, as they seem to take them, are diametrically reversed because if they are going to serve the public interest they will fight with the Grand Trunk Pacific and try to keep down, the cost to the country. When they were going to call the arbitrators in what was their attitude? Mr. Lumsden had resigned his position as chief engineer. No self-respecting man would go on and act as arbitrator, and he says: I resign my position as arbitrator as wrell. The consequence is that this body to which the hon. member for Carleton and the hon. member for Pictou were going to leave all questions before the Hodgins inquiry, has been suddenly and rudely dissolved by the action of the government's own commission. Now, what happens? Still, the Grand Trunk Pacific are objecting, in these many letters that I have produced, to over-classification. They object first to the appointing of a new arbitrator; they say that the old arbitration board has not been dissolved because Mr. Lumsden has resigned. All you have to do is to appoint a new engineer and then the three engineers will decide the matter before them. The biggest bungle and tangle that it is possible to conceive is displayed by the correspondence which has taken place between the commission and the Grand Trunk Pacific in reference to the appointment of a third arbitrator and in reference to getting down to the specific matter that is to be considered by the arbitration board. There, we have what? -the commission fighting tooth and nail and for wThat?-to limit the matters to be arbitrated to those mentioned in the letters from the Grand Trunk Pacific. In other words, they are trying to say to the Grand Trunk Pacific that this arbitration board cannot consider one single question except those questions mentioned in your letters; that is the over-classification to which you have objected in those letters. The Grand Trunk Pacific say: We do not want to be bound to that; we want a full, complete and thorough investigation into the classification over the whole system. In reply the commission say:	You cannot have that. Why should they not have it? Is it not in the interest of the public to know if any monev has oeen misspent
25X7

not only on sections 'B' and 'F' of the Transcontinental railway, but on the whole railway that is being built by this commission? This commission conceived it to be their duty, and they think they are serving the public thereby, to limit the inquiry and have no investigation into other portions of the road, when, as a matter of fact, if they took a diametrically opposite course, they would be best serving the interests of the country.
How is this country interested in the matter? Under the contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific, as hon. members of this House know, we are to furnish the money to build the railway. We pay the interest on the money during the time it is being constructed. We will take -eight years as the time that it will take to construct that railway, and I think I am fair at putting it at eight years. We do not, of course, borrow the whole cost of that railway at the beginning of the eight years, and to be fair we will cut that in two and make it four years. I will say that we pay four per cent for our money, because, while we are not paying that rate of interest, I contend, and the statement of my hon. friend from Montreal, St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) bears out that contention, that when you consider compound interest, brokerage, commissions	and
underwriting, our money will cost us four per cent. What does that mean?	The
estimated cost of the railway, as brought down by the hon. the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) in December last, is a trifle less than $115,000,000. One hundred and fifteen million at four per cent for four years amounts to $18,400,000. We will pay that on the cost of construction providing that $115,000,000 will cover the expenditure. What after that? One hundred and fifteen million dollars plus $18,500,000 is what it is going to cost us. But we must add to that seven years more interest at four per cent which amounts to $37,352,000 because we get no rental for this road for the first seven years. Adding these two together it makes the total amount that we nay in interest $56,752,000, practically $57,000,000 and $57,000,000 is just exactly half of $114,000,000 which is almost the estimated cost of the road. It means that we are paying half of the estimated cost of the railway. It means that every dollar of over-classification costs' this country 50 cents. It means that every million dollars that we pay for that road costs us $500,000 in interest. So, in that way it will be appreciated what we are paying. When Mr. Woods stated in that letter that I have quoted that the over-break alone would be $1,000,000 on one section 'alone, we see that this country will have to pay $500,000 in excess of
what it would otherwise pay. When Mr. Hodgins was trying to keep down the expenditure of section 'F' every dollar that he saved in classification meant fifty cents to this country. When Mr. Grant, of his own volition, went over sections 'B' and 'F' and cut down $647,000 of the estimates, without one single kick from a contractor, he saved this country $323,000. But, in addition to that we have this interest, and it is the country's interest and it is our duty to keep it in view, that we should not only for our own sake but for the sake of the Grand Trunk Pacific keep down the cost of the railway. Why? The greater the excessive cost of that railway the greater will be the freight rates, because their freight rates will depend on the amount of interest they pay and the amount of interest or rental they pay will be three per cent upon the total cost of construction. So, we are interested in that way in keeping down the cost of that road.
The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals said that when it was brought to his attention that the Grand Trunk Pacific purposed to undertake some of the contracts with this commission for the building of a portion of the railway, at first sight he was not quite certain whether it would be proper for him to allow them to do so. I think his first thought was probably the best. What has happened? Here is the Grand Trunk Pacific under contract with this government to lease the railway after it is constructed at a certain rental. Here is the very same company building a portion of the railway. The engineer of the company is the engineer who will oversee their contract. He is the engineer who will say, of his own company, whether or not their contract has been over-classified, whether or not they are getting too much money. It is the same thing as if I were to say to myself that I should be the sole arbitrator as to whether I was getting too much money for the work that I was doing. That is the position they are in. What has been the effect? I am only going to cite two instances. The Grand Trunk Pacific have, I think, five or six contracts with this commission. The first contract is for 50 miles west from Moncton. The estimate of solid rock under that contract as officially given to this government was no solid rock whatever, and the amount certified was 10,000 yards.
We find that the estimate of loose rock was 130,000 yards and the amount certified
850.000	yards so that these two items alone make a difference of $375,000 on the first of the Grand Trunk Pacific contracts. Where is the man, where is the check, where is the engineer who is to say that the Grand

Trunk Pacific is getting too much for that contract? Surely the Grand Trunk Pacific is not going to make any objection; and yet the history of the whole construction of this railroad is that unless objection is made by the Grand Trunk Pacific practically no objection is to be made with reference to any portion of the railroad whatever. All the material above common material is called classified material, and the engineers appointed by the government estimated that the classified material on that section was only 7 per cent whereas it turns out now to be 52 per cent. Here is an increase of $238,000 on that item alone, and on the whole contract an increase of $600,000 for this one section. We say that is because the Grand Trunk Pacific there is occupying a dual position, and its engineer has certified in favour of itself what itself is entitled to. Now, we come to district 'A,' mileage 96 to 164 from Moncton, and the increase in the solid rock there over the estimates, loose rock amounts to- $63,367, and the increase of solid rock out of common excavation-and this is a remarkable thing-amounted to $272,983, a total increase of $341,000 on that section. On these two sections therefore there is a total increase of practically $1,000,000. And where is the check on the Grand Trunk Pacific; where is the check on this increase of $1,000,000 on these two contracts alone? We know that the whole history of the construction of the line is that no check can be applied except by the Grand Trunk Pacific themselves. I would like to ask the right lion, the Prime Minister this question: Suppose that no objection whatever is made by the Grand Trunk Pacific engineers and there is consequently no dispute to be referred to the arbitration tribunal at all, are we to infer that there has been no mismanagement, no dishonesty and no over classification in the construction of this railway? The right hon. gentleman has told us that those things go to the arbitrators which are in dispute between the Grand Trunk Pacific and the government, and even on his own words we are surely entitled to an investigation into the cost of this road in matters where no dispute has arisen, and in reference to which the country may have suffered. It seems to me, Sir, that if the right hon. the Prime Minister expects this to be an effective inquiry, if he expects it to attain the object which he professes to have in view, he has got to give the committee the right to investigate the cause of Mr. Lumsden's resignation. Mr. Lumsden said in so many words that the reason he resigned was because the engineers in districts 'B' and 'F' had over-classed material. In other words they had converted earth at 25 cents a yard into loose rock at 50 cents a yard, and loose rock into solid rock at $1.50 per yard, and in that way money was Mr. MIDDLEBRO
improperly taken out of the treasury of the country. Surely if we are going to ascertain whether or not Mr. Lumsden was justified in losing confidence in the engineers, we cannot possibly attain the desired end unless we are permitted to prove what he alleged and go into this whole question of classification.

speechtext:
CARVELL (Carleton, N.B.) As I was a member of the committee which investigated certain questions in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific two years ago and as I have been referred to by my hon. friend from Grey (Mr. Middlebro), I trust I may be pardoned if I take a few minutes to discuss what to me i3 a very important question. I compliment the leader of the opposition on the good sense shown by him in marshalling his forces on this occasion and leaving it to a man like the hon. gentleman (Mr. Middlebro) to resurrect the Hodgins' charges which have been buried for two years and upon which the people of this country have already passed judgment. The hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) and the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) who know what took place with reference to the Hodgins charges had the good judgment not to discuss them in the manner they have been discussed this afternoon. I am sorry that the action of my hon. friend (Mr. Middlebro) has rendered it necessary to refer to these Hodgins charges at all, because it must be a painful matter to Major Hodgins and his friends, and to the hon. gentlemen opposite as well, to have these things rehashed. The facts of the Hodgins case are simple. Major Hodgins was a district engineer employed by the commission. He did not get along with the engineers under him, he had lots of trouble and the commission sent an officer to investigate the matter and report, and as a result of the investigation Major Hodgins was discharged. Major Hodgins made the statement that he estimated the cost at $12,000,000 and that he had seen in .one of the Toronto newspapers that contractor McArthur had stated that the cost would be about $16,000,000 and therefore he concluded that the increase of $4,000,000 above his estimate was due to the excessive classification which was known as the Quebec classification. He also stated in substance that he had been taken down to Quebec to be taught how the classification was made there, and the inference was that he had been asked and had refused to adopt the Quebec classification in district 'F,' and because he had refused he was dismissed from his position as district engineer. Well, the evidence showed that Major Hodgins went to Quebec in company with 15 or 20 other engineers and the commissioners of the Grand Trunk Pacific, that they examined a certain cut in the vicinity of

La Tuque and the report of the engineers had shown that that cut contained about 87 per cent of solid rock whereas in his judgment 40 per cent of solid rock would be the outside figure to allow. And, because of what he saw in this cut he considered that unfair and dishonest classification had taken place and that he would not apply it to district 'F.' This matter was investigated for about a month and Major Hodgins was assisted by able counsel whose services were paid by the government. Every chance in the world was given Major Hod-gins and the Conservative party to prove the charges, and after a month's inquiry, without any pressure or promise or anything else, Major Hodgins voluntarily stated that he found he was entirely wrong, because the cut to which he referred as having been classified as 87 per cent and upon which he would have allowed 40 per cent solid rock, was actually classified as only 29 per cent solid rock in one. month and 30 per cent in another, and the very month in which he was at the La Tuque cutting it was classified at 29 per cent, while he himself had allowed 40 per cent. When Major Hodgins was brought face to face with this statement of facts, there was nothing for an honourable man to do but to say what he did, that he was wrong, that he had been misled by somebody, he withdrew his charges and that was the end of the whole transaction. My hon. friend tries to resurrect these charges and to show that after Major Hodgins failed to prove that there was anything wrong in Quebec and consequently that- he had been asked to do anything wrong in his district, we should have gone into the question of classification. I do not propose to discuss that because it was threshed out at the time and if the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) had been here he would have exercised the same good judgment displayed by the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) and the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) and refrained from discussing that question at all. My hon. friend says that after Mr. Poulin was made district engineer in 'F' the over-classification amounted to $2,798,000. Why, the hon. gentleman does not know what he is talking about. The amount he cites is a certain conclusion arrived at by the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) and I shall refer to it in a while. But the hon. member for Simcoe does not claim that it is an overclassification, he says it is a difference between the estimate of the engineers who surveyed the work in the first place and the actual result of construction. He does not say it is an over-classification, he says it is an increase in cost. My hon. friend from North Grey who knows nothing about it, comes here and says that since Mr. Poulin was put in charge of the work the
over-classification has amounted to over $2,000,000 and he contradicts the hon. member for Simcoe himself. I am sorry the hon. member for Simcoe is not here; I believe that hon. gentleman tried to give a fair statement of the case as he viewed it. I cannot agree with his conclusions but, so far as his figures are concerned, he took them from the returns furnished. He has been very industrious, he has asked time and again for returns, and I understand he has gathered information, he has codified that information and while I think in some cases he has been unfair, he has given us the result of his investigations, and has something to back it up. The hon. member for North Grey comes here this afternoon and I would not like to say through malice, I would not *be entitled to say it, but I think I have the right to say through sheer inability to understand the purport of these figures, makes the broad statement that after Mr. Poulin, a Frenchman, took charge, the over-classification amounted to more than $2,000,000.
The hon. member for Simcoe in compiling his statements took the amounts and quantities in district *F' from the estimate of Major Hodgins and you will all remember that Major Hodgins stated before the committee of inquiry that as a result of his investigations and re-surveys of his district he was able to reduce the estimated cost from about $13,000,000 to about $12,000,000 or in other words that he was able by a re-survey to reduce the cost of district 'F' by $1,500,000. The hon. member for Simcoe takes that $12,000,000 as being the true estimated cost of district 'F' and builds up a case from that, the result being his statement that it cost $2,798,000 more than it was estimated by the engineers it would cost.
