Mr. Lumsden signed them and adopted them and made them his *own, and has to stand by them. Now, I want to read these specifications'. I am go-' ing to take up the question of solid rock only, and I confine my reading of the specifications to that:
Solid rock excavation will include all rock found in ledges or masses of more than one cubic yard which, in the judgment of the engineer, may be best removed by blasting.
I think it would do many of our hon. friends on the other side a vast amount of good if they would read that, and read it carefully. This presupposes two conditions of affairs to exist. First, it presupposes that there would be rock found in ledges. Every member of this House, and every intelligent member of the reading public of Canada, knows that if you come to ledge rock there is no question that that rock is solid rock. It is the other branch of the specifications over which the difficulty arises-rock in masses; if the rock were all ledge rock, there could not be any question about it. But as it provides also for rock, ' found in masses of more than one cubic yard,' it presupposes that some substance must be classified as solid rock which is not ledge rock. Were this not the case, of course, the specification would have been confined to ledge rock itself. Now, the question arises: What is meant by the term 'rock in masses?' This work commenced early in 1906, I think. Of course, it would not be very long before differences of opinion would arise between the engineers as to what was meant by ' rock in masses of more than one cubic yard.' The Grand Trunk Pacific, who want to keep the price down to thq lowest figure, because they will

have to pay interest on the cost of it for the next forty-three years, contended that it meant practically nothing but boulders which would measure one cubic yard. If it was not a boulder, they contended, it was not solid rock. Other engineers on the work said that it did not mean that at all. And Mr. Lumsden applied to the district engineers, the district engineers to their divisional engineers, and, in some cases, to resident engineers. The contractors applied to their solicitors, and some of the ablest legal minds in Canada were brought to bear on the interpretation of these words. I will not quote any of these opinions, it is enough to say that such legal authorities as Blake, Lash & Cassels, Alexander Lacoste and others were consulted and gave opinions. Eminent engineers also were asked to interpret the words. A variety of interpretations was given, but, with one or two exceptions, every one of these authorities, both technical and legal, held that the specification did include something beyond rock in ledge or in boulders measuring over one cubic yard. Therefore, after a great deal of discussion, Mr. Lumsden, some time, I think, in December, 1907, issued to his engineers, further instructions as to his interpretation of this clause. He then went so far as to say that rock in masses meant rock joined together in such manner that, in the opinion of the engineer, they could be best removed by blasting, so long as the individual pieces of rock in these masses exceeded one cubic foot in size.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock I was endeavouring to point out some of the difficulties of classification in railway construction from a practical standpoint. I had read the instructions given to Mr. Lumsden by his engineers on the 10th of January, 1908, as to his interpretation of the specifications in regard to solid rock. I now refer to clause 35 of the original specification, and here is what Mr. Lumsden says about it:
All large stones and boulders measuring more than one cubic foot and less than one cubic yard, and all loose rock whether in situ or otherwise, that may be removed by hand, pick or bar, all cemented gravel, indurated clay and other materials that cannot in the judgment of the engineer, be ploughed with a ten-inch grading plough, behind a team of six good horses properly handled; and without the necessity of blasting, although blasting may be occasionally resorted to, shall be classified as loose rock.
Under the heading I would include:-
1.	All large stones and boulders more than

one cubic foot and less than one cubic yard not covered under clause 34.
2.	All loose rock in situ or otherwise that mav be removed by hand, pick or bar, ami not covered under clause 34.
3.	All cemented gravel, indurated clay, and other materials that cannot, in the judement of the engineer, be ploughed with a ten-inch grading plough behind a team of six good horses properly handled: and without the necessity of blasting, although blasting may be occasionally resorted to.
That was an interpretation of this clause that might be given by any person, and, let us apply the test. Take material which the engineer may say cannot be classified as solid rock, and then the first question that arises is: Can it he ploughed with a team of six horses and a ten-inch plough? Well, in almost every case that must of necessity lie purely in the judgment of the engineer who is classifying the work, because, of course, you could not by any possibility get a team of six horses and plough on to some of this work. The next question is: Can it be removed by hand, pick or bar? There' is no trouble in telling whether it can be' removed by hand, because a man can get down and try it. But, can it be removed by a pick? Well, a Tailway navvy will take . a pick and if he takes time enough he can remove a solid ledge of rock, or he can' with a crow-bar, if he takes time enough drill a hole three feet deep in solid rock: But, I submit that no engineer ever intended that if it were reasonably a physical impossibility to remove this material by' pick or bar, it must necessarily be classified as loose rock. We must apply common sense to the thing. The question is whether a man engaged in railway construction could fairly and reasonably remove this material by means of a pick or1 bar, or whether in the judgment of the engineers you could with a team of six horses and a ten-inch plough, plough it. If it cannot be ploughed in such a way, then it should not be classified as loose rock, and if it can, then it should be so classified. I merely mention this to point out the large degree of judgment which must be exercised by the engineer whose duty it is to classify the work. I am also endeavouring to show the next to impossibility of you or I, Mr. Speaker, or even an experienced engineer classifying that work on an examination made a year afterwards, when the weathering has caused the face to become smooth and to look different from what it was in its original state. Under the specifications anything other than' solid rock and loose rock would be called common excavation. Let me for . a moment refer to the argument advanced by the hon. member for Simeoe (Mr. Lennox) who has given the question a good deal of consideration, and to whom the country and the House
owe a debt of gratitude for the labour he has expended in preparing his case. I wish to discuss the points raised by the hon. gentleman in a fair manner and to give him credit where credit is due. In one connection the hon. gentleman was manifestly unfair, although perhaps unwittingly. He gave us instances of work which was estimated by the engineers to cost so much, but which had cost more than the estimate, and he said that this increase had arisen on only three items of the contract. Well, there are 104 items in the contract altogether, and while he did not say so, yet the inference was that the discrepancy between the estimate and the cost would proportionately increase in the case of the other 101 items. Well, my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Haggart), who_is somewhat of a railway man, knows that in such a contract as this, the three items of solid rock, loose rock, and common excavation will represent 90 per cent of the total cost of the undertaking, and in some cases more than that. Therefore, when the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox), considering the three items, wants us to believe that' there will be an alarmingly greater increase when the remaining items are taken into account, I am sorry to think that he did not treat the House with that fairness to which we are entitled and which indeed the hon. gentleman usually exhibits. Then, another thing, the hon. gentleman did not touch at all upon the price of the quantities to be removed. The prices range practically from 25 cents a yard for common excavation to 50 or 60 cents for loose rock, and $1.50 for solid rock, but the hon. gentleman omitted to mention what is called train-haul. Under the contract the contractor agrees to remove all cuts down to the grade and to place the material in the nearest hollow on either side or wherever he is instructed to do by the engineer. The contractor has to haul that material 500 feet without extra cost, but when he hauls it beyond 500 'feet he gets, I think, one cent per 100 feet per yard. After all that is done, after the amount of earth taken out of the cut is used in the embankment or fill adjoining it, if there is nothing left at the fill-up, they have to resort to some other method. That is called train-haul. They get from 45 cents to 50 cents a yard for train-haul, and as a rule it must be common excavation unless the engineer authorizes the contractor to take something else. There you see, you have millions of-common excavation which actually figure up at 45 cents to 50 cents a yard instead of 25 cents a yard, and any gentleman who' assumes to discuss quantities and prices' [DOT] of this contract ought to know it. I am1 bound to say the hon. gentleman must havd known it, and it probably has escaped hi? attention.	.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: Is there not a special price for that kind of work?

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: Certainly, that is what I am telling the House, but it is common excavation and it is included in the quantities of earth removed and is a special price. That price is about 45 cents or 50 cents a yard, and that price rules as long as the distance to be carried is not more than, I think, five miles. If, for any reason, they have to go more than five miles for material, they get a certain amount per mile after that, I think one cent a yard per mile for the tram haul. This increases the cost of common excavation in many cases by 100 per cent, and it ac* counts for the increased cost to some extent, but yet my hon. friend took good care not to say anything about it.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: How much of that kind of work is there?

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext:
I know one place in district 'A,' for instance, where there is
300,000	yards of train haul; another place where there would be 250,000 yards. I think in New Brunswick I could pick out in district 'A' probably 1,000,000 yards of train haul and these are things which we must understand if we are to discuss this matter intelligently.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: Does not my hon. friend think that an engineer giving the original estimates would take that into consideration before he gave the estimate?

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext:
I am not a judge of the engineer, and I do not think the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) or any other hon. member will say that any engineer can go over the ground in making preliminary surveys or even locating surveys and figure exactly to a yard what he will have to do to build a railway 1,800 miles in length.
I will take up district 'F' and take the different sections in the order in which they were discussed by the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox). He stated that there would be an increase in the cost when the work was completed of about $2,700,000 over the estimate made by the engineer before the work was commenced. Let us look at this like reasonable business men. The engineer goes over 200 miles of proposed railroad. He looks at the contour of the country, at the hills and hollows, he examines the rivers, he makes up his mind as to whether there will be much rock, and he says: I come to the conclusion that out of 1,000,000 yards of excavation there will be 1,000 yards of solid rock and 200,000 yards of loose rock, and the balance common excavation. I want to know how any man can tell to a thousand yards or a hundred thousand yards or a quarter of a million yards what Mr. CARVELL.
different classes of material there will be in a million yards of excavation. He cannot dig pits, they do not do that in modern engineering. He may drive steel bars down and come to the conclusion that after so many feet of common excavation he will have solid rock. I want to be reasonable and I want the members to be reasonable; I am sorry my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) is not here, in order to ask him to be reasonable and to tell me what no man on earth, no matter what his ability may be, can tell whether he is going to find this cemented material of which Mr. Lumsden speaks, this conglomerate or plum-pudding material _ of which he also speaks, or material which can or cannot be ploughed by a team of six horses when it is found twenty or thirty feet underground.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext:
Does the hon. member mean to argue to this House and to the country that any capable engineer has the slightest difficulty in estimating whether
100,000	or 500,000 yards of material is sand, or solid rock?

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext:
There never was a railway constructed on earth, let alone in Canada, tout that very thing happened, and it is the most common error known to engi-' neers. I shall give an illustration under my own observation. About a year ago, in company with the chief engineer, I visited a large portion of the work in New Brunswick. We came to a cutting in which there are probably 150,000 yards of material. The engineers returned this in their estimate as solid rock. The sub-contractor, a man from Sydney, Nova Scotia, took the work believing he had this 150,000 or 200,000 yards of solid rock, and it turns out there are not 25,000 yards of solid rock in the whole cut, yet the engineers told him it would be solid rock. There is a concrete illustration. If the hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Conmee), a practical railway contractor, were here he would bear out every word I say, and the Temark is true in many cases'. Engineers sajr they believe from looking at the ground it is going to be sand, and it turns out to toe very solid rock. I tell my hon. friends they should go on some of these enormous works and see for themselves, and they will conclude that what I say is true.
Now, we will go to district ' F '. There we have an estimate based on the quantities and the estimated classification of Mr. Hodgins, of $12,000,000. I said before dinner that Major Hodgins left out a number of items in his classification, one of which, the excavating of a foot below grade in all rock cuttings, amounted to half a million dollars. I find in referring to the debates, that it would amount to $495,000, about 300,000 yards of solid rock which he

had not estimated at all. I also looked up Mr. Poulin's evidence at page 485 of the investigation. Mr. Poulin there submitted a statement to which I have already referred, and he states there that Mr. Hod-gins had not estimated work in the contract and in the grading which amounted to $1,500,000, and therefore, instead of this work being estimated to cost $12,000,000 as the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) stated the other day, it should have been estimated by Mr. Hodgins himself, if he had included these things which were left out, at $1,350,000. According to the statement given by my friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) it did cost only $12,892,000, or less than it should have cost according to the^ proper estimate made by Mr. Hodgins himself. I wish to tell my hon. friend another thing concerning this district. This is a matter of which there is no public record, but I will make the statement, and it is the easiest thing in the world for my hon. friends to verify it by asking for a return which will be readily brought down. My hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) complains that in this contract, as in many others, for some unexplained reason-and there was always the insinuation that there was something crooked at the bottom of it-common excavation had constantly dwindled and solid rock had increased. In district ' F ' half a million yards of common excavation disappears and appears as solid rock, and this was done designedly and with the consent of the engineers and of the Grand Trunk Pacific and every body else. It had to be done.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: Give the particulars.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: I will.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: Give them now.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: It was in filling across lakes. The experience of railway contractors and engineers is that, in many places, where you fill up a body of water with common earth-if it were even sand it would not be so bad-it will not stand; it is only mud and will melt away. We have illustrations of that in many places. There is one on the Canadian Pacific railway between here and Montreal, and there is one as my hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. John Haggart) knows in New Brunswick, between St. John and Rothbsay. They have been filling up that New Brunswick hole for 40 years and it is going down all the time. In order to meet these conditions they have taken solid rock out of the cuts and have put it in these embankments and made solid rock embankments.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: You would not get solid rock where there was none.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: It is called rock-borrow, and that is the subject I am going to talk about.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: What was the estimated quantity on that particular section, and how much wa3 it increased by the difficulties the hon. gentleman mentioned?

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: I do not know. But I can tell the hon. member that the solid rock has been increased from the actual requirements of the case, according to the estimates, by half a million cubic yards. The engineers estimated to use half a million yards of common excavation for the fills and they have had to get rock, not from the ordinary cuts, but from outside the cuts. They broadened them out and took half a million yards of solid rock, borrowed it and made the fills.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: Give the mile-post where that occurred.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: I cannot. I think I treated the House fairly

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: The hon. member cannot give it.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: I told the House that I got the facts from the engineers, but that they could be verified by a return.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: The hon. member ought to have given the mile-post.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: I am willing that the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) or any other member should make any criticism of my remarks after I have finished, but I hope the hon. gentleman will not lecture me while I have the floor.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: I want the facts while the hon. member is stating them.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: I would like to show some more rock-borrow. And I can give the hon. member the mileage-I can give him the whole thing. That is, I can give him the stations, and he is railway man enough to know what that means. I have here a return to this House, file No. 12,603, brought down some time before Christmas. This refers to the Kitchen contract, district ' A

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: I thought the hon. gentleman was dealing with Mr. Hodgins.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext:
I was. But my hon. friend (Mr. Barker) wants facts, and I am going to give him facts. Take from stations 500 to 1,070 in District A. That is better than giving the mileage, because it gives every one hundred feet. They required a borrow which ordinarily would be a train haul of 392,000 cubic yards. The engineer reported that it was impossible to find a borrow of common excavation on the Kitchen contract. The proposition was made to borrow rock near the site of these fills or embankments, outside the ordinary line. Now, it was stated by the hon. mem-



ber for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) that earth embankments have what is called a slope of li to 1-that is, for every foot you go perpendicularly your embankment goes out li feet. If the perpendicular distance from the shoulder of the embankment to the bottom is 50 feet, it will be 75 feet from that point to the outside of the embankment. It is known to engineers that rock embankments will not spread out nearly so far. I think they figure out at li to 1. or, in some cases, much less than that.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: Very often perpendicular.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: Not when broken up.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: You can see it often on the Canadian Pacific railway.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext:
I want to tell the hon. member he does not know how roads are constructed to-day. He is about twenty-five years behind the times. They go to a rock cut ten to forty feet deep-I have seen one rock cut on the Grand Trunk Pacific eighty feet. They tunnel into the hill- they call it ' coyuting '-perhaps forty feet. Then they sink a shaft and then spread out from that. After all is ready they put in five or ten tons of explosives, and break up ten or fifteen thousand cubic yards of material at one blast-break it up so small that it is taken out with the steam shovel, hauled and dumped over the embankment. That will not go perpendicular; you have only to tell how it is done to show that the hon. member (Mr. Barker) does not know wliat he is talking about.
Now. let us go back to section * A.' They had to have 392,000 yards of train haul, and the engineers reported they could not get this material on the work. As a rock embankment would not be so wide at the bottom as the other, it would not require so many yards to make it. Then, it is known to all engineers that a yard of common excavation, when placed in an embankment, will not occupy more than a yard of actual space, and it will shrink a little for it will pack closer than when it was in its native position in the earth. Besides that, all measurements of railwav construction are made, as you may say, in situ. That is, when they pay the contractor for rock-borrow they pay for the number of yards, as the material is in the. ledge from which it is taken. But when it is broken up. and hauled out and put in the embankment, a yard of rock will make from I 6-10 to 1 9-10 yards. So, you have more yards in the embankment itself, and you have a smaller number of yards to pay for in situ-you will reduce the number of yards both ways. Then they figure out the cost by train haul. Suppose they had to go fifteen miles. That, in the Kitchen contract, was forty-five cents a yard. So they figured out that the em-Mr. CARVELL.
bankment built out of common earth would cost the country the same amount of money as an embankment built of rock borrow at $1,101. The engineer made a proposition to the Kitchen Company, to give them a special contract to make these embankments at that figure, and they accepted it and did the work. Thus, 400,000 cubic yards of solid rock-

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: Not figured in the specification?

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: No, it had appeared in the specification as about 590,000 or 600,000 yards of common excavation. There you have an illustration of how common excavation dwindled by 600,000 yards, and solid rock excavation increased by 400,000 yards, yet without costing the country a cent.	,

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: If the hon. member would give the mile post we could see if that applied in the other case.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: I have told the hon. member the station.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: The hon. member is giving what occurred in New Brunswick. Give the mile post where you say a similar thing occurred on section ' F.'

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext:
I do not propose to answer my hon. friend (Mr. Barker) on that point. As my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. E. M. Macdonald) suggests, there is nothing the matter in New Brunswick. I am showing that they had to (borrow rock in New Brunswick, and it can be shown also that they had to borrow rock in district ' F.' And it was done with the consent of everybody, it has not cost the country a dollar more, and you have a great deal better work. More than this, I can show places on the Grand Trunk Pacific where the original estimate was for steel viaducts, but the Grand Trunk Pacific Commission thought it would be better to make solid " embankments. Of course, that costs more. In the estimates, these fills did not appear because the places were to be crossed by steel. But the commissioners made up their mind that it would be better to have permanent works. I can show one place on district ' A ' where it has taken 250,000 yarc(s of material to fill up one of these places which, under the original estimate, would have been crossed with steel. That adds to the quantities. More than that, in one of these cases it is being filled with rock because they cannot get the earth. I think that is section ' A.' I hope now I have given enough illustrations to show how these quantities are changed from the original estimates down to the actual quantities afterwards completed. My hon. friend from Simcoe referred to all these, and I will refer to them. He took the first

section west of Moncton. It is a matter of common knowledge that practically all these Grand Trunk Pacific contracts have been handed over to sub-contractors; the Grand Trunk Pacific taking a very small percentage, simply^ enough to pay them for doing some financing, and the balance goes to the contractors. They are not ordinary subcontractors, because a sub-contractor in an ordinary contract probably allows 15 per cent to the main contractor; whereas on these contracts, less than 5 per cent goes to the Grand Trunk Pacific. Now, if any hon. gentleman has the idea that the Grand Trunk Pacific are not watching this matter very carefully all over the line of railway, he is very much mistaken. I can state that there is a feeling on the part of engineers all over this line, and I have met most of them, that the Grand Trunk Pacific are acting in a really unfriendly spirit, and are finding fault with everything that is going on. They are not objecting down in New Brunswick, as they are probably in every other part of their work. There are very few objections in New Brunswick. In one of these contracts, No. 2, there has not been a solitary protest. On the Kitchen works, which my hon. friend referred to as costing much more than they should, there have been very few protests. But that is not a Grand Trunk Pacific contract. My hon. friend says that in the first estimate of No. 2 contract there was no solid rock at all. It turns out now that there is something like 10,000 or 20,000 yards of solid rock on that whole contract. Now, I want to know if you are going (to condemn an engineer as being a dishonest scoundrel because, in a work 50 miles long, he *says he did not think there was any solid rock, and did not get within 20,000 yards of what turned out to be the fact. You have only to read the specifications to know that any man might make a mistake like that. It is only an error in judgment, and the marvel to me is that these engineers get as near to the facts as they do in their first estimates.
He takes up next No. 3, that is from Chipman to the Intercolonial. There, he says, they have also an increase of 231,289 cubic yards of solid rock which should be called excavation, giving a total increase in this one item alone of $341,000. I want to tell my hon. friend that there is a place on that contract where soft work has been cut out and a solid embankment put in the place of it, and that accounts for 200.000 yards of this work, and it has been done with the consent of the Grand Trunk Pacific's engineer and the commissioners' engineer. Yet my hon. friends say that because of these apparent discrepancies in the figures, somebody has been guilty of fraud, and somebody should be brought to the bar of this House, and somebody should be disgraced for the Test of his natural life, 81J
as an engineer who had sold himself out to the contractor. I want to know if that is the standard by which my hon. friends would want one of their friends, or sons, or brothers, or their friends' sons or brothers to be judged? I wont use any harsher term. I think I have shown some reasons why these discrepancies appear between the estimate and the actual results, and if they will make a thorough investigation they will come to the conclusion that there is very little real fault to find.
Next, we have the contract from 164* to 195, that is the Kitchen contract. On that contract, no doubt, the cost has very much increased over the original estimate. I am bound to say, however, that on that contract the engineers made a mistake as to the amount of solid rock to be found. But I have accounted to you for 400,000 yards of solid rock, which has been borrowed entirely elsewhere and put in there, and as I said before, it does not cost the country one dollar more than it would if the work had been completed according to the specifications, and if they had got a rock embankment instead of an earth embankment. Then he goes on to the lines in white. That is hardly worth discussing because the increase is so very slights Now I am not going to discuss the case in the province of Quebec, because I have no personal knowledge of it. No doubt there has been an increase in quantity, no doubt the matter will be investigated, and if there is anything wrong it will be cut out; But I am only talking of things of which I know, or of which I have evidence before me in the returns from which I can discuss the question intelligently.
Then that brings us back to the object of all this discussion. My hon. friend from Simcoe says that there has been dishonest classification on the part of the engineers, he says that the quantities of solid rock and loose rock have materially increased, and the quantities of excavation have decreased. I have pointed out some of the reasons why solid rock was increased, and I have given you actual illustrations. But, there is another matter to which I want to refer as showing why solid rock has increased. Any hon. member who knows anything about railway construction knows that when you go into a cut, say 20 or 30 or 40 feet deep, of solid rock, you dont take this out by pick and bar, or by a little stick of dynamite, it would cost you $10 a yard to do it; but you take it out by putting in monstrous charges of explosives of dynamite, or nitro glycerine, or things of that kind. Is it nossible for any man actually to gauge the width of that explosion when he is taking down 10,000 or 15,000 yards at a time? If that overlaps the actual width of the cutting according tq

the prism, as it is called, then the balance ' is called an overbreak, and on the Canadian Pacific railway they admit there ought to be at most 15 to 25 per cent al' lowed for overbreak. That adds to the cost. When engineers are estimating ' quantities they estimate actual quantities according to the prism as laid down on the 'plan; and when you add to that ten per cent or twenty-five per cent, which of neces sity must happen in the way of overbreak you have that much added to your origina
*	estimate. In all these cases more rock i? broken than they expected. Then that be
[DOT] comes a question for negotiation. Is r. fair to allow the contractor for this extra amount, or not? That is a matter to be decided mutually.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says that the estimate is formed on the prism quantity.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: I do.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: How is it that the prism quantities are less than the actual quantities? The actual quantities generally taken out are a great deal less than the prism quantities.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: They are a great deal more than the prism quantities. My hon. friend has got it reversed.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: The quantities that were estimated by the engineers are less than the amounts taken out.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: My hon. friend is at liberty to say that, I say it is the other way.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: No, I went carefully into it, and I find that the amounts estimated by the engineers are the actual quantities paid for.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext:
With the hon. gentleman's permission-according tio the figures brought down by the hon. member
*	for Simcoe yesterday, which figures were .not disputed by the Minister of Railways,
because they were compiled from information brought down by the minister himself, these figures show that in one case, while the estimate of the amount to be ex-[DOT]cavated was 15.000,000 yards, there was actually taken out, according to his certificate, only 10,000,000.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: I do not propose to discuss this matter with mv hon. friends, they will have all the chance they want to tell their side of the case.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: But we want the facts.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext:
I think I know as much about the facts in this case as my hon. friend does and perhaps before I am through Mr. CARVELL.
he will think I do. There is this question of overbreak. The hon. member for North Grey made the statement this afternoon that after Mr. Grant was appointed district engineer he went over the work and, of his own volition, deducted something like $350,000 from the work on districts 'B' and TV I can tell my hon. friend, and perhaps he does not know this, but he could get it by asking for a return, that of that portion of the $350,000 belonging to district 'F' $100,000 o* it is a question of overbreak and not a question of classification at all. So, therefore, you have reduced the actual amount in dispute as to classification within districts 'F' and 'B' down almost to a minimum. The total amount in dispute between the Grand Trunk Pacific engineers and the commission engineers is less than $1,000,000 on $50,000,000 worth of work; or less than two per cent of the whole work in question is in dispute between these engineers. When you consider the difficulties of classifying material, as I have pointed out here to-night, under Mr. Lumsden's instructions, ought any engineer to be branded as a scoundrel because there happens to be a difference of two per cent between the estimates by himself or his predecessor and the actual results of the excavation? I think you have only to state the proposition to see the unfairness of it and it is a remarkable thing that the engineers were able to estimate these quantities and costs as accurately as they have done. I stated in the early part of my remarks, and I wish to repeat it here, in order to have it emphasized, that according to the figures of the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), there is only an increase of $7,-
500,000	over the estimates, which are only estimates made by the engineers at the beginning of this work.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: I would like that authoritatively. I suppose the hon. gentleman gets it from the minister?

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: Authoritatively? Why, I figured it out from the figures given by the hon. member for Simcoe on Tuesday, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Haggart) or any hon. gentleman can figure it out for himself and see. I have taken the figures [DOT]is he gave them and that is the result.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: I thought they were figures given to you.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen say ' hear, hear.' I stand by my statement. I think every hon. gentleman in this House, if he will let his reason sway him, will stand by the same statement because of the absolute nonsense of a proposition like this. Then, they say we want to do more than that. We want to investigate everything that has taken place in the conduct
of this work. We want to investigate whether this or that engineer exercised proper judgment in locating the line, whether he should have located it half a mile east or a quarter of a mile west. Let me give an illustration. Hon. gentlemen bring up Major Hodgins here as the acme of perfection in all engineering matters. I will showr you what it will amount to. There is a place-I cannot give the name, but I can get it for hon. gentlemen if they desire it-where an engineer located on the work on Major Hodgins' district, when he was district engineer, a five per cent curve in order to get around the edge of the lake. Major Hodgins said: That should only have been a four per cent curve, and because you have located a five per cent curve you are wrong, your judgment is no good. He fired him. That man has gone forth a dismissed engineer and to this day is looking for a position because he is sent off, his reputation is injured, and has no means of redress. Worse than all that, on the advice of this same Major Hodgins, $40,000 was expended on the line which he projected, or caused to be projected, and they had to go back and abandon that $40,000 worth of work and adopt the line projected by the very engineer who was fired because he exercised his common sense and judgment in laying out this line. These are seme of the things that my hon. friends want to have investigated, and they want to have a hundred and one things like this investigated all over the country. You have only to enunciate the proposition in order to see the absolute nonsense of it.
Now, Sir, I submit that these are very grave charges which have been made by Mr. Lumsden. Mr. Lumsden has said in effect, that these engineers were dishonest. Perhaps I am putting it too strongly. Well I will modify it. He says his engineers failed to carry out his instructions of the 10th January, 1908. I have pointed out to the House what these instructions were. If an engineer takes a certain view of the classification of a certain cut under the instructions of Mr. Lumsden, and if Mr. Lumsden says to him, I cannot go there myself, you are on the work, you are the only man that can do it, I want to know, Sir, whether we have the right to bring that man up and allow a prejudiced engineer to investigate him and say that because you have exercised your judgment in one way and our engineers would exercise their judgment in another way, that man is a scoundrel and is entitled to the castigation given to him by Mr. Lumsden. Therefore, I am driven to the conclusion that the only logical thing we can do is to have a committee appointed as suggested by the Prime Minister. We can bring Mr. Lumsden before the committee and ask him as business men whom he means when he speaks of those who did not carry out the

instructions which he gave them. Then, it will he up to Mr. Lumsden to say who these men are. Then, let us bring before this committee a commission of expert engineers and let this commission say whether or not, in their opinion, the engineers who have been so severely reprimanded or castigated Iby Mr. Lumsden are guilty or not. If they are, dismiss them. If the committee find that they have been wilfully guilty of a crime, prosecute them.

speechtext: How are you going to make the inquiry? I pointed out the impossibility of it from a business, standpoint. We would make laughing stocks of ourselves all over the country if we were to attempt to carry out the proposition of hon. gentlemen opposite.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext: I am glad to hear my hon. friends opposite applaud that; I am glad they are coming round to a reasonable view of the case and that they will vote against their own motion.

They are the men created by parliament to have the right to give the evidence, and I can say more than that, there is one man on that commission who has visited every cut and every fill on the Grand Trunk Pacific from Moncton to Winnipeg, and I say that that man has information which it would take the best engineer in Canada ten years to obtain if he spent the whole of his time doing it, and even then he could not do it because Mr. Grant has seen this work in the actual course of excavation; and visited it month after month as inspecting engineer, and he knows and has first hand knowledge which the most expert engineer on earth could ;not get now. Therefore, no committee of Mr. CARVELL.
engineers that could be sent out is in as good a position to judge fairly between Mr. Lumsden and these engineers whom he has charged with incompetency or worse, as is the commission which is created by parliament, and for that reason I submit that the amendment should be voted down and the resolution moved by the right hon. the Prime Minister adopted by the House.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: It may be truly said of the hon. member (Mr. Carveil) as it has been said is all that has reference to either the motion, that the very last part of his address is all that has reference to either the motion or to the amendment, and therefore the hon. gentleman will understand why I shall first reply to his closing remarks. The hon. gentleman gave as a reason why he was going to support the motion that, before the committee proposed by the First Minister, a committee of engineers could be called who would give evidence as to whether or not there had been bad faith on the part of the sub-engineers in not following the instructions of the chief engineer of the Transcontinental, but only a moment before that he said that no matter what any engineer said as to whether or not these sub-engineers followed the instructions, that would be no evidence of bad faith because they might in perfect good faith have given a different classification from that given by the chief engineer.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext: I must correct my hon. friend. I did not say: if they did not follow the instructions; I said: if they did not interpret the instructions as Mr. Lumsden would interpret them.

maintopic: NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAIL WAV-CLASSIFICATION OF MATERIAL.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Carve'll) stated that no matter how great the divergence in the classification, that would be no evidence of bad faith on the part of the under engineers. Then, if that would be no evidence, and if that is the only evidence these arbitrators could give, there absolutely could be no evidence offered to the committee as to the bad faith of any of these men in the matter of over classification. Consequently if the resolution moved by the right hon. the First Minister is adopted, under the argument adduced by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Carveil) there cannot possibly be brought in a finding of bad faith. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Carveil) has given a speech and he has got through with it, and I have been at a loss to find one word or one sentence in that speech which argued any more against the amendment than it argued against the resolution, because whatever he may have said against investigation applied equally as well against the alleged investigation suggested by the First Minister in his motion as against the investigation asked for by the amendment. For fear I

should do any injustice to the hon. member by not paying the attention to his speech which it merits, I shall briefly refer to a few points which he adduced. Let me premise by saying that I do not for one minute expect that I can add as much to the knowledge of this House from the point of view of the skilled engineer as has been furnished by the hon. member (Mr. Car-veil). I do not conceive that it is my duty to take part in this debate for the purpose of adding anything to the text-books on the subject of engineering; I conceive rather that my duty is to show why the amendment moved by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) should prevail against the resolution of the First Minister. Probably 75 per cent of the speech of the hon. member for Carleton was directed towards trying to show that it was impossible for engineers to make correct estimates by the yard of what would be solid rock, what loose rock, and what common excavation. I do not contend and nobody will contend that it is possible for absolute estimates so to be made. But, it is stated on the authority of engineers, and no engineering authority has been adduced to the contrary, that a margin of 20 per cent was ample to allow any engineer who could pretend to make a careful or competent survey.
Now, the point advanced by the hon. member for North Simcoe was that in district *F' which is the principal district in dispute there had been a mistake, not of 20 per cent, but a very gross mistake which was sufficient to raise a prima facie case against the honesty or the competency of the estimate, or the honesty of the calculations at the time the excavations were made. The facts are that in district *F' some 3,500,000 cubic yards were estimated by the engineers as solid rock, some 700,000 yards as loose rock, and 11,200,000 yards as common excavation. But, instead of this, the Minister of Railways has told the House that the actual figures are 6,500,000 cubic yards of solid rock, 2,100,000 cubic yards of loose rock, and about 3,000,000 yards of common excavation. There is a difference between the estimate and the result, not of 20 per cent, but of almost 100 per cent in the first case, and about 200 per cent in the second case, and less than one-third of the total estimated amount of common excavation. And, the hon. member for Carleton comes before the House and he gives it as his opinion as an engineering expert that it is a marvel to him how the engineers made so close an estimate as that. The only palliation he has to offer is that in district 'F,' somewhere he knows not where, he has heard that some 500,000 cubic yards of rock were used for the purpose of filling in lakes. Well, he can allow his 500,000 cubic yards whenever he wants to, and there will be almost
8.000.	000 yards of excavation left which he has failed to explain away. Now, Mr. Speaker, we can take for the purposes of this inquiry whichever horn of the dilemma the hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) wants to sit upon. He can argue that it is a first-class estimate, and then I will ask him of what use are any such estimates at all for the purposes of constructing a railway; of what use was it for the government to go to such great expense to be able to inform this country for the purposes of an election, that there were
11.000.	000 cubic yards of common excavation in district 'F' when as a matter of fact there were only 3,000,000 yards. Of what use was it to go to the trouble of ascertaining that there were 3,500,000 cubic yards of solid rock when as a matter of fact there were 6,500,000 cubic yards of solid rock. And, of what use was it to inform the House 'and the country on the authority of competent engineers-as the Minister of Finance said-that there were
700,000	cubic yards of loose rock when as a matter of fact there were 2,100,000. Let me say to the member for Carleton and to the House, that if it is not possible to estimate within closer limits than that, if that is a marvellously correct estimate, then, the presentation of these estimates at all can only have been intended to deceive the House and the country and they should never have been made. If 20 per cent is the utmost that may be allowed for a divergence between the estimate and the actuality, surely a divergence of 200 per cent cannot be explained on any hypothesis consistent with honesty. The hon. member (Mr. Carvell) pointed out that there was considerable more excavation required on account of the overbreak, and which he said would not be estimated by the engineers in the first place. I do not think the hon. member is correct in that, although on points of engineering of course I bow to his opinion as an exceedingly high one, judging from the assurance with which he gave it to the House. But at the same time, Sir, at page 12, of the report brought down by the First Minister, there will be found words of the assistant chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific, Mr. Woods, which are utterly inconsistent with the supposition that overbreak was not allowed for in the original estimates. Mr. Woods says, under date of June 19, 1908:
I have nothing to show how this overbreak is estimated. Articles 37 and 38 would indicate that a large amount of this overbreak might have been estimated as loose rock rather than solid. Can you say if this has been done? None of my reports indicate such to be the case. I think you will readily agree with me that if these cuttings are being measured month to month by actual quantities taken out, and no allowance deducted, little effort will be made by the contractors

to keep overbreak within reasonable limit and in the end we shall undoubtedly be paying $1,000,000 additional for the work on this section probably not contemplated in your approximate estimates.
How can any man say that that statement is consistent with the statement of the hon. member for Carleton, New Brunswick (Mr. Carvell) that overbreak would not be allowed in the first instance? An examination of district ' F ' clearly proves, and the figures in rough were given by the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middle-bro), that there was a total estimate of 15,056,063 cubic yards, and the total excavation actually taken out to the date of return was 10,068,032, or a deduction of almost
5,000,000 cubic yards. But in the return there was embodied the statement that 94-66 per cent of the work only was done. Allowing for the balance of 5 -.33 per cent, there will altogether be only in district ' F ' 11,222,433 cubic yards or about 4,400,000 cubic yards less actually taken out in the ultimate than was originally estimated by the engineers. Notwithstanding that the cost has far exceeded the estimate and will in the ultimate, to use the word of the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), outrageously exceed the estimate. Surely an hon. member -cannot expect sensible men to think engineers will give an estimate of loose rock or solid rock simply by taking a view of the country and not making any borings? Surely if the engineers did such a thing, the members of the government would not give the reports to the House as reliable. Surely the men who made the estimate would not' reduce it to a single yard oi_ rock, if they were going on the assumption that if they could come within 200 per cent of the correct figure they would consider, in the words of the hon. member (Mr. Carvell), that they were .doing marvellously well.
The hon. member for Carleton, with a wise discretion which I have observed in many cases, got away from section * F ' with remarkable speed. He got down to a district near Moncton, and tried to show that there were there some lakes and that borrowed rock had to be used to fill, so that it did not cost the country any more.
I must confess I did not understand his argument that this borrowed rock did not cost the country any more, but assuming him to be correct he must produce to the House the actual basis for the ultimate result that has ensued, that it is costing the country more.
