speechtext:
On this district near Moncton it was brought out by the member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox)-and it has not been denied except by the remark of the member for Carleton, New Brunswick, that the member for Simcoe, like the member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker), and the member for North Grey did not know what he was talking about-that in the eastern 50 miles there had been an error not of 20 per cent, but of 556 per cent, in the estimate of loose rock. Will the hon. member say that this is explained by the fact that some little rock was dumped into a lake? An estimate of 135,000 yards of loose rock grows into 850,000 yards, an increase of 556 per cent. The solid rock is not quite so marvellous, it was estimated at nothing and grew to 10,000 yards. But the excavation estimated at 1,900,000 was reduced to a paltry 600,000 and the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) still assures the House that he considers these estimates marvellously accurate.
Then we come to the next section, 50 to 58. The hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) shows that in that very section there was an increase in the cost of 166 per cent, and if, as the hon. member for Carleton, New Brunswick, argued, there was nothing added to the cost by means of the borrowed rock, what accounts for the increase of nearly three times in that section. In the next section, 58 and 96, the hon. member for Simcoe shows by a return that the percentage of solid rock had increased not 20 per cent but 240 per cent, and that also, to use the words of the hon. member for Carleton, New Brunswick, is a marvellously accurate estimate.
Take section 96 to 164, the increase of solid rock there, if the other is marvellously accurate, will be still more so for it is 95 per cent. Surely the member for Carleton does not pretend to be able to convince this House that estimates are worth one -dollar to the country, are not a positive detriment to the country as tending to deceive, if they cannot come infinitely nearer the mark than has been the case in almost any division of this whole Transcontinental line.
The hon. member for Carleton gave some figures of $15,000,000 in the total cost. I confess I could not understand his argument where he stated that the increase would be only $15,000,000. The figures are in ' Hansard ' and are to be found in the returns. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) assured this House that the cost would be $54,000,000 and he stated that his authority was not, as the member for

(Jarieton (Mr. Carvell) represented this afternoon, his own. I would like these two gentlemen to get together and reconcile their differences, because while the Minister of Finance assures the House he would not give the House an estimate based on his own authority, the member for Carle-ton, N.B., says that these estimates are not given on competent authority, but by members of the House. The Minister of Finance assured us that the co3t would be $54,000,000 and in that the minister estimated the interest during construction because without that it would be only some $44,000;000. The figures brought down last December show an estimated cost of $114.000,000, a rise from $27,000 per mile to over $63,000 a mile on the average. I do not know what the hon. member for Carle-ton, N.B., meant by referring to an increase of $15,000,000. Before he got through he also said: What is the use of appointing a committee to look into this matter of classification when the total amount at variance between the two contending parties at the present time is only two per cent? If the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., had been able to prove to the House that the total amount at variance was not two per cent but 1-100 of one per cent he would only have added to the strength of the argument that we require a committee to go into the rest of the over-classification. Why is there only two per cent now in dispute? It is because of the ingenuity of this Transcontinental Commission, assisted, as we were informed yesterday, by the Minister of Railways and Canals himself, by a document dated January 10, 1908, persisted in with a wonderful loyalty throughout two years and nearly three, with a marvellous tenacity, because by the ingenuity of that resolution they were able to shut out the whole burden of the complaint of the Grand Trunk Pacific from the purview of the arbitration board. It is more to revise and extend the scope of the investigation than for what is within the jurisdiction of the arbitrators that we require a committee for the purpose of investigation. I shall come to that point later on.
The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell), in that part of his speech before six o'clock, laid great stress on the fact that it was absolutely impossible, once an excavation was taken out and the road laid down, to make an investigation and determine as to over-classification. He said it was a mere farce. Let us assume that the hon. member's knowledge of engineering leads him to a correct conclusion on that point. Then, what is the use of the arbitration board now sitting? What is the use of putting the country to the expense of that board appointed last November to investigate work done prior to January, 1908? The hon. member's argument is that the whole principle of the arbitrations propounded by this agreement of which the government is the father, is a farce.
Now, I wish to refer for a few minutes to the resolution, and I confess that I cannot make the point stronger or clearer than it was made by the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro). Still I submit, in my own humble way, that this resolution of the First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) means absolutely nothing;- plainly and on its face it can result in nothing. As the hon. member for South Simeoe (Mr. Lennox) said, it is a gold brick, it is made for the purpose of being announced from the house-tops as showing the Prime Minister's desire for pure politics. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) avoided the point that nothing could result from this investigation. If the committee is appointed in pursuance of the resolution, the hon. member for Carleton and possibly the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) will be members of that committee. For I have learned this, if nothing else, since I came to this House, that the cold and frigid logic-or perhaps I should say the narrow scrutinizing method-of these hon. members confining the limits of investigations in this House appeals with great force to this government for the hon. member for Carleton in particular appears to have a perpetual retainer from the government for committees of this description. Should that hon. member be appointed as one of this committee, I cannot conceive that he will remain the man he has always been unless he contends before the committee that nothing can be investigated except according to the strict language of the resolution as interpreted and explained by the mover. Then it must be pointed out in the first place that the First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is careful to include and quote only such language of Mr. Lumsden as meets his purpose, that he leaves out Mr. Lumsden's charges that there . was over-classification in districts 'B' and 'F.' The only thing quoted is to the effect that there was a disregard of the instructions of Mr. Lumsden and that Mr. Lumsden had lost confidence in his staff. Consequently, all that will come within the purview of this committee is whether or not Mr. Lumsden had lost confidence in his staff and whether or not they disregarded his instructions. Investigating that narrowest of all points before the committee, the committee would be hemmed in by the fact that, as soon as they used the matter of over-classification to prove that these men had disregarded instructions they would be stopped by the hon. member for Carleton and the hon. member for Pictou on the ground that this over-classification, whether it results from bad faith or incompetence, is not within the purview of

the committee. If bad faith, if insubordination-if you call it such-on the part of these district engineers is not to be proven by over-classification, you cannot prove it at all, and it does not matter whether it existed or not. So, the only element by which insubordination could be proved is shut out from the domain of the committee altogether. If there ever was a resolution cunningly devised to forbid investigation, this is the one. The hands of Judge Cassels when he went to investigate the affairs of the Department of Marine were not anything like so securely tied as those of the committee will be when started on its narrow course. The resolution of the First Minister is not the whole truth; it is ' the seeming truth that cunning times put on ' to entrap the people. But the people cannot be deceived, because the facts have been clearly pointed out three times in this House, and no attempt made to meet the points raised.
Now, let me approach that point from another side. If any committee should be appointed by this House that would in any way duplicate the work of the arbitration board, there would be no work for that committee to do. This committee, as I want to argue later on, has infinitely greater work before it, if it is given power to do that work, than any arbitration board, because there is so much excluded from the jurisdiction of the board as to justify the appointment of the committee anyway. If they could not investigate any of these two per cent difficulties which the hon. member for Oarleton has spoken as between the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental Commission, they could not investigate the point of bad faith, because that point is inextricably involved in these two per cent difficulties.
The question before the House is whether or not we, having for our clients, not the Transcontinental or the government, but the people of the country, are justified in inquiring into all the facts regarding this expenditure of public money. My remarks will be almost exclusively along the line that we should have such an investigation. And in this we are supported by the powerful authority of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway itself. What we ask for is little if anything more than what the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company have been asking for for over two years-as evidenced by the very return brought down by the government-and what the government, through its commission, has been steadfastly refusing. I am relieved of the necessity, in order to form a basis for my argument, of placing on 'Hansard' the letters of Mr. Woods in which he argues against the classification as made by the district engineers of the Transcontinental. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) thought Mr. MEIGHEN.
he did justice to himself and the people by putting on record certain letters consistent with his own position, without putting on record those that were against his position. But these other documents have been placed on record by the hon. member for North Grey. Before I proceed further, I wish to correct the Minister of Railways -I regret to see he is not in his place, but perhaps his absence and his inattention to this debate is the measure of the importance that he attaches to the resolution of the First Minister-in regard to one statement he made, yesterday. The hon. gentleman said that since the appointment of Mr. Grant as chief engineer of the Transcontinental Commission, there had not been any new objections to the classification. If the minister-or those behind him who are present-will take a look at the return brought down, pages 35, 36 and 69, they will see that that statement of the minister is incorrect. Let me read from page 69. In a letter to Mr. Woods by Mr. Gordon Grant, dated October 21, 1909- several months after Mr. Grant was appointed-in reply to a letter written by Mr. Woods to Mr. Grant, of October 5, 1901, an acknowledgment of the criticisms of Mr. Woods is made.
I must comment here on the fact that throughout this return there is a marked absence of copies of the letters, in the first place, written by Mr. Lumsden to Mr. Woods. There are only the letters written by Mr. Woods to Mr. Lumsden, and they are more or less unintelligble without the replies of Mr. Lumsden. Not only is there a marked absence of those letters, but there is an absence even of the letter from Woods to Lumsden of October 5, 1909. At all events, in the reply, the purpose of Mr. Woods' letter is clearly shown, because Mr. Lumsden writes as follows:
I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 5th instant in which you file objections to the classification as returned on contracts 4 and 5 in district ' A.'
And so on. These objections cover the work done one or two years ago, notwithstanding that they were the same as the objections found by his engineers. This is pointed out by Mr. Lumsden. Further on, Mr. Gordon Grant acknowledges the receipt of objections to the following classifications as having been received, which objections are not referred to prior to the appointment of Mr. Grant, and which consequently, I take it, were made after Mr. Grant's appointment :
In district ' A ' 24, Grand Trunk Pacific Company: in district ' A ' 25, district ' B ' 15, Macdonell & O'Brien, districts ' C ' and ' B ' 14, Grand Trunk Pacific; district ' F,' O'Brien & Macdonell.
All these objections were made after the resignation of Mr. Lumsden, although it

was stated by the Minister of Railways none were made. It is worth while to refer to the objections made after Mr. Lumsden's resignation by Mr. Woods, as shown on page 35 of the return, where Mr. Woods says:
Referring to our recent visit to the work on district ' IS J east of the St. Lawrence river, our examination of classification as rendered at points visited, and our conversation regarding the same, I hope to repeat in writing what I stated to you verbally, that we still vigorously protest to the classification as returned to date. For example:-
And he proceeds to give examples covering several inches of the page of the return. Further on he says:
I take it that the above are fair samples of classification on this residency, if not on the entire division.
Emphasizing the point that the instances mentioned by himself are typical only. He says:
In the aggregate you can readily see the effect upon the cost of construction.
Now, Sir, the importance of the great divergence between the estimate and the result, is illustrated by the latter part of the letter which I read a few moments ago, found on page 5 of the return, in which Mr. Woods charges that if the overbreak on this district ' F ' is allowed to go on in the haphazard, unchecked style in which it had been going on, the loss on that connection alone would be $1,000,000 from overbreak. Now surely if, on one section of the road from Winnipeg to Moncton the loss in overbreak is estimated by Mr. Woods, through the error, through the dishonesty, of the officials of the Transcontinental, to be nearly $1,000,000, what would be the loss, not on overbreak alone, but on classification also on the whole district from Moncton to Winnipeg? Surely the importance of it was worth the while of the commission, in the first place, to grant an investigation from Winnipeg to Moncton, and if they did not do it, then it is for this House to take the matter in hand.
I now come to a point which I think will be of interest to members of this House, because it bears most directly on the necessity for a thorough investigation, I refer to the arbitration that was to take place last summer by Mr. Lumsden, Mr. Kelliher and Mr. Schreiber, the last being the third arbitrator called in. In the first place, I say that if ever there has been anything in the whole conduct of the construction of this road that reflects upon the Transcontinental Commission, and through it on the members of the government of the day-because the government countenanced and tacitly approved of all the Transcontinental Commission did-if I say, there is anything that establishes the discredit of
that commission it is the arbitration farce that proceeded in the matter of overclassification and overbreak during the months of May and June, 1909. Now what are the facts? Throughout the whole of 1908 and part of 1907, the Grand Trunk Pacific Company and the Transcontinental Commission had been unable to agree in the matter of classification. Objections had been filed early in 1907, they continued throughout all of 1908. The summer was the only time, admittedly, when arbitration proceedings could be intelligently gone on with. But the harvest was past, the summer was ended, and nothing was done. The Minister of Railways has been pleased to account for the delay by ascribing it entirely to the officials of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and quoting Mr. Lumsden as his authority. But I can equally well quote Mr. Kelliher, and Mr. Woods, and Mr. Chamberlain as authorities for stating that the delay was caused just as much by the Transcontinental Commission as by the Grand Trunk Pacific. In the month of May, when the Prime Minister wrote the letter which was quoted by the Minister of Railways, in which he asked for an investigation, and when he stated that, as a result of that letter, proceedings were at once taken for an investigation, I say that he stated what was incorrect, and what this return proves to be incorrect. It is a remarkable fact that in the month of May, the Hodgins investigation was taking place, it is a remarkable fact that throughout this month and the previous month, the press and members of the government were contending that there was no over-classification. At any rate, on the 11th of May, the first minister writes to the Transcontinental Commission and suggests that an inquiry be instituted, and suggests the appointment of an arbitration board. Notwithstanding the fact that the letter was written at that time, and that it was answered by the chairman of the commission with the assertion that proceedings had already been instituted, there is no record to show that until the 22nd of July, or over two months after, the first step had been taken towards pushing these arbitration proceedings. Mr. Lumsden's letter written in October, says that on the 22nd of July last he wrote a letter to Mr. Kelliher asking that an arbitration be started. So the letter of the Prime Minister, whether it was intended to be peremptory or not, at all events had no peremptory effect, because they stood still until the 22nd of July. Then one dilatory step was taken and then another, until the winter came on; and then the letters of Mr. Lumsden and Mr. Kelliher show that to attempt an arbitration xn the winter months was an absolute farce, that no arbi-

tration and no investigation eould take place when snow was on the ground. I commend these words to the Minister of Railways, who assured this House yesterday that since the 18th of November, and during the winter of 1909 when snow was on the ground, arbitration has actually proceeded. These words in the House, and the statement made -by the minister's own engineer on previous occasions mean that the present arbitration also is an absolute farce.
Well, after a while, and after much correspondence, an arbitration board is constituted in the winter months. They can do nothing until May. In the letter appointing Mr. Schreiber as third arbitrator, in the very last sentence of that letter, it is stated that if he accepts, a formal submission to the arbitration board will be drawn up for execution. Mr. Schreiber accepted, his acceptance appears appended to that letter. And notwithstanding the fact that the engineer, with the authority of the Transcontinental Commission, signed that letter and assured Mr. Schreiber and all interested in the arbitration, that a formal submission would be drawn up for execution, no such formal submission was ever executed by the commission, or by any one representing it. A formal submission was drawn up by the Grand Trunk Pacific, a very fair, a very comprehensive, a very useful document, but the Transcontinental Commission knew too much about the game to sign that and they further knew too much about the game to give the actual reasons why they refused to execute it, I stated in reference to the submission that it was a very fair and reasonable one. I want to read that submission, I want to read the agreement that the Grand Trunk Pacific laid before the Transcontinental Railway Commission for execution and to ask the members of this House whether it was not a fair and reasonable agreement and whether it was too comprehensive as it was at a much later time stated to be by the Transcontinental Railway Commission. At page 17 of the return that agreement ap-ppnrs The usual recitals appear in the first place setting forth the fact that an Act of parliament calls for the arbitration of all differences, and the fact that differences have arisen. Then, it goes on to say:
Therefore this agreement witnesseth that the following question dn regard to the specifications and the work in respect of which the said engineers have differed shall be submitted for determination to the said engineers and the said Collingwood Schreiber, Esquire, as third arbitrator, namely
(a) The interpretation of the specifications as applied to the actual work, each party under this heading to be at liberty to ask for the construction or interpretation of any particular clause of the specifications not already Mr. MEIGHEN.
approved by the engineers and such construction or interpretation when given to be conclusive as to all work already done, and to be thereafter binding in regard to all future work to he done.
is that unreasonable? is there anything ;:i fear by an honest Transcontinental Railway Commission or by honest engineers in asking that certain clauses which may coni in an ambiguity, or which may be difficult of interpretation, shall be settled as to their interpretation, once and for all? Nothing unfair to my mind.
(b) Classification of material handled by contractors in the formation of the roadbed, or incident to other work forming part of any of the contracts on the eastern division.
Surely it will be in the interest at least of the people of this country, if it is not in the interest of the commission, that that natter shall be investigated. Glassification of material handled by contractors. The technical point is raised and is persisted in with a steadfastness, a perpetuity, if I may use the word, that would never be expected of the most technical lawyer in a court of law, .that unless you put in your objection at a specified time and put in your objection to a certain mile there is nothing to dispute over as to that and consequently nothing to investigate. As Mr. Kelliher and Mr. Lumsden went over the road, if Mr. Kelliher found something that was over-classified, could not he object then and would not that be a question in dispute? Would not a question in dispute be raised the moment Mr. Kelliher said: There is over-classification and Mr. Kelliher having stated that and that point in dispute having arisen, was it not in the interest of the people of the country that that point in dispute be settled there and not be relegated to obscurity and refused settlement for all time? Surely it was. Would it not have been absolutely fair to have investigated a dispute raised by Mr. Kelliher on the ground? He is looking over the work. He goes over a mile and he says: There is over-classification amounting to 100, or 200, or 500 per cent and I want you to investigate that. If Mr. Lumsden did not agree with him let Mr. Collingwood Schreiber decide it. That is what the Grand Trunk Pacific asked for and that is what the commission refused. The attitude of the commission on that point is consistent only with the proposition that they wanted to confine the limits of the overbreak and over-classification, they wanted to confine the dollars that the country had lost in the construction of this road by these frauds-and these incompetencies of various people in order that Liberal politicians might go through the country and say, as did the hon. member for Carleton: Why, there is only two per cent; there is only $1,000,000 out of $50,000,000. That could

have been the only result. They could not have had the interests of the people at heart. They could not have cared one single straw for the treasury of this country, or thev would not have allowed the Grand Trunk Pacific to have raised objections and refused to have allowed these to be fairly and amicably settled by the tribunal appointed to discharge this duty under an Act of parliament. This agreement goes on:
(c)	Payment to contractors for handling material in cutting in excess of the theoretic section to be excavated, whether caused by slides, excessive use of explosives or otherwise, and commonly termed overbreak.
They wanted that investigated, but the commission refused to investigate that unless it also was bound within the narrow and frigid letters which happily Mr. Woods happened to write on a previous occasion and since the 10th January. The commission not only absolutely refused to investigate anything except such as was within each specific mile post embodied in Mir. Woods' letters, but they refused to investigate anything embodied in Mr. Woods' letters prior to the 10th January, 1908. Later, the Transcontinental railway secretary of the commission addressed to Mr. Schreiber, as appears in the return under date of about the 20th January, 1909, a letter which shows clearly that the commission had absolutely made up their minds that no objection, however specific, raised by Mr. Woods, prior to the 10th January, 1908, would be allowed to be investigated. They shut the door first to all objections raised on the ground, they shut the door to Mr. Woods' objections wherein he says the whole division is wrong, they shut the door lastly, and they locked it, and said that no matter how .specific your objections, if they were made before the 10th January, 1908, they are shut within a dark closet and you cannot investigate them now. Then they go on. Here is a general clause and could [DOT]anything be fairer?
(d)	All other matters not included in the foregoing but which may properly form the subject to arbitration under clause 7.
How could anything be fairer? Everything that could properly form the subject of arbitration under clause 7 of the Act passed by this parliament in 1903 should be investigated. Let me ask any member of the government who may be present-[DOT] and if there are none present who know anything about it, then let me ask any hon. member of this House who is interested in the people's behalf-what right had the commission, what jurisdiction had the Minister of Railways and Canals to limit the powers of investigation granted by the House of Commons in an Act passed in 1903?

In reference to that motion, I have only to say that I cannot accept it at all as a reasonable censure on the government, or as a reasonable censure on the minister. It is true that when a prolonged debate occurs, as in this case, the ministers have to leave the House occasionally. It is true that at this present moment the minister in charge of this particular question is not in the House, but at the same time there are ministers here. We have frequently seen what is practically the same thing on the other side of the House. Members on the front bench of the opposition make a motion, then leave the House, pay no more attention to it afterwards in any shape or form, and even leave the House during the speeches which are being made by members on that side. A rule of this kind should certainly work both ways. It should work on one side just as much as it does on the other. When a debate is prolonged to a very consider-, able extent, one cannot expect that any one individual or any number of individuals shall remain in the House during the whole time of the debate. I regret very much indeed that members frequently leave the House, and that applies to all members. That is perhaps one of the reasons why our sessions are so prolonged. But it comes with ill grace from any^ member of the opposition to take exception to that condition which they so largely bring

about, or to oast a reflection upon the Minister- of Railways who is one of the hardest working ministers of the Crown, and who attends as constantly and continuously to his arduous duties as any member of any government ever did. I feel- under these circumstances that the strictures made by the hon. member (Mr. Foster) are entirely uncalled for.

speechtext:
I wa3 referring, before this very convenient recess took place, tc the celebrated memorandum of the 10th ol Mr. FISHER.
January, 1908, which the Minister of Railways assured us yesterday he was the father of,-I am very glad, indeed, to see that the Minister of Public Works appears on the scene in this debate as in much the same manner he flitted over the scene in the Transcontinental Commission correspondence, just at the close of the incident. That memorandum of the 10th of January purports to be made in pursuance of clause 7 of the agreement, ratified by the Act of parliament of 1903, and it reads:
Monthly estimates for contractors shall be submitted promptly from time to time by the chief engineer of the commissioners to the company's assistant chief engineer at Montreal for approval. If he has any objection to such estimates he shall promptly file the same with the chief engineer of the commissioners, and any objections from time te time filed shall thereupon be considered, and, if possible, determined by the said engineers, and in case of their failure to agree, may then or at any time before or at the time of the final payment, at the option of either party, be considered and determined by arbitration as provided in the agreement of the 29tli July, 1903, but in no ease shall the payment of monthly estimates be delayed except with the consent of the commissioners.
Now, that agreement purports to be in. pursuance of the Act of parliament of 1903 -I am sorry to say the Minister of Railways avows himself the father of it-but tljat agreement distinctly limits the operation of that Act of parliament, confines the powers of arbitrations, restricts within very narrow limits the possibilities of arbitration, and confines within bounds so as to render almost useless the only protection that the people of this country had under the Act of 1903. I want to know by what authority the Minister of Railways or the Transcontinental Commission limited the powers of arbitration granted by the Act of parliament within the narrow confines of the memorandum of the 10th of January? What right had the Minister of Railways and what right had the Transcontinental Commission to say that matters that might have been arbitrated under the statute cannot hereafter be arbitrated. I say that the ingenuity and purpose of that agreement is only too plain, and I say that it has worked disastrously for the people of this country. However, the winter months passed and the arbitration board proceeded to its work on the 21st May, 1909, and finished their work on division ' F ' on the 5th day of June of that year. During that time Mr. Collingwood Schrei-ber, in whom the Minister of Finance professed such unlimited confidence, Mr. Lumsden, who was the choice of all engineers of the world as the chief engineer of the Trancontinental, and Mr. Kelli-her, selected by the Grand Trunk as their chief engineer, devoted their time to an

investigation of the classification and overbreak on district * F I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if the argument of the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., is right: that after the work was done no classification could be made that could compare with the work of the engineers on the spot at the time of excavation, then, surely Mr. Lumsden, and Mr. Kelliher, and Mr. Col-lingwood Schreiber would not have addressed themselves to a task, which, if the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., (Mr. Car-vell) is correct, they must have known was a farce from beginning to end. Surely, they were in a position to make the classification or else they would not have come back, and while not presenting a formal report, practically reported through the mouth of Mr. Lumsden that they found against the honesty or the competency of the classification that had been made. The very words of Mr. Lumsden, and the tacit concurrence in them of Mr. Collingwood Schreiber and Mr. Kelliher, give denial to the argument of the hon. member (Mr. Car-vell) that it is impossible to properly classify such work, unless the engineers were there when the actual excavations were made. They finished with district ' F ' oyer which Mr. Foulin presided, on the 5th of June, and on the 6th of June they proceeded to district ' B ' and finished there on the 22nd of that month. These three men, the most competent engineers in the country, the choice of the government, considered that they competently did discharge their duties, and they must be conceived to have acted honestly. Now then, I say that the facts in connection with that arbitration which appear from the record as brought down by the government, facts that are undeniable on the very face of that return, clearly show that no sooner did that board which was the creation of the Transcontinental Commission, with the ratification of the government; no sooner did these men finish their work than the Transcontinental Railway Commission started to wreck it. No sooner was the work of their own arbitration board completed, and no sooner had they got an inkling of what their finding was, than they set deliberately to work to wreck the rejport, and if possible obviate the possibility of a report at all.
On what do I base that? It is a remarkable coincidence, and I notice that this has already been brought to the attention of the Minister of Railways or he would pay more attention to it, he knows it as well as I do, he absolutely knows that it is impossible on reasonable grounds to believe that the letters of Messrs. Poulin, Doucet and Huestes were written otherwie than at the instigation or with the concurrence of the Transcontinental Commission, in the light of the return brought down. The Minister of Railways asked this House, whether, if we had been engineers in the case of Messrs. Poulin and Doucet we would not have acted exactly as they did. I tell the minister no, and I say further that no engineer could possibly have done so, acting as a reasonable man, if he conceived he was being wronged by an arbitration board. What does Poulin do? Notwithstanding the fact that the work of arbitrating on the over-classification on section ' F ', his own section, was finished on June 5, he sits silent under it and says not a word until June 22, about two and a half weeks afterwards. How does the minister explain that, that a man so grossly wronged as Poulin said he was, by his own superior officer, would not protest or open his mouth until the 22nd day of June, some 16 days after the whole work was done. It is a remarkable fact also, and I do not need to draw this to the minister's attention, because he knows it, that Poulin says nothing from his head office in Winnipeg, nothing from the ground, but he waits until he gets down here, within the sanctum or within the influence of the Transcontinental Commission, and there makes known his complaint, because his letter is dated not from Winnipeg, but from Ottawa on the 22nd of June, 1909. Not only that but section ' B ' was finished on June 22, the very day that Mr. Poulin made his complaint. Mr. Doucet immediately, on the 23rd of June, the very day after Mr. Poulin makes his complaint, also writes to the chairman of the Transcontinental Commission and complains as well. The same day that occurs Mr. Huestes writes a memorandum and makes his complaint. Let me say to the minister that neither he nor any other man can justify these district engineers in making their first complaint to the Transcontinental Railway Commission instead of through the medium of their own superior officer, Mr. Lumsden, except on the hypothesis that the whole thing was instigated by the Transcontinental Railway Commission itself. Furthermore it is a remarkable fact that Mr. J. D. McArthur, the contractor on a large part if not all of district ' F ', about the same time and also two weeks after they got through with his work, by a wonderful coincidence writes to the chairman of the Transcontinental Railway Commission and he protests also against the work of the Arbitration Board. On the 22nd or 23rd of June, at the very time these engineers are making their protests, another remarkable coincidence occurs, and Messrs. Macdonell and O'Brien also write a letter to the chairman of the Transcontinental Commission, making complaint exactly along the line of Mr. McArthur's. It is also difficult to explain and it would be interesting to know the cause of a clause in Mr. McArthur's letter wherein he states that he is informed an examination of the district engineers

was made by the arbitration board, and as a matter of fact notwithstanding that sub-sequently_the commission upset the whole findings -of the arbitration board on the presumption that the engineers were not examined notwithstanding the fact that Mr. McArthur says they were. We have all those facts coinciding. We have Mr. Doucet's letter written from Ottawa on the 22nd of June, Mr. Huestes' memorandum written on the 23rd, and Mr. Poulin's on the 23rd, all along the same line, and we have Mr. McArthur's letter on the 19th and Mr. Macdonell's on the 23rd. How do you explain the fact that all those men came to write on the very same line to the chairman of the Transcontinental Railway Commission, all to the same man, just at about the same time, and for the same obvious effect? Surely that is not a coincidence. What do they do? What does this Railway Commission, in which the Minister of Railways places such confidence do? A most remarkable thing, and for that act no other is responsible than the government of this country and the Minister of Railways in particular, because that act was made known at once to the Minister of Railways by a letter from the secretary of the Transcontinental Railway Commission and there is no protest against it and the Minister of Railways subsequently concurs in the action of the Transcontinental Railway Commission wherein they disallow and utterly condemn the work of the first arbitration board.
The commission did the following with the tacit concurrence of the Minister of Railways: On June 25, at IX o'clock in the morning, the commission held a meeting, and they read the letters written to them by Messrs. Doucet, Huestes and Poulin. They also read the letters written by Messrs. McArthur and Macdonell & O'Brien, and in the light of those letters, taking those letters as correct, even although those letters assumed that Mr. Col-lingwood Schreiber, in whom the government have absolute confidence, Mr. Lums-den, the man whom they appointed themselves, and Mr. Kelliher, acted like perfect school boys, the Transcontinental Railway Commission, with the concurrence of this Minister of Railways took those letters without question and immediately stamped the whole proceedings as illegal. Sir, if it is unfair and wrong, as the Minister of Railways contended yesterday, for any one to find these district engineers guilty without a hearing-and nobody asked that they should be found guiltv without a hearing- was it not far more wrong, was it not an outrage, for the Transcontinental Commission on June 25, to pronounce on the authority of engineers, without the other parties being heard, that Messrs. Lumsden and Kelliher and Schreiber had been so abso-Mr. MEIGHEN.
lutely derelict in their duty, had so absolutely forgotten the fidelity they owed to the people of this country, as to upset without a hearing the finding these three engineers on the authority of understrappers.
The Minister of Railways yesterday pronounced as an outrage in a hypothetical case that he ascribed to the mover of the amendment, an act which he himself condoned on the 25th of June, 1909, an act which on that day was certainly outdone by the Transcontinental Railway Commission that absolutely overtopped anything that would be done were we to find these men guilty without a hearing; and the Minister of Railways, by his tacit concurrence in that act is responsible for that outrage on the 25th of June last. There is no reasonable deduction from this correspondence other than that a deliberate conspiracy was entered into on that day to annihilate the report of that .arbitration board simply because it resulted in finding a large amount of over-classification which would have brought discredit on this government and on this country, and if there is any bad faith to examine, if there is reason for an investigation with the object of finding bad faith, this government and the right hon. the First Minister who moved for this committee, would far better act in the service of the people if they investigated bad faith on the part of their own commission instead of (as they only pretend to do) on the part of certain unmentioned understrappers on the engineering force.
The Transcontinental Railway Commission, at 11 o'clock in the morning on the 25th of June, pronounced the following remarkable words on the authority of letters written to them, which should never have been written to them, in reference to the conduct of Messrs. Schreiber, Kelliher and Lumsden:
Whereas, it is inconceivable that proceedings of such great importance, and possibly involving a very large sum of money, and which may result in much expensive and troublesome litigation between the contractors and the commissioners, should have been conducted in such a hasty and superficial manner, without a sufficient hearing being grant-to the engineers on the work.
If Mr. Collingwood Schreiber was guilty of inconceivable conduct, if he was guilty of conducting a great public duty, in a-hasty and superficial manner, why does the government, and why does the Minister of Railways, assent to his appointment again on the same arbitration board? Surely, if he was guilty of such conduct as that, if he was so absolutely forgetful of the duty he owed to the people of this country and to the government, he is not a fit man to .conduct proceedings of such importance. But they go further and ar-
2570

gue-and here is a most remarkable thing -that Mr, Schreiber, Mr. Lumsden and Mr. Kelliher, in the course of that investigation, proceeded along lines of this awful memorandum of submission which I read to the House some time ago, and which called for no more and no less than arbitration on matters that were properly the subject of arbitration under clause 7 of the Act passed by this parliament. Because they did such a heinous thing, because they so absolutely forgot their duty to the country as to follow the provisions of this Act of parliament instead of doing as directed by the Transcontinental Railway Commission, their whole finding is illegal and void. Did anybody ever hear of such an argument? Can the Transcontinental Railway Commission or the government of Canada produce a reputable lawyer who will say that, because they proceeded under the authority of a form of submission which provided only that such matters should be submitted to them as provided by Act of parliament, therefore the whole proceeding must be upset for illegality? The Transcontinental Commission had no authority whatever for that statement. Furthermore, there is nothing to show that the arbitrators had proceeded under that authority. But even if they had, Mr. Collingwood Schreiber was justified in doing so by the very document to which the Transcontinental Commission is a party. In the document appointing him and which he signed, it is clearly stated that a form of submission would be presented to him. It was never presented to him, unless it was the form of submission under which, they charge, they acted; they never presented any other. And when they refused the form of submission which was sent, they did not apprise him of the fact. They, wrote, if not to their own engineer, then to Mr. Kelliher, that they did not see any necessity for it. If the Commission wanted to be above board in the matter, why did they not say that it would be illegal to proceed along that line and state specifically their objections to that form of submission, instead of saying in an offhand way: 'We do not think any submission is necessary?'
On June 25, at eleven o'clock in the morning, these gentlemen, or three of them, held a meeting to pass a resolution, which is reported at page 30, protesting against the proceedings of the arbitrator as being ' improper and illegal,' in that they were based in all or in part on the draft agreement of May 14, 1909, which had been rejected, and which had no existence in fact-and for that they had the authority only of a district engineer under Mr. Lumsden, and against it they gave Mr. Lumsden, Mr. Kelliher and Mr. Colling-82
wood Schreiber no hearing at all. The report goes on:-
That the engineers on the line who classified the work were not afforded a sufficient hearing or an opportunity of presenting evidence.
What right had they to say that the engineers must be heard by the arbitration board? Did the Act of 1903 say that arbitrations should be upset by the Transcontinental Railway Commission unless these engineers, who were charged with being guilty of wrong-doing, were on the spot to argue the matter out? I do not think so. But, further, Mr. McArthur's letter was by that time in the hands of the Commission in which it was stated that the engineers were heard before the arbi tration board.
Again, I ask the Minister of Railways and Canals-though I know he will not listen- and I ask the Secretary of State (Hon. Mr. Murphy), did the Act of parliament state that contractors must be heard before the proceedings could be legal? The Minister of Railways and Canals said the findings would be of no use unless they were heard, because the government wanted such evidence as would be taken bv the Exchequer Court. The minister is not a lawyer, and I do not pose as a very great lawyer myself. Still, it does not require a great lawyer to know that even if they had been heard the evidence would not be binding upon them before the Exchequer Court. Evidence against a third party would not be taken by a court in a subsequent case. So the hon. minister's argument falls to the ground, though I confess that it had the best face of any that could be given in support of clause (D) of the resolution of this Transcontinental Commission of June 25th last. They say that the contractors were not heard. That was a significant statement. But there is the significant fact that, on the 19th of June, when the conspiracy referred to was being hatched, Mr. McArthur wrote a letter saying he was not heard before the arbitration board, and he protested against it. Yet, on the second arbitration board being formed, and Mr. McArthur notified, he immediately writes to the commission that he has nothing to do with the arbitration and does not want to be heard. Is it not most remarkable that the commissioners should upset the findings of an arbitration on the ground that the contractors were not heard, when in the first place, there was no legal authority for their being heard, and, in the second piace, they did not want to be heard? After the commission makes the finding condemning Mr. Lumsden, Mr. Kelliher and Mr. Schreiber as being superficial, as being derelict in their duty-as well paraphrased by the hon. member for Carleton- as not knowing what they were talking about

-Mr. Lumsden resigns. The Minister of Railways said there was no justification for his resigning. There will be plenty of opportunity for the Minister of Railways to answer, but surely he will never contend before any sane audience that an engineer, the head official under a commission, could possibly retain his office after being censured in such language by his superiors, by the very board that had appointed him- being called, almost in plain words, a school boy and told that he was derelict in his trust. Under such conditions no self-respecting man could retain his job. The minister said that he did not know whether the letter was written before the meeting or after it, but if he had read the return he would have seen that it was pointed out under the authority of the chairman that Mr. Lumsden resigned after the meeting held at eleven o'clock in the morning. What is the authority for the hon. member for Pictou and the Minister of Railways and Canals saying that Mr. Lumsden resigned in a huff because his men disobeyed his instructions? He could do nothing but resign, and the Minister of Railways knows it. And, what is more, the Transcontinental Commission knew that he could do nothing but resign, and that is why they passed the resolution on the 25th of June. They intended that he should resign, and that there should be no doubt about it, and not only that he should resign as engineer, but they made sure also that he should resign as arbitrator as well. Read , his second letter of June 26th:
Ottawa, June 26. 1909.
The Commissioners of the Transcontinental
Railway,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sirs,-
How he must have emphasized the adjective.
