I stated that I have lost confidence in the engineering staff, I would like to state .that this does not apply to the whole staff, but applies only to a portion of the staff who were responsible for the measurement, classification, supervision and inspection of considerable portions in district ' B ' and east of Rennie Crossing in district 'I" lately gone over by me.

maintopic: HUGH D. LUMSDEN.

speechtext:
Apd here is a most significant postscript.
P.S. In order to make the matter clear, I may say I assume my resignation as chief engineer also carries with it my resignation as arbitrator in matters of dispute with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, but as there is a doubt raised by you, I also resign as arbitrator.

maintopic: HUGH D. LUMSDEN.

speechtext: So, to be absolutely certain that the work of wreck was complete, that they had utterly annihilated the work of this arbitra

maintopic: HUGH D. LUMSDEN.
speechtext: tion board which was so disastrous to them, they come to Lumsden after he has resigned on the 25th of June, and say there is a doubt whether he was not still arbitrator and he had better remove that doubt. And so, he resigns as arbitrator too. Surely they must be given credit at least for the greatest possible efficiency in carrying out their evident determination of having Mr. Lumsden out of the road and the arbitration proceedings made null and void.

maintopic: HUGH D. LUMSDEN.
speechtext: Was that expression of doubt verbal?

maintopic: HUGH D. LUMSDEN.
speechtext:
There is a distinction between this intimation on ,the part of Mr., Lumsden, and other intimations of Mr. Lumsden. that seem to favour the contention of the board. Mr. Lumsden says over his own signature that the doubt as to this was raised by the members of the Transcontinental Commission, whereas ail these statements of the board launched out before the public to the effect that engineers on the ground are the only persons who can make a competent estimate, were made only on the authority of the Transcontinental Commission, as a memo, by the secretary.
Now we go on. The work of wreckage, they contend, is complete. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company take another view; they say that notwithstanding the fact that Mr. Lumsden resigned, his successor is ex-officio arbitrator, and notwithstanding the fact that he resigned as arbitrator, there is nothing to hinder Mr. Sohreiber making his report. There may be some doubt about that. There is no doubt in my opinion that the work of the arbitration board up to that point. was absolutely valid; at all events, the Grand Thunk Pacific claimed that it was valid, notwithstanding the resignation of Mr. Lumsden. At all events, if .the Grand Trunk Pacific were content to call it valid, there -was no reason why the commission should not call it valid, too. But they chose not to do so. They say: No, we want things done de novo, and we will try a new man, we want some different resiult. Then what occurs? They go ahead and appoint a new arbitration board, and after a long time they start again, notwithstanding the protest of the Grand Trunk Pacific. But in the meantime there is a remarkable coincidence. On the 25th of June, Mr. Lumsden writes his letter of resignation, he says in that letter that there has been overclassification carried on to a very large amount. He says that owing to this, and owing to the disregard of his instructions, he has lost confidence in the staff. That letter was written to the Minister of Railways or to the commission; at all events, the commission transmitted it to the minister on the 25th of June. The Minister of Railways was in the city on the 26th day

of June, and until the 30th of June, 1909, because on the 30th of June there is a nice letter pTit on file by the minister, and I must compliment him on the graceful language he uses. He writes to Mr. Lumsden, who has been in the plainest way fired by the commission, or has been put in a position where his self-respect demanded his resignation. The minister writes thus on the 30th of June:
Dear Sir,-I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 25th instant, inclosing correspondence sent by you to the Transcontinental Railway Commissioners, and also proffering your resignation as chief engineer. It will be considered in due course.
That must have been news to Mr. Lumsden; at all events, it shows that the Minister of Railways was in the city from the 25th day of June to the 30th. Later on he evidently went across the water, 'because on the 31st of Augwst he writes a letter to the Transcontinental Railway Commission. And I want to say that I cannot understand this correspondence on any other hypothesis than that it was born of a laudable ambition on the part of the Minister of Railways to make the correspondence look as nice as possible, to give it a high moral tone, notwithstanding the awful facts that had transpired. I cannot see anything in it but a nice piece of stage-play. Here is the letter, and I invite the attention of the House to the matter, because the spectacle of the Minister of Railways breaking the bread of official fidelity to the Transcontinental Commission, is a most inspiring one. The letter is found on page 48:
Dear Mr. Parent,-As I was leaving for Europe some time ago the resignation of the chief engineer of the commission, Mr. Lumsden, was received, and X left it with my colleagues for consideration. I find on my return-
Remember, the Minister of Railways did not find this until he got back. During the five days he was in Ottawa it did not come to his notice.
-I find on my return that in his letter of resignation Mr. Lumsden intimated that he had lost confidence in certain of his staff. 1 have no doubt that this intimation is unnecessary, hut wish to emphasize the government's attitude in this matter. Should it he found that any member of the staff has been dishonest or wilfully negligent in the performance of his duty he should he summarily dealt with.
Now, that must have been news to the Transcontinental Commission.
What you desire and what we all desire is justice to all parties and the fullest protection of the public interest. Any employee who has forgotten this, or has failed to act on this principle, cannot be retained for a moment.
Now surely the Minister of Railways will concede that if there was any occasion for 82J
writing a letter like that to the Transcontinental Commission, he must have had grave doubts as to the fidelity with which that commission was discharging its duties. So it looks to me as a piece of stage play, put on in order to make the correspondence look wholesome. Then the chairman of the Transcontinental Commission, not to be lacking in his share of the pantomine, comes forward and writes thus to the Minister of Railways, he actually expresses the startling fact that the minister's view's that dishonest officials must be fired, exactly coincides with his own; and the Minister of Railways, with sober face, read that correspondence to the House as emphasizing the high moral tone which the government of this country adopts in connection with the Transcontinental Railway. It does seem strange that notwithstanding the fact that the minister was here for five days, and that he discussed the matter with his colleagues, as appears by his letter, he never noticed Mr. Lumsden's statement that he had lost confidence in his staff until two months afterwards, and he never thought there was any occasion, during the whole of two months, to preach the doctrine of honesty to the chairman of the Transcontinental Commission. The chairman of the Transcontinental Commission actually goes on to say:
Should any reasonable proof be brought that employees in our service have been guilty of serious negligence or wrong-doing, yon can rest assured that the commissioners would deal prompt justice, as we have done already in several cases.
But the whole correspondence up to that point, and subsequently, shows that there was no object so dear to the chairman of that commission as to see that all the avenues of proof should be closed, so far as he could close them. Now for two years the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company were paraded in this country, during the election campaign of 1904, as the guardian of the people's rights in the matter of the construction of this road. The electors were told that the company was in such a position that they had actually to fight the battles of the people in order to preserve their own rights. Then the railway company, during two years, urges and struggles with the chairman of the commission that a proper and complete investigation be made of all matters complained of. Throughout those two years we have the spectacle of the chairman and the commission resisting, with every weapon in their power, the attempt of the Grand Trunk Pacific to preserve their own rights, and through them in some degree the people's rights. If the powers had been granted to that arbitration board, or to the second arbitration board which is now in existence, the powers which the Grand Trunk Pacific so ably con-

tended should be granted, then there would not be so much reason for the amendment of the hon. member for South Simcoe as there is. It is because the request made throughout those years by that company that the investigation should be thorough, was denied by the commission, that there is all the more need for an investigation now. What supports the position I take that the railway company, throughout these years, struggled for a complete investigation? Turn to page 52 of the return. Mr, Chamberlin, vice-president and general manager of the company writes as follows to the chairman of the commission under *date of September 15, 1909:
Dear Sir,-Referring to conversation had with you to-day relative to Arbitration Committee.
We are ready to have the commission go on with their examination, and consent to their re-examining matters complained of and looked into by the former commission consisting of Mr. Collingwood Sehreiber, third arbitrator, Mr. Hugh D. Lumsden, government engineer and Mr. B. B. Kelliher as chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific.
X presume this committee will start their examination from Winnipeg and work east to Moncton.
That is a presumption that unfortunately Mr. Parent could not agree with.
Mr. Kelliher is now in Winnipeg, and will be ready to start any day which will suit the *convenience of Mr. Sehreiber and Mr. Grant. Will you kindly advise me as early as possible when Mr. Grant and Mr. Sehreiber will be ready to start, so that we may arrange the affairs of our engineering department accordingly-	.	.	.	,
VVe trust that this examination will be very thorough and will be continued over the entire line, taking up and settling all matters under question.
That is a simple trust and one would think an honest and useful trust, but the commission, having the interests of this country at heart, could not coincide in it. Right on the next page, in a letter dated the 18th September, Mr. Chamberlin says:
I am quite willing as you propose and as mentioned in my former letter, that the arbitrators should go over all questions in dispute from the beginning, letting the two engineers discuss all differences on the ground as they go along and where they cannot agree call in Mr. Sehreiber.
And that also is a willingness, in which the chairman of the Railway Commission, as guardian of the people's rights, refused to coincide. Then, on page 55, Mr. Chamberlin still urgently presses the same point. In a letter dated Winnipeg, 8th October, 1909, and addressed to Mr. Parent, he says:
You seem to misunderstand position Grand Trunk Pacific railway. My agreement with you which is outlined in your letter fifteenth was that all differences were to be discussed on the ground in accordance with article Mr. MEIGHEN.
seven of the agreement between the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and your government, and we are ready at any time to proceed on that basis. Mr. Grant declined to discuss and settle differences as above suggested, therefore delay rests entirely with your commission.
Mr. Grant refused to proceed on the lines laid-down by the parliament of Canada under clause 7 of the agreement of 1903, and he persisted in proceeding within the narrow, small and almost useless limits of the agreement of the 10th January, 1910, of which the Minister of Railways boasts that he himself is the father. On page 58, Mr. Chamberlin still continues the same struggle-the struggle that we are continuing now.
Have wired Kelliher

He says under date of October 5:
To sign letter appointing third arbitrator and to proceed at once with arbitration, as per our letters. Trust you instruct Mr. Grant to make examination thorough, and to take all the time necessary to settle all differences between Winnipeg and Moncton.
If the commission had agreed to make a thorough investigation and discuss the difference between Winnipeg and Moncton the matter would have gone ahead, but they did not agree, they have not agreed yet, and consequently the amendment is absolutely imperative if the public interests are to be protected. At page 59 Mr. Ryan, secretary of the commission, writes instructions to Mr. Grant that if Mr. Kelliher re-, fuses to go on within the narrow limits of the subsidiary agreement then they must stop altogether. He says:
Kelliher's attitude again delaying arbitration. Persistence in this will perhaps indefinitely delay it. If he adheres to refusal to sign joint letter, your instructions are to return to Ottawa. Show this telegram to Killi-her, and advise result.
Then Mr. Chamberlin says on October 6:
We now find engineer Grant refused to take up anything but a few specific cases and not make arbitration cover all matters in dispute as you agreed when I saw you in Ottawa, and by your letter later, therefore Mr. Kelliher rightly refused to go on with arbitration. When Mr. Grant is prepared to take up all matters in dispute, Mr, Kelliher will be ready to meet him.
But Mr. Grant was not so prepared, because the commission refused to let him be so prepared. Then at page 60 Mr. Parent writes to Mr. Chamberlin on October 7, as follows:
For reasons which have been explained it is in the public interest-
Mr. Parent is very fond of that expression :
-that these differences should be promptly adjusted, and I hope, therefore, that you will

instruct Mr. Kellilier to prevent further delay by consenting to sign the ioint letter, and proceed at the earliest possible date in the matter.
At page 61 Mr. Gordon Grant admits the whole point in a letter dated October 11, to the chairman of the commission. Mr. Grant says:
Mr. ICelliher also insisted in spite of the advice of the Deputy Minister of Justice to the contrary that I had no say in the appointment of a third arbitrator, that Mr. Lumsden's previous choice of Mr. Schreiber still held, and that another joint letter was not necessary. This, of course, was all in accordance with his instructions dated September 18. Not only was this the attitude assumed by Mr. Kellilier, but he also informed me that, before we went out, I would have to sign a formal agreement or submission similar to the one previously prepared by the authorities of the Grand Trunk Pacific.
So that if Mr. Grant had been willing to sign the general agreement which I read to the House the first arbitration authorized by the government and bv parliament in 1903 would have been ready to go on, but Mr. Grant refused and the commission backed him up in refusing to allow the law laid down by this House in 1903 and which at that time was considered ample for the protection of the people's interest to be carried out; consequently the arbitration was delayed in 1908 and 1909. I might go on but surely the Minister of Railways will admit that the point is established. On October 21 the point is again raised by Mr. Kelliher and the letters all through that period establish the same contention. The matter is still in dispute. The deadlock still ensues, the deadlock which the Minister of Railways was able to remove, but the deadlock which was only removed when the serene presence of the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugslev), appeared on the scene about the 18th November last. It is a strange thing, it is a matter certainlv that this return does not explain, but it is a remarkable fact that just as soon as the Minister of Public Works, carrying peace and blessing in his train, appears upon the scene in the middle of November last the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, with a complacency childlike in the extreme, without any explanation, without any introductory letters, without any reason being given, without anything to explain it, quietly submit in toto to the contention of the Transcontinental Railway Commission, evidently under the spell of the Minister of Public Works. Now, Sir, an agreement appears on page 74 of the return under which the whole thing is submitted to arbitration and absolutely within the limits urged by Mr. Gordon Grant throughout this controversy. What
explanation can be offered for this docility? What explanation can be offered for the rapidity with which the Grand Trunk Pacific, the guardian of the people's rights, the only guardian of them, threw down the bulwarks behind which they had been doing battle all along and without qualification coincided with the contention of Mr. Grant and of the Transcontinental Railway Commission? Under mat submission this board of arbitration now can only arbitrate as to matters specially mentioned in letters prior to 10th January, 1908, and subsequent letters wherein specific points are mentioned such as are in conformity with the limited agreement of the 10th January. The whole contention disappears. All the clouds of difficulty are removed in a moment, the sun shines serene and the whole operation of this arbitration board is limited, as the hon. member for Carleton correctly says to the two per cent difference contended for all along by Mr. Grant and the commission. That is the whole history of the affair. There is quite a little stage play which it may be interesting to glance at. After Mr. Grant had written repeatedly to the Transcontinental Commission explaining Mr. Kelliher's attitude at Winnipeg and after Mr. Chamberlin had written to the Transcontinental Commission a letter in which he stated very innocently that the commission had called Mr. Lumsden back to Ottawa away from his duty as arbitrator, a letter appears on the file in which the secretary of the commission asked Mr. Grant to again report on this Kelliher matter. I have been unable to find what reason in the world there could be for that other report, and I should-be glad if any gentleman on the other side can explain. But here is where the stage play comes in. In the course of that report Mr. Grant very correctly says that he has covered the whole matter in former reports so far as Kelliher's conduct is concerned, but he says that Mr. Chamberlin's letter saying that the commission called Mr. Lumsden back to Ottawa is incorrect. Now, what suggested to Mr. Gordon Grant to report on that point in Mr. Chamberlin's letter? Was not the whole purpose of that correspondence to, if possible, remove from the public mind the evidence of the conspiracy that Mr. Lumsden was called back. On page 67 of the return will be found the letter of the secretary of the Transcontinental Railway Commission and Mr. Grant's reply. The secretary very innocently asked Mr. Grant for a report, and inclosed Mr. Chamberlin's letter, and Mr. Grant replied:
With reference to Mr. Chamberlin's statement that Mr. Lumsden was called back to. Ottawa by the commission, I understand from you that you did not call Mr. Lumsden back

to Ottawa, and in the records of my office I find a letter addressed by Mr. Lumsden to Mr. Schreiber, dated June 22, 1909, in which
he says:-
Now, June 22nd is the date of the completion of the investigation in district 'B,i district 'F' having been gone over before; and as soon as the inspection was completed in district ' B ' Mr. Lumsden evidently wrote this letter to Mr. Schreiber:
As it is important that I should be in Ottawa on the 21th instant and the work of inspection of the Macdonell and O'Brien contract in connection with matters in dispute between the .chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and myself having been completed, I am unable to proceed further with the work at the present time.
Mr. Lumsden states in that letter, that it is important he should be in Ottawa on the 24th of the month, and I cannot see anything which would make that important, except that the commission wanted him there. Now, Mr. Grant's explanation of that paragraph in Mr. Lumsden's letter is:-
I understand from my secretary who was also Mr. Lumsden's secretary, that the first time he wrote this letter to Mr. Schreiber, Mr. Lumsden stated that it was important that he should be in England early next month, that is, he, in his second letter, changed ' England ' to ' Ottawa.'
There is a most peculiar thing there. Mr. Lumsden wrote saying he had to be in England early in July and Mr. Grant says on the authority of the secretary that he afterwards changed the word 'England' to 'Ottawa,' meaning that he had to be in Ottawa early next month.

maintopic: HUGH D. LUMSDEN.
speechtext: He said he only changed one word.

maintopic: HUGH D. LUMSDEN.
speechtext:
Yes, that would mean that he had to be in Ottawa early in July, but as a matter of fact, if he makes any sense out of it at all, he changes the original letter saying he had to be in England early in July, say that he had to be in Ottawa within two days.
Why did he so suddenly change his intention to go across the Atlantic, into an intention to go immediately to Ottawa, unless there was some urgent call.	Mr. Grant's letter, while it is fairly well designed to wipe away this peculiar fact, appears only too clearly to show that Mr. Lumsden was called back by the Commission and it supports the position taken by Mr. Chamberlin, that Mr. Lumsden was called off the work of arbitration by peremptory orders from Ottawa.
During the course of his speech, I asked the Minister of Railways a question. I then had in mind the point that even under the original agreement the people were not adequately protected in the mat-Mr. MEIGHEN.
ter of over-classification. I may be wrong, but my opinion is that the matter of overclassification and the consequent increased cost was not in the contemplation of this House when that original agreement was entered into, because I think the wording of clause 7 of the original agreement would not necessarily or obviously lead to the conclusion that the matter of cost by overclassification or by any other cause was in contemplation of parliament as a matter to be referred to arbitration. Assuming that the arbitration is empowered under the original agreement to cover the question of over-classification-and we must assume it because all parties have assumed that that shall be within the purview of the arbitration board-then it turns out that the people have practically no protection at all. Even if the arbitration has the tho rough and complete scope that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company contended it should have, and that we contend it should have, even so the people have not adequate protection under that agreement. I asked the Minister of Railways how he could explain where the engineer of the Transcontinental Commission would represent the people in the matter of over-classification, and as the Minister of Railways did not answer at the time, I was in doubt whether to complement him or his sincerity in acknowledging that he could not understand the point or on the skill with which he avoided it. Later on in the evening, he did attempt to answer it, and with I should think about three per cent of success. In so far as the legal liability of the government to charge the 3 per cent interest on the cost of construction was concerned, his explanation had something in it. But what about the 100 per cent principle cost of construction? How in connection with that could that engineer possibly represent the people? Why, Sir, no dispute could arise unless the Grand Trunk Pacific chief engineer takes the position that there is over-classification, and that consequently the cost is too great. It is inconceivable that the Grand Trunk Pacific would take the position that there is under-classification, and the cost estimated at too little. Before any dispute can arise, then the Grand Trunk Pacific must take the position that the cost is too great through over-classification, and then the representative of the Commission must say: 'No, the cost is not too great and I shall not let yon reduce it.' Now, in arguing out that position, how can he be said to represent the people of Canada, when he urges that the cost should be as great as it is? How in the world can he represent the people of the country in urging for the increased cost? It may he that he is establishing the right of the people to interest on that increased cost, but the Minister of Railways cannot have studied the position.

seeing that as to the 100 per cent, the principal cost of the construction which the people of Canada had to put up, the engineer of the Transcontinental Commission was acting directly antagonistic to the interests of the people. Therefore, all along there was no protection in the matter of over-classification, except such as might be afforded by the engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and I say that under the circumstances, in matters of over-classification that did not constitute a sufficient protection for the people of Canada. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company pays the 3 per cent interest, it is true, but it is a well known principle of railway management nowadays that the freight rates are fixed to meet such charges, and that the interest in the end comes out of the people. I do not -want to say it is a matter of no concern to the Grand Trunk Pacific to see that the cost is kept down, but it is a matter of comparatively little relative concern to them compared with the concern it is to the people of this country. Consequently I say that even should the arbitration have the thorough powers it was intended to have, it did not constitute in the matter of over-classification a sufficient protection for the people of Canada. The interest of the parties who are only relatively slightly interested was not a sufficient interest to be placed as a bulwark for the protection of the interests of the people, who, to an extent 40 times as great were interested in the cost of the construction.
That being the case, and I think it must be taken as clearly established, surely when we are in that position, surely when we have little enough protection at the best, it is the duty of this House to see that that protection is exercised in the most liberal possible degree. Surely the action of the Transcontinental Commission should have been not antagonistic to the limits of the arbitration, they should have taken a position all along in favour of the widest possible scope for that arbitration board. But when they refuse to take that position, it is the duty of the House to take it for them and to investigate the matter which they refused to investigate. The Transcontinental Commission all through these proceedings should rightly have been looked to by the people of this country as ranging themselves in all matters of dispute in favour of the people as against the contractors, but they have ranged themselves on the opposite side and in every dispute that has occurred have stood up alongside the contractor and fought his battles and the people's interests have been' left to take care of themselves. We do not represent the Transcontinental Commission or the government, we represent the people of Canada. They are our clients alone, and unless the light is let into them through the instrumentality of the resolution of the hon. member for South Sim-'on it is never going to be let in, absolutely no light can be let in by the resolution of the first minister and ho member on either side can show how there is any possibility of the slightest pretense of investigation under it. As this parliament is constituted, the House of Commons should have the interests of the people and no other at.heart, the people are their clients and they should have no other clients. It is our duty to see that they know the facts, and _ they knowing the facts we can rely on their intelligence.

maintopic: HUGH D. LUMSDEN.
speechtext:
At this late hour I shall try to be as brief as I possibly can in discussing this question. What are we discussing? A resolution of the right hon. gentleman the leader of the government purporting to make inquiries into certain charges made by one Hugh D. Lumsden, engineer in chief of the Transcontinental railway, in which he uses certain words which I had better read. He says:
That neither the general specifications nor my instructions regarding classification have been adhered to, but on the contrary large amounts of material have been returned as solid rock, which should only have been classified as loose rock or common excavation, and material has been returned as loose rock which was, or could have been handled by ploughing or scraping.
He goes over a lot of charges in which he accuses his subordinates of not carrying out his instructions. Why does not the right hon. gentleman leave that to the committee to inquire as to whether the allegations of the chief engineer are true or not? He carefully avoids it. Look at his resolution. What is it? It says:
And whereas, while this House deems it not desirable to take any action which might prejudice the position of either of the parties to the arbitration proceedings now in progress between the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway company and the said commissioners, yet the said recited allegations of said Hugh D. Lums-den, stated by him as the reasons for his resignation of the said position of chief engineer, are in the opinion of this House of such great public interest.
In the opinion of this House it is of great public interest whether a subordinate carried out his instructions. The-gravamen of the charge is that the country is being robbed by over-classification on certain of the work, and that is the charge made by Mr. Lmmsden in his letter to the commissioners, yet this House is debarred from inquiring into it. Why? Because an arbitration board was provided under the Act and the question is, as the hon. gentlemen who have spoken from the othefi side of the House say, sub judice; as we bad given powers to this arbitration, or

at least delegated them, we should not inquire into the classification or the question whether there has 'been over-classification or not. These questions are not to be considered at all. What a farce appointing a committee of this House for the purpose of inquiring whether some subordinates' of the chief engineer had performed their duty or not. That is all that the right hon. gentleman is willing to submit to the House for its consideration. A greater farce never was heard of in this House. He could not get past the fact that his chief engineer, the party selected by him to superintend the construction of the Transcontinental railway, was obliged to state that there was over-classification, or, in other words, robbery of the country.
Let us first look at the manner in which an estimate as to the probable cost of a railway is prepared. The bon. gentlemen stated that a specification had been prepared for this work by his depmty minister and by the engineer in charge of the Grand Trunk Pacific. I think they put their heads together and consulted some United States works as to what the proper specification. should be. I have not the slightest doubt in the world that the specifications provided by them are proper specifications. I am perfectly content, too, that the interpretation in the first instance put on them by Mr. Lumsden, that even his amended interpretation after the opinion of the Minister of Justice had been obtained, was perfectly in accordance with what is correct. If these instructions were carried out, we would have honest construction of the Grand Tnunk Pacific. An estimate of the cost of the construction of the road is made by engineers. Engineers are employed to locate the road. , When the road is located, they say that there may be mistakes in reference to the quantities along the line of road. They examine it most carefully, test pits are sunk at every part of the road, and the variation ought not to be more than the amount the Minister of Railways said, 20 per cent. It never is 20 per cent with true engineers. They ought to know within 20 per cent anyway every piece of rock, every piece of loose rock, and every piece of earth upon the road. That is demanded by the Minister of Railways. Under these estimates of quantity the department lets contracts, and strange to say in this case the same parties who located the road, as I drew from the Minister of Railways, are the engineers who are on the construction. They furnish information to the country stating what the quantities are and from time to time as the work progresses and the measurements come in, the quantities a.re found to be in some cases three times in excess of what they estimated. Not a word from the Minister of Railways, not a word from the Railway Commissioners who have charge of the con-Mr. JOHN HAGGART.
struction of this road, saying: How is it, gentlemen, you estimated certain quantities in reference to this particular construction at one time and now by your return you find there in some cases three times the amount? Not an explanation asked, no reason given. I drew the attention of the Minister of Railways a couple of years ago, and a year ago, to the fact that it was notorious that the quantities on this road greatly exceeded the estimates jinade of them. I asked whether this was by reason of the interpretation put upon the contract by the Minister of Justice. If it were so, I could not understand the position of the chief engineer. These contracts were let on specifications prepared by him-. They were changed by the Minister of Justice putting a certain interpretation uporf them. But why were not the specifications* altered for the new contracts so as to carry out in these what was intended in the first place? I do not see this matter referred to in The correspondence. The simple fact is that the parties who had change of the work for the government returned quantities largely in excess'->as to cost-of the quantities estimated by themselves to be in the work. And no complaint was made by the government or by the commissioners; no report was made by the engineer, nor does any evidence appear 'as having been given before any commission with a view to exculpating .those who were thus proven to be in error.
The Minister of Raidways and Canals (Mr. Graham), and the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), in their remarks, found it necessary, in order to defend the government, to say: We have done all we possibly could, but powers were delegated to the Railway Commission and board of arbitrators and not to the Minister of Railways. I was careful, when the commission was appointed, to state that the responsibility of the minister to this parliament should not cease, that whatever commissioners or arbitrators were appointed, we would not divest ourselves of authority for this purpose. We may have- delegated our authority to a certain extent for our own convenience, hut the ministerial responsibility must always continue. The member for Pictou asked us: What has the Minister of Railways or the head o.f the government to do with the question whether classification is right cr wrong?- the matter is referred to the arbitrators to decide the matter according to the law, and by that we are all hound. But the doctrine I laid down is that this House goes to the minister direct. The minister can exculpate himself by justifying the action of his subordinates and showing that the calculations have been correctly made.
The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Car-veil) dealt with the tender question of the arbitration between the Grand Trunk Paci-

lie and the government in reference to this work. I may be wrong, but in my judgment the arbitrators had nothing to do with deciding any question arising between the contractors and the government. The only questions that the arbitrators can decide, and the only ones intended to be referred to them under the Act, are disputes be-between the Grand Trunk Pacific Company and the government in reference to the construction of the road. The power of decision of matters between the government and the arbitrators is entirely with the government. I might read the statute on this subject, but instead I will read from the report brought down a section embodied in the contract which the government have let:
The engineer shall be the sole judge of work and material in respect of both quantity and quality, and his decisions on questions in dispute with regard to work and material, shall be final.
No arbitration is referred to there.
No extra additional work or changes shall be deemed to have been executed, nor shall the contractor be entitled to demand payment for the same, unless the same shall have been executed to the satisfaction of the engineer.
Thus, the Railway Department has entire control over any dispute between the contractor and the government, and the only questions the arbitrators have to deal with are questions arising between the Grand Trunk Pacific and the government in reference to the construction of this road.
Now, why are we asking this inquiry! It is one of the most important that has come before the House. We were promised the construction of this road for $53,000,000. The Minister of Finance states that, in giving this estimate, he did not speak on his own authority but on that of the engineers. But the minister is responsible to this House and he has no right to hide himself behind the officers of the government. If an officer of the government makes a misstatement to him, it is his duty to correct that officer, to suspend him, or, if necessary, to dismiss him. The statement was prepared by Mr. Schreiber, prepared on certain quantities, furnished to his department by the location engineer I have looked carefully over the returns, and I find the total prism quantities are less than the amount found by actual construction of the road. I think that in the case of every contract let on the Transcontinental Railway, the locatees of the road made the quantities a little in excess of what has been found. What, then, is the difficulty? It is on the question of classification. If you have a million yards of earth to take out, and, instead of classifying it as earth, you classify 700,000 yards as loose rock at 50 cents, instead of at 25 cents for loose earth, or solid rock at $1.50, the
difference is very serious. But where the government is responsible, and what we want to inquire into is as to these changes of classification. We want to inquire whether there has been falsification of the classification or not. That is the only real question. The question before the country is not whether the country has received good work. Why go to the trouble of surveying, and locating a line, taking out the quantities, preparing specifications and letting contracts if we are not allowed to inquire afterwards whether the expenditure has been in accordance with the contracts, and not only whether the country has got good work or not. The question of honour, of proper management of the public works is far above every consideration of money value. Honour should never be linked with dishonour. We ought to have in our public men honour and reputation. No country can exist unless it has the means of knowing that the money entrusted to_ the care of the government is spent in the interest and to the honour of the country. What we want to investigate is charges that have been rife from one end of the country to the other. It is the duty of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways to assist the opposition in finding out whether there has been a proper and honest spirit, an economical spirit in the expenditure of public moneys, and whether contracts have been carried out properly or not.
That is his duty; we ought to be assisted in that. Do not burk the inquiry. We do not want an inquiry to investigate even the charges made by Mr. Lumsden, we want an inquiry as to whether there has been over-classification or not. But the Prime Minister says we are simply to inquire whether the charge made by Mr. Lumsden against his subordinates is correct, whether they (carried out his instructions. You would think that the inquiry should give us the right to look into the question of classification. But no, the right hon. gentleman does not intend anything of that kind, we are to be completely debarred from going into the question of over-classification. Now, I think the House will agree with me that an inquiry should be made into these charges, which are rung from one end of the country to the other. They are selfapparent upon the papers brought down. Is there not a prima facie case -when you see 600,000 yards of solid rock in a contract increased to 1,200,000; when you see loose rock multiplied in quantitv three or four times; and when, to make up the quantity taken from the prism, they have to reduce earth excavation reduced to the standard of rock? Then the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) made a statement which, if true, bears evidence of fraud committed upon the government. He says that on some portions of the line where there

have been excavations returned as solid rock, the slope upon that excavation is one and a half to one. That very fact shows that there was earth present, they are passing through earth. If that statement is correct, it is evidence sufficient to convict the engineers of having returned clay instead of rock. I shall have another opportunity of discussing these questions. The hour is late now, and I know the House is anxious to have a vote. But for the honour of the House, for the honour of the country, let us not be debarred from making an inquiry into the charges which are specifically made in this House. Mr. Lums-den has made charges of fraud, of overclassification on the part of his engineers, who refused to follow his instructions, which sometimes amounted to two-fold or three-fold actual quantities. Do not prevent the opposition from exercising the right of making this inquiry, in order to iustify themselves before the country. If we are refused it will be worse for the government. I state here in the papers brought down the evidence is so conclusive that fraud has been practised upon the government, that the government should hasten to inquire into the matter. The Minister of Railways himself stated that the location of this road was under the charge of a certain class of engineers. They reported the amount of loose rock, the amount of solid Tock, and the amount of clay excavated that would require to be taken out; and these same engineers, be it remembered, are now engaged in the construction of that railway. There has not been a proper tab kept upon the excavation, there has not been proper reports made from month to month to the department. The department ought to have known that the payments were largely in excess of the estimates. But no inquiries were made, the chief engineer is not even consulted, even those gentlemen who made the estimate are not asked to explain the difference, and the poor country has been left entirely at their mercy.

maintopic: HUGH D. LUMSDEN.
speechtext:
- CROTHERS (West Elgin). There are one or two matters in connection with_ this question which seem to me of considerable importance, and which I have not heard discussed during this debate. Even at this late hour I take the risk of wearying the House for a few minutes to bring these matters to its attention. I read the observations made bv the Prime Minister in introducing this motion; I had the advantage of hearing the somewhat lengthy and heated address delivered by the Minister of Railways; I listened to the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), and to the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Car-veil), and I have endeavoured to find some logical, consistent and bona fide position for gentlemen on the other side of the Mr. JOHN HAGGART.
House to take on this question, and I must confess my inability to reach the conclusion that this motion is presented to the House with any sincere desire to'preserve the interest of the people. Gentlemen who have spoken on the other side have given us quite lengthy addresses, all of which are equally applicable to the motion proposed by the Prime Minister and to that which has been proposed by way of amendment. Hon. gentlemen have put up a very plausible argument, I must confess; they tell us that this parliament, in Dasing the Transcontinental Railway Act in 1903, provided that a board of arbitrators should be constituted composed of the chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, the chief engineer of the Board of Transcontinental Railway Commissioners, and, in the event of their being unable to agree, they should choose a third arbitrator. They call your attention to section 7 which provides for that board in these words:
It is hereby agreed that the specifications for the construction of the eastern division shall be submitted to and approved of by the company before the commencement of the work, and that the said work shall be done according to said specifications, and shall be subject to the joint supervision, inspection and acceptance of the chief engineer appointed by the government and the chief engineer of the company, and in the event of differences as to the specifications, or in case the said engineers shall differ as to the work, the question in dispute shall be determined by the said engineers and a third arbitrator to be chosen in the manner provided in paragraph -1 of this agreement.
So in that section of the agreement this parliament has provided a board of arbitrators to determine questions of a certain character that may arise. Gentlemen opposite have told us time and time again that the people are safeguarded by that board of arbitrators; that board, we are told, is composed of an independent, high minded body of experts. Now, Sir, I have just noticed, during the last few minutes, a communication from the commissioners to the members of this board, which is really astounding, and alarming, and startling, if you stop for a moment to look at it. , It is contained on pages 28, 29, 30 and 31 of this return. In it the commissioners undertake to criticise, discipline and intimidate this board of arbitrators. One would scarcely believe it possible. Let us see, at the bottom of page 30, what this communication says. It comes from Mr. Parent, chairman of the commission, and P. E. Ryan, secretary.
Resolved, that the secretary be, and is hereby directed to write to the three arbitrators, transmitting a copy of the letters of District Engineer Doucet and notes of Assistant District Engineer Huestes, each dated 23rd June instant; a copy of the letter of Messrs. Mac-donell and O'Brien, dated 24th instant; *

copy of the letter of Mr. J. D. McArthur, dated 19th instant, and a copy of report of District Engineer Poulin, dated 22nd instant, all relating to the proceedings of the arbitration Tribunal

	'
Here you find these commissioners forwarding to the arbitrators letters signed by these subordinate engineers and by two or three contractors. What do these commissioners then say?
-and to say that the commissioners object to and protest against the proceedings of the arbitrators as being improper and illegal, for the following reasons, viz.:- _	.
(a)	That they were based in whole or in part on the said draft agreement of May 14, 1909, which had been rejected, and which had no existence in fact;
(b)	That the examination of the work was of a hasty, insufficient and superficial character.
Fancy a person interested in litigation before a court having the audacity to w,rite a letter of that kind to the court to criticise the conduct -of the eouTt. Here they say that the examination made by these arbitrators, this independent tribunal, provided by this parliament for the protection of the people of Canada was hasty, insufficient and superficial, and they undertake (to discipline and intimidate it. But, that is not all.
(c)	That the engineers on the line who classified the work were not afforded a sufficient hearing and an opportunity of presenting evidence.
Further:
(d)	That the contractors were not afforded an opportunity of showing cause; and further to say that the commissioners insist, in the public interest, that the proceedings of the arbitration tribunal shall be exhaustive, final and conclusive; shall cover all the objections filed on behalf of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and that the report of the arbitrators, when made, shall be supported by substantial evidence, including details of quantities.
There is the communication sent from the commissioners to this board of arbitration, alleged by gentleman after gentleman on the other side of the House to be composed of competent experts, virtuous arbitrators, independent men, and yet intimidated by this board of commissioners. Did anything of the kind ever occur in a civilized community before? I read this because the importance of it warrants it. We find these commissioners appointed by this government, criticising, disciplining and intimidating an independent board, constituted for the purpose of safeguarding the interests of the people.

maintopic: HUGH D. LUMSDEN.
speechtext: And by a statute.

maintopic: HUGH D. LUMSDEN.
speechtext:
And by a statute. That communication was brought to the
knowledge of the Minister of Railways and Canals by a letter sent to him by the secretary of the commissioners, dated the 26th June. What step did the Minister of Railways and his colleagues take in regard to this? Did they point out to these commissioners that they had drifted outside of their jurisdiction, that they had no legal right and that it was simply an outrage for them to attempt to intimidate an independent board of arbitrators appointed for the protection of the people of the country? Not one word, not one line do we find coming from the Prime Minister to say to these commissioners: You must not interfere with this board, this board has been appointed by the parliament of Canada to safeguard the interests of the people; it must be held to be an independent board and you must not attempt to dictate to it. Did the right hon. gentleman send a single word of that character to this commission? Not a word. Did the Minister of Railways send a single word of that character, reprimanding or rebuking the commissioners for having taken that stand, for having attempted to pervert the judgment of this board of arbitrators, said to be independent, in the interests of the people? Not a single word. Is there any reason why a high minded gentleman like Mr. Dumsden should not resign hi3 position when the government permitted the members of the commission to send him such an insulting letter as that? Could any gentleman having a grain of self-respect submit to any such position as that? You will notice that these commissioners are not writing the arbitrators-they would not be justified in doing that even-in the interest of the people, but they are writing them to influence them in the interests of the contractors. They say that the contractors ' were not afforded an opportunity of showing cause that ' the examination of the work was of a hasty, insufficient and superficial character,' and that ' the engineers on the line who classified the work were not afforded a sufficient hearing and an opportunity of presenting evidence.' That is what we get from the commissioners. One of the primary reasons for this is that the commissioners were appointed for political purposes and had no special qualifications for the office. A great deal of this difficulty has arisen from the fact that these commissioners knew nothing of the construction of railways. They were men who had been appointed by reason of political services rendered to the government and there was added to that commission a few weeks ago a very estimable gentleman, a member of this House, but I never heard that he ever had had any experience as an expert engineer or that he knew anything about the construction of railways. Do the railway companies who are striving to get large dividends for their shareholders ap-

point political friends to positions of trust as managers of their companies? No, you will find that the managers of the large raiiwaycorporationsaremen who have come up from the bottom, who know every step in the process of construction and operation of railways. These are the men who are placed in these high positions to manage these great railway corporations and they are men who know something about it. But here we have a commission appointed who know nothing about the positions that they are called upon to fill, but who are appointed by reason of political services rendered to the government which is in accord with most of the appointments made by this government. I submit that it would have been a more proper position for the government to have taken to have said to Mr. Lumsden: We will not accept your resignation, we will dismiss the commissioners who had the audacity to perpetrate this outrage upon the people in attempting to intimidate you in the position which you occupy. But, instead of doing that what do we find the government doing to-day? We have the government saying to this Hou3e and to the people of Canada that they have lost confidence in their chief engineer, not that they have lost confidence in the commissioners, not that they have lost confidence in any of the subordinate engineers, but that they have lost confidence in Mr. Lumsden because that is what this motion means, if it means anything. It was said here by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) that Mr. Lumsden had made a statement and that the government were going to appoint a committee to ascertain whether Mr. Lumsden was telling the truth or not. At page 2483 of ' Hansard ' it will be found that the hon. member for Pictou, in a speech which he made in this House yesterday, used the following words with reference to a statement made by Mr. Lumsden:
My right lion, friend the leader of the House asks this House to investigate that statement and to ascertain whether it is a fact or not.
That is the position they take. Here was the chief engineer of the largest project that this country has ever undertaken, appointed by this government, making a statement in reference to several of his subordinates. Hi3 statement alone should have secured the dismissal of these men instanter. Instead of that we have the government saying:	We do not believe Mr. Lumsden; we are going to appoint a committee to ascertain whether the statement he has made is true or not. Is not that the position? They accept his resignation.
I have here a copy of this motion proposed by the Prime Minister, and in it he cites portions of two letters written by Mr. Mr. CROTHERS
Lumsden, in which letters Mr. Lumsden states, speaking of his engineering staff generally, he says:
In view of the general disregard of my instructions and having lost confidence in the engineering staff I have concluded to resign iny position as chief engineer.
Is it possible to conceive that Mr Lumsden sent in that resignation without having been misused not only by the commissioners but by this government. We would like a committee to ascertain what Mr. Lumsden said to the government in regard to the manner in which he had been treated by the commissioners, whether he called the attention of the government to this intimidation practised upon him by the commissioners and if so what answer he got from the government. Did the government tell him: We are going to stand by the commissioners, to stand by the engineers, to stand by the contractors even if you go down. I cannot conceive of his resigning without his having some intimation of that sort from the government. In the second letter he says:
1 beg to state that this does not apply to' the whole staff but applies only to the portion of the staff who were responsible for the measurement, classification, supervision and inspection of considerable portions in district B and east of Rennie crossing in district ' P/ lately gone over by me.
What Mr. Lumsden says is that he has lo3t confidence in these engineers in respect to their measurement, classification, supervision, and inspection. Now, the Prime Minister proposes a committee to ascertain whether that statement is a fact or not. We are told that the board of arbitrators is the ,only tribunal properly qualified by expert knowledge to determine questions of measurement, classification, and inspection, and yet the Prime Minister proposes to appoint a committee of three partisans to determine whether the statement made by Mr. Lumsden be true or not. I would like any man to explain to us how a committee of five are to investigate and ascertain whether Mr. Lumsden was justified in making that statement or not, without making an inquiry into the measurement, classification, inspection, and supervision. I submit to you Mr. Speaker, that it would be utterly impossible for any committee to make any inquiry with a view to ascertaining whether Mr. Lumsden was justified in saying that these men had made over-classification, without having inquired respecting that classification. That is as plain as two and two are four. And yet we are told by hon. gentlemen opposite that this committee will not be permitted to ask any questions respecting the supervision, classification, or inspection. Then, how is the committee to ascertain whether this

classification and inspection was properly or improperly done. Of course it would be utterly impossible. It seems therefore as clear as the noon day sun that the proposition to appoint this committee is not made with a sincere desire in the interests of this country but is suggested for the purpose of making nice reading campaign literature for distribution among the people. Mr. Lumsden was a qualified man, a man of knowledge and experience and capacity and integrity, or he was not. Hon. gentlemen opposite now say in substance: We doubt whether he was or not, because we are going to appoint a committee to ascertain, as the hon. member for Pictou says, whether the statement he made was true or not. Now, if the position taken by the government in that regard be sound, that itself is a very good reason why we should investigate the whole' matter, because Mr. Lumsden has been in office for years and if the government had no confidence in him and are not able to accept his word on a statement of that kind, then how are they to expect the members of this House and the people of Canada to accept without question what he has been doing for the last 4 or 5 years? And if he be a man of capacity, experience, and integrity, then his word should have been accepted at once by the government, and his subordinates who were accused of misconduct should have been dismissed at once-one or the other. Therefore I say that all the arguments hon. gentlemen on the other side have presented against the adoption of this amendment are equally applicable against the motion presented by the First Minister. A great many things arouse suspicion about the Transcontinental Railway. It has been iterated and reiterated that the people of this country were deceived by the government-I * do not say intentionally-but certain it is that they were deceived and grossly deceived with reference to the cost of this great work. They were told by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Finance that the whole road from Winnipeg to Moncton could be constructed for about $50,000,000. The government were then urged to take more time to become familiar with the project, and to get more information with regard to the character of the country through which the railway would run, but the Prime Minister told us that the archives contained material enough to make anv member of this House as familiar with that country as he might be with his own home in the city of Ottawa. He told us he had mountains of information, and that there was no necessity whatever for getting further information with regard to the matter. The Minister of Finance yesterday gave the name of a gentleman upon whom he relied as authority for the statement that it would cost only $51,000,000.
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the House that one of two things must exist with reference to the estimates that were made before this country embarked on this project, and also with reference to the estimates that have been made on the different parts of the road that have been let to	contractors-either
the engineers who gave that information were incompetent or they lent their hand to deceiving the people of this country. There is only one alternative. Would any one attempt to make you believe, Mr. Speaker, that it was impossible for a competent engineer to get within one-third of the cost of the road, and yet it is admitted now that this road will cost three times as much as we estimated. What do we find with reference to these estimates as detailed to the House yesterday by the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Lennox). We find that in contract after contract, he took up, the alleged measurement exceeded from 75 to 520 per cent more solid rock than the engineers estimated, and that in every case the amount of solid rock grew enormously while the amount of sand and clay. diminished enormously. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that in this respect, and I submit it guardedly, one of two things must be admitted: Either the engineer was incompetent or he was dishonest. One could very easily understand that an engineer may make a mistake and over estimate one mile and under estimate the next, but every one knows that if there are such variations they would be found on both sides if the estimate were made by an honest and competent man. But here we have hundreds of miles and in every instance the alleged under estimate of from 200 per cent to 500 per cent varied on the one side only. Go out to the plain, honest people of this country whether Liberals or Conservatives and tell them that, and I submit there is not a sensible man amongst them who will accept it without very strong suspicion. He will likely say if he is a Liberal: I had confidence in the government when they made that statement to me four or five years ago, I have confidence in the government yet, there must be something wrong with the commission apnointed to manage the construction of the railroad or there must be something wrong with the engineers who were appointed to carry out the instructions. I have not lost confidence in the government, I believe they were honest at the time they made that statement to us; ydu cannot blame them much. But they will say further: The cost of the 'railway is so enormously beyond what they told us; the fact of these commissioners

not being experts, the faci oi their being appointed for political purposes the fact that they know nothing about the construction of railways, the fact that they have attempted to intimidate the independent and righteous board of arbitrators that we supposed was standing between us and the contractors, all these things have established in our minds a well grounded suspicion that things are not right, and unless our leader, unless this government which we have been following for many _ years will give us an impartial, and a fair, and an open, and full investigation of this matter from the top to the bottom we will lose confidnce in the whole outfit. Why, the very first thing I see in this return is a letter dated 7th October, 1907, written by the assistant chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific, from which I quote:
Let me give you some illustrations.
Take the cutting from station 5818 to 5826, estimated 71 per cent solid rock and 29 pel cent loose rock; slopes taken out 1 i to 1.
Showing that this is not solid rock because if it were there would be no such slopes, for even if the solid rock stood up perpendicular it would be safe. But where there is sand and earth they have to slope back li to 1. And the engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific says:
Very little ledge in this cut. Some large boulders, but a very large percentage is common excavation.
Then again he says:
Station 5842 to station 5850. Classified 94 per cent solid rock, 6 per cent loose rock. Slopes taken out li to 1. Solid rock over classified at least 100 per cent.
Then again he says:
Station 5866 to 5875. Estimated . 80 per cent solid rook, 20 per cent loose rock. No rock in place in this cut.
No rock whatever although this classic fication gave 80 per cent solid rock and 20 per cent loose rock.

maintopic: HUGH D. LUMSDEN.
speechtext: Is that an engineer who says that?

maintopic: HUGH D. LUMSDEN.
speechtext:
Yes, it is an engineer who says that. That letter was written October 7, 1907, and these same engineers are operating on the road to-day; notwithstanding the finding they thus made, they are still in the employ of the government and still giving estimates on the construction of that road. Is it any wonder that the members of this House and the people of this country are demanding an impartial investigation of this whole matter from the beginning to the end.
Station 5882 to 5901. Estimated 78 per cent solid rock, 22 per cent loose rock. A large amount of this cut wasted with slip scrapers Mr. CROTHERS.
and ploughing being done with two horses. There are hundreds oi yards of earth here without a stone, large or small.
Station 6030 to 6046. Estimated 40 per cent solid rock, 10 per cent loose rock. This is the large sand cut west of O'Brien's camp. Of the 95,000 yards moved to August" 31 in this cut at least 80,000 yards were pure sand.
And yet these engineers are on the work to-day and hon. gentlemen opposite say: 'We boast that we have the same engineers now that we started with, we. have kept them all along.' The government got notice of this in October, 1907, that is two years ago last October, and they are there still.
Station 6071 to 6078. Estimated 99 per cent solid rock, 1 per cent loose rock. Very little solid rock in place. Slopes taken out If- to 1.
I would have made it 100 per cent. The slope of li to 1 indicates sand. They did put in 1 per cent for loose rock and 99 per cent for solid rock. Yet these engineers are on the work still and the Commissioners are still in the employ of the government, notwithstanding these Commissioners have, kept these men at work all this time, notwithstanding that these Commissioners have been intimidating, criticising and stultifying the righteous and independent board of arbitrators appointed by this House for the protection of the people,- they are all there yet, they will stay with us until the end, all of a piece, from the right hon. the Prime Minister down, they all must be kept in order that they may finish their work.
I have another half-page of that letter making similar objections which I might read. But let me give one or two words that are very significant:
As before stated, these over-classifications are not made through error in judgment nor upon the decision of the resident or division engineers, who are fully acquainted with the character of the work, but by arbitrary orders from their superior.
Who were these superiors? This .letter was written to Mr. Lumsden, the chief engineer, and it certainly is not referring to him. Who are the superiors? That statement is made by Mr. Woods, the assistant Engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific two years ago last October. They are still with the Commission and yet the right hon. gentleman proposes a resolution here to appoint three partisans-I do not suppose there will be more than two from this side -to ascertain whether this is so or not, whether Mr. Lumsden was telling the truth or not. How can one of us go out on the streets to-morrow and meet a fellow citizen without a blush of shame on his cheek? If this proposition contained in this amendment be defeated this evening, what will it be saying to the people of this country? It will be saying: 'We refuse to investigate charges of this kind, saying that your moneys are being sacrificed by the million,

but we refuse to investigate.' What are we to say? The Minister of Railways was asked two or three times, several others have been asked what this committee suggested by the Prime Minister is to inquire into. The hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) suggested two or three questions that might be asked of Mr. Lumsden if he were in the box before that committee. One would be: 'Did you find these men honest?' He might answer: 'Yes, or no.' He might be asked: 'What are the names of the men?' He might answer that.' He might be asked: 'In what respect did you find them dishonest?' Then we would hear: 'Hold, you must not answer that question, I object.' They told us so in so many words, this committee would have no right to investigate anything of that kind, they have said: 'This has been relegated to a board of arbitrators.' It has been relegated to a board of arbitrators under the intimidation of the political partisans who constitute that Commission, who are labouring in the interests of the contractor as shown by this letter. What are they to inquire into? We have been told by hon. gentlemen on the other side, in speaking against the amendment, that it is only expert engineers who should inquire into such matters; but you have the statement of the chief engineer of the Commission, in the person of Mr. Lumsden, and the Prime Minister actually proposes to this House and to the country, that he will set aside the statement of that celebrated and distinguished expert and leave it to three of his partisans behind him. I submit that I do not think there is a single hon. gentleman in this House who, if he were left to his head and his heart and his patriotism, would not say that there has been a sufficient ease made out to warrant this House in appointing a commission or committee or some independent tribunal, to investigate this matter from the top to the bottom.
Nobody, I say, has been able to tell us what this committee is to investigate, and how they are to carry on their work. I submit that the very recital of the motion proposed by the right hon. Prime Minister shows that this committee could not do this work without inquiring into the matters of classification, supervision anu inspection. So that if what has been said by hon. gentlemen on the., other side in opposition to our proposal to have the whole matter investigated be well taken, it is just as well taken as against the motion proposed by the Prime Minister. I was very much surprised to find in the remarks of the Prime Minister a statement to the effect that he himself doubted Mr. Lumsden. I have never heard that there was a word to be said against Mr. Lumsden. He seems to have had the confidence of this government at the time he was appointed and for many
years thereafter. There is no suggestion that I have ever heard that he was a man unworthy of - confidence. I shall not take up more time of the House, but I cannot emphasize too strongly the point I started out with. I want to call the attention of the House, and particulary of the people of this country, to the fact that the tribunal provided by the statute of this parliament in 1903, and section 7 of the agreement to stand as a safeguard between greedy grafters and dishonest contractors and the people, this government has permitted the commissioners to discipline and criticise and intimidate, not in the interest of the people, but in the interest of the contractors who are trying to bleed the people.

I regret, Mr. Speaker, that I should be a party to prolong this debate to any extent, and, to use a phrase I have heard many a time at the opening of lengthy addresses, that I should take up the valuable time of the House; but, I would deem it on my part a breach of duty to give a silent vote on such a question.
Viewing the matter in.the most unselfish spirit and apart from all sectional or party considerations of any kind, I am satisfied, and thoroughly so, that a general inquiry is desirable, not an inquiry narrowed down to a single district, or dealing merely with quantities, classification, supervision and inspection; but an inquiry concerned with the methods followed in connection with the building of the National Transcontinental, east section, from one end of the line to the other, and I contend that public opinion demands it.
On the above grounds, I ask for an investigation of a general, fair, public, and thorough character, untrammelled by legal technicalities or political bias, as laid down in the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) ; and not a summary, curtailed investigation, held behind

-closed doors, hide-bound and out-of-date, such as is looked for in the resolution submitted by the right hon. Prime Minister.
Considering the grievious nature of the charge made by Mr. Lumsden, considering the high standing of that gentleman, his .unassailable reputation, his ability and prestige which no hon. member is justified in questioning; considering the alarming and inexplicable discrepancy between the estimated cost of the Transcontinental-a mere trifle it was to be, these hon. gentlemen assured us at the outset-and the monstrous amount it actually comes to and will .grow to in the end, I say, Mr. Speaker, that a general inquiry is in order; and all that these hon. gentlemen on the other side have said, satisfies one as to the slackness of their principles of political morality and fairness much more than it impairs the force of my statement.
After listening to their expressions of .opinion, I wonder, Mr. Speaker, through what perversion of the most elementary principles of logic-not to. say honesty- these hon. gentlemen feel an inclination, and apparently rejoice in directing from the bitter shafts of malice and suspicion against the honest and faithful servant who has been courageous enough to fulfil his duty, though the loser by it, in the sole interest of the country; and how is it that their goodly disposition goes wholly to those whom a prima facia case exists, and who should be the object of suspicion. However, my short stay in this House has taught me that this government has tender mercies for their prevaricating political friends, much more so than for honest judges; and whenever, as the result of an inquiry, graft and extortion have been brought to light, the guilty parties have always found in this House ministers willing to discredit and even disgrace tribunals in order to better absolve and clear those whom these tribunals had convicted.

I do not think so. My hon. friend asked me what there is to investigate? There is the charge made by Mr. Lumsden that he has been deceived by the engineers of certain districts. As to how it should be investigated, of course that will depend upon the answers given by Mr. Lumsden himself. I do not know what reasons he may have, and the only way to ascertain what reasons he has for coming to the conclusion he does is to investigate. It is premature to say what course the investigation shall take. The leader of the opposition began his speech very dramatically by asking: ' Can you say that the- public interest will be prejudiced by this investigation?" Certainly, I do say so. An investigation here on the back of the investigation now going on would cettainly prejudice the public in-

terest. I do not say at this moment that the door is to be closed against investigation-nothing of the kind. Parliament can exercise supreme power. I think the hon. gentleman put the case better when he said that parliament in its wisdom would determine whether there was to be an investigation. I agree with that. But I say that parliament in its wisdom will not feel called upon to investigate the matter, but will investigate the facts covered by this motion and will reserve its judgment for a future occasion.
