Or 'upon the character of Mr. Lumsden; and he has read the statement which he did make in his speech. The statement which he made involves an inference which, while I will not say it goes so far as to touch the moral character of Mr. Lumsden, certainly goes so far as to touch the stand he took, and his judgment, becamse the Prime Minister as the head of the government says that he questions his judgment. Well, if he questions his judgment, he has gone a long way to losing confidence in Mr. Lumsden, and he has taken the opportunity of letting the world as well as this House know that he no longer has confidence in Mr. Lumsden's judgment.
Well, let that go. He then took up the letter of Mr. Woods, and the statement of the leader of the opposition, a very strong statement, which consisted in putting the letter of Mr. Woods on record. Nothing could be stronger than Mr. Woods' letter. Now, who is Mr. Woods? Is Mr. Woods a nonentity? Is he a scrub engi* neer? Is he a man of no standing in his profession? How often have we heard the greatness and the grandeur of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway described to us, and Mr. Woods is a trusted servant, a picked engineer, a trusted employee in engineering matters of that great Grand Trunk Pacific Company, which knows how to employ the best, and, which so far as I know, always
does employ the best. That is what Mr. Woods is. When he speaks, he speaks with authority, the authority of a man who is trained in his profession, and he places at the bottom of that- the observation and experience of a man who has gone over every foot of the ground he is talking about. Now, is no credence to be given, is no weight to be attached to the judgment, to the statement, to the repeated statements of Mr. Woods in that respect? In 1907 Mr. Woods wrote that letter. In 1909, two years afterwards, he is writing exactly similar letters and along the same line, and from 1907 to the present time Mr. Woods has never ceased writing letters, and no letter of his can be quoted in which he does not reiterate the same broad, strong and specific statements with reference to over-classification, giving the mile, giving the section, and giving the quality of the overclassification. I think that is something that cannot be explained away.
Bait that is not all. Mr. Woods has the backing of his district engineers. Amongst them is Mr. Armstrong, who called the attention of Mr. Woods to what was going on, and who gave him the basis of the information upon which Mr. Woods acted, and upon which, after he had acted, he wrote these repeated letters. More than that, in this stand of Mr. Woods on behalf of his company first, which is a stand, so far as it goes, on behalf of the people of this country, in the second place-because every dollar that Mr. Woods and the Grand Trunk Pacific get taken off on the cost of that road is a dollar taken off from what the people of this country have to contribute, that is what it means. Alongside Mr. Woods stands his district engineer and his sub-engineers. Alongside of Mr. Woods stands Mr. Kelliher, and alongside of Mr. Woods stands Mr. Chamberlin, who is the vice-president of the road; alongside Mr. Woods, in his charges, there is ranged up the whole line of the Grand Trunk Pacific engineering staff, and, there is not one of them but backs him, not one of them but will substantiate his statements. Now that means something.
The Prime Minister asks: If it were true, would Mr. Dumsden have done nothing? And he demolishes the leader of the opposition in saying that an investigation has been held. What was the investigation? Mr. Lumsden writes a letter, or he has a personal conference with the engineers on that part of the road which was the subject of Mr. Woods' letters. The letter was read here to-night, and what did the letter say? Mr. Lumsden says that he questioned them upon it, and they denied it was so. That is the investigation. What a lovely kind of an investigation that is, Merwin likes an investigation like that, Lodge likes an investigation like that, Pearson delights in that kind of an investigation,

the saw-dust wharf heroes love that kind of an investigation. Just ask whether it is so or not, and when they deny it, give it all up, and three years afterwards when you are taunted with it say: But there was an investigation; we asked the chap ii it was true and he said it was not. Rut what an example that would be foT our judges. Why, all you have to do when any one does something criminal is to call the chap up and say: Did you do that? He denies it, the judge immediately throws off his robes, his work is done; and when you ask him what was the result of the triah he says: I could do nothing further, the chap denies it.
Now I put another question to the Prime Minister and the government. The government cannot get out of their responsibility in this matter. When the dommission bullyrags an independent tribunal, the arbitrators appointed, it is the government that is bullyragging them. But we do not need to labour that. The Prime Minister takes the whole glory of doing it. When an independent tribunal of judges is appointed to decide upon great issues between two opposing forces, between the government of this country and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, when that independent and scientific tribunal is arranged for and constituted, the government commences to say: You are hasty, you have no judgment, you have acted like school children, dont do it again. And so they intimidate them for carrying on all work that they have to do afterwards. I put it to the Prime Minister if, two years and some months ago, a statement like that from a reputable engineer whom the Prime Minister dares not impugn, either as to his character or his ability, if two years ago that statement came to the notice of the government, if two years ago their engineer did not take proper action upon it, and they waited for two years and some months, and yet no proper action has been taken upon it, whose fault is it? It is the government's fault? You were erecting a building with another man's money, you appointed the foreman, the man came and told you that the foreman was not doing his duty, that the workmen were stealing, that they were putting in material below the specifications, and charging high prices for it. You got that information, you did not compel your foreman to investigate it. The first thing a business man would have done would be to bring up his foreman and say: Here, this is what is said of you, is the statement true?-Well, I do not know.- Have you investigated it?-No.-Well, do something. The foreman goes down and asks the men that are putting in bad lumber and charging high prices, is it true that you are doing that? They say, no. Your foreman comes back to you. Have Mr. FOSTER.	'	.
you investigated this?-Yes-How far?- I asked the men whether they were putting in bad stuff and charging high prices, and they said, no.-Quite satisfactory, quite satisfactory. After two long years of spending the other man's money, under the same foreman, under the same contractors and under the same workmen. That is the astoundingly adequate idea that the Prime Minister has of his duties as leader of a government. Why, when you translate it into ordinary business, does not every man see what it means? I charge the Prime Minister to-night with full knowledge of this thing two years ago, and I charge him, the trustee for the people, with having spent since then more than $58,000,000 of the peoples' money, and during all that 24 months he has never seen fit to investigate allegations like that, involving such outrageous, such tremendously costly violations of the spirit and of the letter of the contract.
The Prime Minister then takes the full responsibility of the bullyragging that the commissioners have given the tribunal. He stands at the back of his creatures. Who were they? Take Mr. Woods, take Mr. Chamberlin, take the engineers of the Grand Trunk Pacific, men of experience, knowing their business, and put them against the three men who call themselves the commissioners. Who are the men, who, acting for the government, undertake to whip and lash these independent, scientific members of the tribunal?-a box-maker, a grain dealer and a promoter. These are the high and mighty, the scientific, who, standing for the government, whip men like Mr. Schreiber, Mr. Kelliher and Mr. bums-den, who know more than these men one hundred times over. The government, instead of dismissing these box-makers, grain dealers and promoters, who transgress so abominably against the interest of	the people, comes and apologizes
for them. Well, you may say that to a certain extent, they were his crea-tars. Mr. Parent, Mr. Young and Mr. Reid did yeoman's work-and some of it was not very well thought of, if I have read the history of the last few years correctly -to put him and his party in. Why should not they, as having created him, keep the whip hand of him? But the Prime Minister says, in trying to refute the argument of my hon. friend from South Simcoe, that the cost has been greatly in excess and that is the reason my hon. friend asks for a fuller investigation. I will repay to the Prime Minister and send him back without charge a little of the taffy that he was good enough to give me, and I will say that I think he is too bright to have ever conceived such an idea as that that was the reason given by my hon. friend from South Simcoe for desiring a fuller investigation. It was not, Mr. Speaker, that the
*2621

*cost was greatly over the estimate, but that the reason of this increased cost was because sand was transformed into loose Tock and loose rock was made into solid granite by processes unknown, but to such an extent that millions of dollars were put into the pockets of contractors more than were supposed to go there when the contracts were let upon the information of the government's engineers appointed by themselves. I put it to the Prime Minister, who knows it well enough. It is impossible for mysteries like this to exist in open day; this is not an age of miracles by any manner of means. Once before we had an example of something like this in the devious course of this government's history. I remember that there was a section of country in the Northwest which, at a certain time in a certain month and in a certain year, was arid sands and desert, worth little, sold for a dollar an acre, fifty cents in scrip, and I remember that in less than three years that whole section of country was a garden of Eden selling at from $8 to $15 per acre. That was another example of those mysterious processes of nature which, through the alliance which existed between them and the right hon. gentleman, worked these wonders. The same mysterious alliance, the same occult influences have been kept at work on sundry nights and days along the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific, which was no more a wilderness than the streets of Ottawa, and which suddenly and wonderfully, but most effectively, turned nature into an object of ridicule, smiled defiance and scorn at the slow work of Providence for millions of years, turned loose sand, all at once, . i a jiffy, into cemented rock and turned cemented rock into solid rock by some strange twentieth century processes. That is why my hon. friend from South Simcoe asked for an investigation.
Now, it has been put here a hundred times in this debate but my hon. friends on the other side of the House do not seem to get it in their minds and I will put it to my right hon. friend again. I will ask the right hon. gentleman one question: Why did the government go to the expense of hundreds of thousands of dollars, nay, millions of dollars, in order to have engineers travel the route, have engineers make borings, have engineers dig test pits, have engineers take advantage of every device that was known to their science? They did this in order to do what?-to locate the line and to measure up the kind of soil and rock which were within the limits of that road bed and put the result in the shape of cubic yards. Was that all done for fun? It was all done for one purpose and one purpose only and that was that the government might be able to give an enlightened and reasonable contract for the excavation of the roadbed and not allow
the people's money to go for what it should not. Your engineers, the same that you have got now-minus the best one because that one you have taken care to get rid of, whom your commission followed as a sleuth hound follows a scent and whom they treated in such a way that no man of honour could hold that position for a single moment-^-made these surveys, they took out these quantities, they handed them to the government and upon these the government gave us the cost of the road. I do not need to go over it all again. Suddenly sand grew into rock, rock grew from loose to solid and the expenditures therefore grew and it is because that could only take place through gross incompetence or gross dishonesty, because one or the other is the necesary reason for it, and because of the waste of the people's money thereby that my hon. friend from South Simcoe asks for a full investigation. Oh, says the Prime Minister, it may not be dishonesty or incompetence; it may be that there are physical reasons. What were the enginers foT and what did the engineers do? The engineers were for the purpose of finding just what the physical configuration and physical properties of the road and you could not let a single mile of contract until these men scoured every foot of it, found that out and reported. It was not until they had found out the physical properties and qualities of the whole line that they could give you the amount to be taken out and make that the basis for giving contracts and asking for tenders. The right hon. gentleman, in his quick grasping at a reason to get himself out of that dilemma, never thought that the physical difficulties were the very things that the engineers first had to overcome and find out before a single measurement could be made and before a single contract could be let. After all that was done, then the extra cost arose because there was a displacement of quantities-sand, found out by these engineers of yours and reported by those engineers of yours and upon which you founded the terms of the contract, sand which when the excavations were made and the quantities taken out did not happen to be there. Somebody or something had come down and taken the loose rock and put solid rock in its place. That is the charge; that is the charge that Mr. Lumsden makes; that is the charge that Mr. Wood makes; that is the charge that the Grand Trunk Pacific gives all through the series of complaints. But of all the arguments one of the flimsiest was the attempt of the Prime Minister in this House of Commons in the 20th century, to fortify this gross displacement of quantities and this consequent transfer of millions of money from the peoples pockets to the contractors pockets, to buttress up his position by saying: Oh, it did'nt cost any

too much because some of you people on the other side of the House prophesied that it would cost a great deal more. That needs only to be mentioned for any one to be ashamed of having attempted an argument like that on a serious question. My right hon. friend is asked why he does not grant an investigation and he sees and he knows the weakness of his position and so he is not like Winston Churchill, he has not banged, bolted, and barred the dooi entirely; he says the door is not banged yet and that parliament has it in its power. Parliament has it in its power to-night, but will parliament give an investigation? Sir, we know, and the country is learning to know, that parliament of to-day means Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He does not give it now, and Mr. Parent will have lost his power and his cunning if he allows him to give it at any time. He holds out the hope to us-not to us for it is no hope to us- but he puts the glittering lure before the people: Oh, some time or other when I get good and ready there may be an investigation of these things, but at present: No, no, it would interfere. If there are to be two, the only two we have in sight is the one proposed by the Prime Minister, and the inquiry by the three arbitrators. And it seems to me there is a clear and distinct difference between the two subjects. I have read section 7 very carefully, and what it provides for is in short this: A road is being built which the Grand Trunk Pacific is to take over; the road is being built, not by the Grand Trunk Pacific, but by the government, and specifications are agreed upon between the two as to what should be the character of the road; if a disagreement arises between the govern-Mr. FOSTER.
ment and the Grand Trunk Pacific authorities as to whether any section of the road comes up to or falls below these specifications, the three arbitrators are to arbitrate under section 7. That is one thing. But there is another branch of the subject equally strong and equally imperative, and it is that this government is building a railway in various sections by its own engineers and by contractors who are absolutely subject to these engineers. These contractors put in progress estimates month by month, which on certification by the engineer are paid by the government from time to time, and there is no cause, no right, no power in the Grand Trunk Pacific to interfere between this government and its contractors. The contractors are building the railroad for the government, the payments are made by the government, and they are certified to by the government employees. And, the verv moment it comes out that there have *been displacements in the classification greatly increasing the cost over and above what should have been paid according to the estimates, that very moment it is the duty of the government and of the Minister of Railways to settle that point then and there before the contractors get their pay. The Grand Trunk Pacific had nothing to do with that; that is a matter between the government and its employees and its contractors. But here we have the odd spectacle of a government professing to be strenuous in getting the people's money into the right channels, living for two long years under accusations and documentary evidence that their contractors have been getting more than they ought to, and yet they don't seem to have taken the first step to get these matters straightened out between themselves and their contractors. That is the singular thing about it. Now, it seems to me that that must be done from month to month and from year to year as between the government and its contractors, whatever may be done by arbitrators between the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific looking to the road coming up to the specifications which have been agreed to by both. I asked the right hon. gentleman, as I asked the Minister of Railways, as I asked the member for Carleton, and I do not know that I slighted the member for Pictou; every man on that side who has spoken, tried to get from thege gentlemen, not what this proposed committee is not to examine but what it is to investigate. My first question elicited the illuminating answer given in the last paragraph of the resolution of the Prime Minister. My repeated question elicited no answer that went beyond that, and when I came back to the metropolis and put the question to my right hon. friend as I have done just now I got no

more information that I got at first. The member for Carleton was very explicit. His answer was:	'That this committee
would investigate the matter in this way;' they would say to Mr. Lumsden: 'Have you lost confidence in your staff,' and Mr. Lumsden would say: 'Yes.' The next question would be: 'Mr. Lumsden, have you lost confidence in all your staff,' and Mr. Lumsden would say: 'No.' The next question would be: 'Mr. Lumsden, would you give us the names of those in whom you have lost confidence,' and Mr. Lumsden would give the names. Then the question which would follow, would naturally be: ' Now, Mr. Lumsden, how was it that you lost confidence in these gentlemen,' and Mr. Lumsden would begin to say: ' Because there was displacement of materials in the classification, over-payments, loose rock substituted for sand, solid rock substituted for loose rock and for sand, and these engineers, contrary to my instruction, passed that and therefore I have lost confidence in them.' Well, he would not get out ten words of that sentence before he would be objected to. And why do I say that? I say it, because the Prime Minister has said so; and every speaker on that side of the House has said so. They have said that the whole matter of classification is now before the arbitrators, that it must remain there and that it cannot be investigated elsewhere. Now, I ask. my right hon. friend: How far is he going to get with his investigation? Why have this debate? Why have this committee appointed to waste its time ? My right hon. friend could get all the information he professes to wish from this committee by simply asking Mr. Lumsden :
Mr. Lumsden, you told me in your letter you have lost faith in some of your staff. Will you please tell the names of those persons? Mr. Lumsden will give the names in two minutes. Why have you lost faith? Why, Mr. Premier, I have lost faith in them for the reason I gave in my letter-and the Premier has those Teasons. I have no greater fault to find with the First Minister than this, that when rumours came to his ears that the members of the opposition proposed to probe the reasons for Mr. Lumsden's resignation, and when he felt that there was looming up in parliament a motion and a demand for an investigation, true to his instinct which has led him on other occasions to do the same thing, he thought he would be cute enough if he possibly could to forestall it with this kind of a resolution. The fault I have to find with the Prime Minister is not that he tried to forestall it, but that he has not been honest with the country in his attempt at forestalling it. Mr. Lumsden gave the Prime Minister his reasons in a letter and the Prime Minister selected from that letter two
sentences which excluded the reasons entirely. If the Prime Minister wished to deal honestly and fairly with the people of this country, why did not he put in his resolution the identical reasons that Mr. Lumsden gave him for his resignation? What were those reasons? I will read what they are so it may go on 'Hansard' with this part of the discussion. He says that certain things
Have led me to the conclusion that neither the general specifications nor my instructions regarding classification have been adhered to.
That is strong, but it is not so strong as what follows. What follows is this:
But on the contrary large amounts of material have been returned as solid rock, which should only have been classified as loose rock or common excavation, and material has been returned as loose rock which was or could have been handled by ploughing or scraping, and should have been returned as common excavation.
There is the statement the engineer gives as to the reasons for his lost of confidence. Would it not have been fair to the people of this country, would it not have been more in accordance with the honest treatment both of Mr. Lumsden and the people , of this country, if those reasons of Mr. Lumsden had been quoted as well as the two excerpts from the letter put in by the minister to the exclusion of everything else. Further:
On several residencies there seems to have been no attempt by the engineers to carry out my instructions and measure rock returned, either by showing the same on cross sections, or by measurements of individual pieces, but they simply appear to have guessed at the amount by taking percentages of the total cutting. In some cases where cross sections were prepared showing ledge rock, they prove to be erroneous, resulting in a very much larger amount of the solid rock being returned than actually existed. What is known as overbreak has also been returned in many places where it was caused by excessive use of explosives, and where the material was wasted this should not have been done.
You could not get an engineer to be more explicit with all the faults in the catalogue that can be urged against a resident or supervising engineer or a set of them than the statements made by Mr. Lumsden in that letter. Do the people of the country know anything of these reasons insofar as the motion of my hon. friend is concerned? He purports to give Mr. Lumsden's reasons, he absolutely conceals Mr. Lumsden's reasons, and yet he and his followers and his newspapers will be distributing all over this country the startling and wonderful statement that this government is so honest, so desirous to protect the people, that before a motion is made the Prime Minister comes down and orders a full, free and impartial

investigation. I say that is about the gravest charge that can be made against the Prime Minister; he is not attempting to deal fairly and straightly with the people of the country. He has concealed Mr. Lumsden's reasons and so far as he is concerned in his resolution he has not given Mr. Lumsden's reasons. He avoided giving them. There is not a man on that side, from the Prime Minister down, who has read to the full the reasons given by Mr. Lumsden for his resignation.

I have puzzled my ingenuity to find out what the next question would be. I have imagined it would be this: You have lost confidence in certain men, why did you lose confidence in them? Then we come back to the reasons in that letter. But my right hon. friend says he will not be allowed before this committee to prosecute his reasons and give them to the committee, 'because wrongful classification is the reason why he lost confidence^ as he says and- all matters of classification are already before another tribunal and will not be allowed to be taken up by this tribunal. Then where are we to get? It is a blind, it is an attempt to throw dust into the eyes of this country. It throws no dust into the eyes of the members of the House of Commons on either side, they are all clearsighted as to just what this means. They know, but the country that looks to the Prime Minister as the first commoner in the land, as its leader, is treated in that way, dust is thrown into its eyes and that, I think, is not fair.
My right hon. friend had a little jerk-up [DOT]on me. He said I made a very great mistake when I stated he had said that Mr. Lumsden had not been over a portion of that line himself. The statement my right hon. friend made was that Mr. Lumsden had never been over a foot of the line in his. life. The point I wash to bring out is that Mr. Lumsden, the chosen engineer of standing, of character, of ability, makes his charges on the 25th day of June, 1909, and Mr. Lumsden's charges on the 25th day of June, 1909, are an exact fae simile of the charges made by Mr. Woods in October, 1907, two years ago. With singular unanimity, every man, who has

the interest of the country at heart, every man who has at heart the interest of the Grand Trunk Pacific, which is to a certain extent the interest of the country in keeping down expenditures, every man is a unit, and altogether consistent and persistent in his statement, that this sort of thing is going on. Mr. Lumsden, the government's engineer, states it as his last message to this government, when he resigns. He makes that charge. Not two years ago, nor at any time since, nor now, will this government and the Prime Minister, as its leader, allow the people to see what has become of their money in the face of these great allegations of fraud, misconduct and incompetence.
Now, Sir, I say that the people of this country have that right. We ought to get out of the idea that this is not the people's money that we are dispensing, it is the people's money. Who stands for the people, if we cannot get such an investigation as that? The government's motion does not stand for the people, the government's commission is throwing itself with all its length and all its strength against the people's getting a chance to look into these expenditures from month to month and year to year. They have not only thrown their length against getting at once all the information they can, but they seek to narrow instead of widening the investigation. The government have introduced this motion against the interests of the people. The Grand Trunk Pacific stands for its own interests and not primarily for the interests of the people. There is nobody to-day looking after the interests of the people. The government's motion is looking after the interests of the contractors and of the sub-engineers who disobeyed orders. The Grand Trunk Pacific is looking after it own interest, and when we come and ask the Prime Minister for a chance to let the people see the truth, he refuses. It is 'better for the Prime Minister himself, if anything is wrong, it will redound to the strength of the government and of the Prime Minister, to let the people know it. The people ought to know it. If there is a suspicion of wrong there ought to be an investigation full and free in order that that suspicion may be removed from the administration.
